WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: District heating
======================================================================

{{short description|Centralized heat distribution system}}
[[Image:District heating plant spittelau ssw crop1.png|thumb|right|The Spittelau incineration plant is one of several plants that provide district heating in [[Vienna]], Austria.]]
[[File:District heating.gif|thumb|Animated image showing how district heating works]]
'''District heating''' (also known as '''heat networks''') is a system for distributing heat generated in a centralized location through a system of [[insulated pipe]]s for residential and commercial heating requirements such as [[Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning#Heating|space heating]] and [[water heating]]. The heat is often obtained from a [[cogeneration]] plant burning [[fossil fuels]] or [[biomass]], but [[heating plant|heat-only boiler station]]s, [[geothermal heating]], [[heat pump]]s and [[central solar heating]] are also used, as well as heat waste from factories and [[nuclear power]] electricity generation. District heating plants can provide higher efficiencies and better pollution control than localized boilers. According to some research, district heating with combined heat and power (CHPDH) is the cheapest method of cutting [[carbon emissions]], and has one of the lowest [[carbon footprints]] of all fossil generation plants.<ref name="claverton-energy.com">{{cite web |url=http://www.claverton-energy.com/carbon-footprints-of-various-sources-of-heat-chpdh-comes-out-lowest.html |title=Carbon footprints of various sources of heat – CHPDH comes out lowest |publisher=Claverton Group |access-date=2011-09-25}}</ref>

District heating is ranked number 27 in [[Drawdown (book)|Project Drawdown's]] 100 solutions to [[climate change|global warming]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.burnhamnationwide.com/final-review-blog/-benefits-of-district-energy-systems |title=The Overlooked Benefits of District Energy Systems |last=Haas |first=Arlene |date=April 12, 2018 |website=Burnham Nationwide |language=en |access-date=2019-09-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.drawdown.org/solutions/buildings-and-cities/district-heating |title=District Heating |date=2017-02-07 |website=Drawdown |language=en |access-date=2019-09-28 |archive-date=2019-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502011307/https://www.drawdown.org/solutions/buildings-and-cities/district-heating |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==History==
District heating traces its roots to the hot water-heated baths and greenhouses of ancient times, perhaps today most known in the [[Roman Empire]]. A hot water distribution system in [[Chaudes-Aigues]] in France is generally regarded as the first real district heating system. It used geothermal energy to provide heat for about 30 houses and started operation in the 14th century.<ref name="Mazhar 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Mazhar |first1=Abdul Rehman|display-authors=et al |date=2018 |title=a state of art review on district heating systems |journal=[[Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews]] |volume=96 |pages=420–439 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2018.08.005 |bibcode=2018RSERv..96..420M |s2cid=116827557}}</ref>

The [[U.S. Naval Academy]] in [[Annapolis]] began [[steam]] district heating service in 1853.{{Citation needed|date=February 2023}} [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] began [[coal]]-fired [[steam]] district heating in 1916 when it moved to [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Powering Innovation {{!}} MIT 2016 |url=https://mit2016.mit.edu/campus-cambridge/evolving-frontier/powering-innovation |access-date=2023-02-26 |website=mit2016.mit.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Energy Efficiency {{!}} MIT Sustainability |url=https://sustainability.mit.edu/energy-efficiency |access-date=2023-02-26 |website=sustainability.mit.edu}}</ref>

Although these and numerous other systems have operated over the centuries, the first commercially successful district heating system was launched in [[Lockport, New York]], in 1877 by American hydraulic engineer [[Birdsill Holly]], considered the founder of modern district heating.

=== Generations of district heating ===
[[File:Generations of district heating systems EN.svg|thumb|The four different generations of conventional district heating systems and their energy sources (fifth-generation cold district heating systems not included)]]
Generally, all modern district heating systems are demand driven, meaning that the heat supplier reacts to the demand from the consumers and ensures that there is sufficient temperature and water pressure to deliver the demanded heat to the users. Each generation has a defining feature that sets it apart from the prior generations. The feature of each generation can be used to give an indication of the development status of an existing district heating system.

==== First generation ====
The first generation was a steam-based system fueled by [[coal]] and was first introduced in the US in the 1880s and became popular in some European countries, too. It was state of the art until the 1930s. These systems piped very high-temperature steam through concrete ducts, and were therefore not very efficient, reliable, or safe. Nowadays, this generation is technologically outdated. However, some of these systems are still in use, for example in New York or Paris. Other systems originally built have subsequently been upgraded.<ref name="Lund 2014">{{cite journal |last1=Lund |first1=Henrik|display-authors=et al |date=2014 |title=4th Generation District Heating (4GDH): Integrating smart thermal grids into future sustainable energy systems |journal=[[Energy (journal)|Energy]] |volume=68 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1016/j.energy.2014.02.089 |author1-link=Henrik Lund (academic)}}</ref>

==== Second generation ====
The second generation was developed in the 1930s and was built until the 1970s. It burned coal and oil, and the energy was transmitted through pressurized hot water as the heat carrier. The systems usually had supply temperatures above 100&nbsp;°C, and used water pipes in concrete ducts, mostly assembled on site, and heavy equipment. A main reason for these systems was the primary energy savings, which arose from using combined heat and power plants. While also used in other countries, typical systems of this generation were the Soviet-style district heating systems that were built after World War II in several countries in Eastern Europe.<ref name="Lund 2014" />

==== Third generation ====
In the 1970s the third generation was developed and was subsequently used in most of the following systems all over the world. This generation is also called the "Scandinavian district heating technology" because many of the district heating component manufacturers are based in Scandinavia. The third generation uses prefabricated, pre-insulated pipes, which are directly buried into the ground, and operates with lower temperatures, usually below 100&nbsp;°C. A primary motivation for building these systems was security of supply by improving the [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] after the two oil crises led to disruption of the oil supply. Therefore, those systems usually used coal, biomass and waste as energy sources, in preference to oil. In some systems, [[geothermal energy]] and [[solar energy]] are also used in the energy mix.<ref name="Lund 2014" /> For example, Paris has been using geothermal heating from a 55–70&nbsp;°C source 1–2&nbsp;km below the surface for domestic heating since the 1970s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=18 December 2006 |title=Energy from Beneath the Rocks |url=http://www.bbm.me.uk/portsdown/PH_450_Energy.htm |archive-date=18 December 2006 |access-date=30 July 2022 |website=The Geology of Portsdown Hill |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061218081732/http://www.bbm.me.uk/portsdown/PH_450_Energy.htm}}</ref> Especially in the former [[Eastern Bloc]] [[Nuclear power|nuclear energy]] has been used for district heating<ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/31304794649.pdf |title=Nuclear district heating in CMEA countries |author1=V.L. Losev |author2=M.V. Sigal |author3=G.E. Soldatov |journal=IAEA Bulletin |volume=3 |year=1989 |pages=46–49 |publisher=[[International Atomic Energy Agency]] |access-date=15 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.powermag.com/district-heating-supply-from-nuclear-power-plants/ |title=District Heating Supply from Nuclear Power Plants |first=Ishai |last=Oliker |magazine=POWER |date=1 February 2022 |access-date=15 August 2025 }}</ref> and new systems keep being installed in China.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/China-starts-building-long-distance-nuclear-heatin | title=China starts building long-distance nuclear heating pipeline | newspaper=World Nuclear News | publisher=[[World Nuclear Association]] | date=17 February 2023 | access-date=15 August 2025 }}</ref> The source of the heat of nuclear district heating is virtually always waste heat from power reactors, but proposals to build dedicated heating reactors or to use the waste heat from repurposed [[spent fuel pool]]s<ref>{{cite news |url=https://p.dw.com/p/3rTH2 |title=Nuclear heating: A low-cost, greener option? |first=Lubos |last=Palata |newspaper=[[Deutsche Welle]] |date=7 April 2021 |access-date=15 August 2025}}</ref> have been brought forth.<ref>{{Cite conference |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-99-1023-6_2 |title=Development Prospect and Application of Nuclear District Heating in China |first1=Yifan |last1=Zhang |first2=Wenan |last2=Li |first3=Qian |last3=Yu |editor-first=Chengmin |editor-last=Liu |conference=Proceedings of the 23rd Pacific Basin Nuclear Conference |volume=1 |book-title=Springer Proceedings in Physics, vol. 283 |location=Beijing |publisher=China Nuclear Power Engineering Corporation |pages=8–17 |doi=10.1007/978-981-99-1023-6_2 |isbn=978-981-99-1022-9 |date=12 April 2023 |access-date=15 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite report |url=https://cris.vtt.fi/en/publications/a-review-of-district-heating-reactor-technology |title=A Review of District Heating Reactor Technology |first=Jaakko |last=Leppänen |work=VTT Research Report No. VTT-R-06895-18 |location=Espoo |publisher=[[VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland]] |date=10 January 2019 |access-date=15 August 2025}}</ref>

==== Fourth generation ====
The fourth generation is being developed,<ref name="Lund 2014" /> with the transition to the fourth generation already in process in [[Denmark]].<ref>{{cite web |title=District heating and cooling as part of Danish energy and climate policy |url=https://danskfjernvarme.dk/english/english/climate-policy |website=danskfjernvarme.dk |date=5 May 2025 |quote=400,000 Danish homes that are heated with natural gas. For 30-50 percent of them, the government estimates that district heating will be the best alternative}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Fjernvarmen driver elektrificeringen i Danmark |url=https://danskfjernvarme.dk/aktuelt/nyheder/2025/fjernvarmen-driver-elektrificeringen-i-danmark |website=DanskFjernvarme |language=da |date=11 November 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Xiaochen|display-authors=et al |date=2016 |title=Energy, economy and exergy evaluations of the solutions for supplying domestic hot water from low-temperature district heating in Denmark |url= http://orbit.dtu.dk/ws/files/140685927/Perez_Mora_et_al_2017_International_Journal_of_Energy_Research.pdf |journal=[[Energy Conversion and Management]] |volume=122 |pages=142–152 |doi=10.1016/j.enconman.2016.05.057 |bibcode=2016ECM...122..142Y |s2cid=54185636 }}</ref> The fourth generation is designed to [[climate change mitigation|combat climate change]] and integrate high shares of variable renewable energy into the district heating by providing high flexibility to the electricity system.<ref name="Lund 2014" />

According to the review by Lund et al.<ref name="Lund 2014" /> those systems have to have the following abilities:
# "Ability to supply low-temperature district heating for space heating and domestic hot water (DHW) to existing buildings, energy-renovated existing buildings and new low-energy buildings."
# "Ability to distribute heat in networks with low grid losses."
# "Ability to recycle heat from low-temperature sources and integrate renewable heat sources such as solar and geothermal heat."
# "Ability to be an integrated part of smart energy systems (i.e. integrated smart electricity, gas, fluid and thermal grids) including being an integrated part of 4th Generation District Cooling systems."
# "Ability to ensure suitable planning, cost and motivation structures in relation to the operation as well as to strategic investments related to the transformation into future sustainable energy systems".

Compared to the previous generations the temperature levels have been reduced to increase the energy efficiency of the system, with supply side temperatures of 70&nbsp;°C and lower. Potential heat sources are waste heat from industry, CHP plants burning waste, [[Bioenergy|biomass power plants]], geothermal and solar thermal energy (central solar heating), large scale [[heat pump]]s, waste heat from cooling purposes and [[data center]]s and other sustainable energy sources. With those energy sources and large scale [[thermal energy storage]], including [[seasonal thermal energy storage]], fourth-generation district heating systems are expected to provide flexibility for balancing [[Wind power|wind]] and [[solar power]] generation, for example by using heat pumps to integrate surplus electric power as heat when there is much wind energy or providing electricity from biomass plants when back-up power is needed.<ref name="Lund 2014" /> Therefore, large scale heat pumps are regarded as a key technology for smart energy systems with high shares of [[renewable energy]] up to 100% and advanced fourth-generation district heating systems.<ref name="David">{{cite journal |last1=David |first1=Andrei|display-authors=et al |date=2018 |title=Heat Roadmap Europe: Large-Scale Electric Heat Pumps in District Heating Systems |journal=[[Energies]] |volume=10 |issue= 4|page=578 |doi=10.3390/en10040578 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Lund 2014" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sayegh |first1=M. A.|display-authors=et al |date=2018 |title=Heat pump placement, connection and operational modes in European district heating |url= http://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/15834|journal=Energy and Buildings |volume=166 |pages=122–144 |doi=10.1016/j.enbuild.2018.02.006 |bibcode=2018EneBu.166..122S }}</ref>

==== Fifth generation/cold district heating ====
[[Image:Cold District heating, schematic function.png|thumb|right|Schematic function of a "cold district heating" system]]
{{main|Cold district heating}}
A fifth-generation district heating and cooling network (5GDHC),<ref>{{cite journal|author=S.Buffa|display-authors=et al|title=5th generation district heating and cooling systems: A review of existing cases in Europe|journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews|volume=104|pages=504–522|doi=10.1016/j.rser.2018.12.059|year=2019|doi-access=free|bibcode=2019RSERv.104..504B }}</ref> also called ''cold district heating'', distributes heat at near ambient ground temperature: this in principle minimizes heat losses to the ground and reduces the need for extensive insulation. Each building on the network uses a heat pump in its own plant room to extract heat from the ambient circuit when it needs heat, and uses the same heat pump in reverse to reject heat when it needs cooling. In periods of simultaneous cooling and heating demands this allows waste heat from cooling to be used in heat pumps at those buildings which need heating.<ref>{{cite web|title=Heat Sharing Network |url=https://www.icax.co.uk/Heat_Sharing.html}}</ref> The overall temperature within the ambient circuit is preferably controlled by heat exchange with an aquifer or another low temperature water source to remain within a temperature range from 10&nbsp;°C to 25&nbsp;°C.

While network piping for ambient ground temperature networks is less expensive to install per pipe diameter than in earlier generations, as it does not need the same degree of insulation for the piping circuits, it has to be kept in mind that the lower temperature difference of the pipe network leads to significantly larger pipe diameters than in prior generations. Due to the requirement of each connected building in the fifth-generation district heating and cooling systems to have their own heat pump the system can be used as both a heat source and a heat sink for the heat pump, depending on if it is operated in heating or cooling mode. As with prior generations the pipe network is an infrastructure that in principle provides open access for various low-temperature heat sources, such as ambient heat, ambient water from rivers, lakes, sea, or lagoons, and waste heat from industrial or commercial sources.<ref name="Pellegrini">{{cite journal |last1=Pellegrini |first1=Marco |last2=Bianchini |first2=Augusto |date=2018 |title=The Innovative Concept of Cold District Heating Networks: A Literature Review |journal=[[Energies]] |volume=11 |pages=236pp |doi=10.3390/en11010236 |doi-access=free |hdl=11585/624860 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Based on the above description it is clear that there is a fundamental difference between the 5GDHC and the prior generations of district heating, particularly in the individualization of the heat generation. This critical system has a significant impact when comparing the efficiencies between the different generations, as the individualization of the heat generation moves the comparison from being a simple distribution system efficiency comparison to a supply system efficiency comparison, where both the heat generation efficiency as well as the distribution system efficiency needs to be included.

A modern building with a low-temperature internal heat distribution system can install an efficient heat pump delivering heat output at 45&nbsp;°C. An older building with a higher-temperature internal distribution system, e.g. using radiators, will require a high-temperature heat pump to deliver heat output.

A larger example of a fifth-generation heating and cooling grid is Mijnwater in Heerlen, the Netherlands.<ref name="Mijnwater2013">{{cite conference
| doi = 10.1016/j.egypro.2014.01.158
| title = Minewater 2.0 Project in Heerlen the Netherlands: Transformation of a Geothermal Mine Water Pilot Project into a Full Scale Hybrid Sustainable Energy Infrastructure for Heating and Cooling
| first = R. |last=Verhoeven
| display-authors = et al
| date = 2014
| volume = 46
| publisher = Energy Procedia, 46 (2014)
| book-title = IRES 2013 Conference, Strassbourg
| pages = 58–67
| doi-access = free
}}</ref><ref name="Mijnwater2019">{{cite web |title=Heerlen case study and roadmap |url=https://guidetodistrictheating.eu/heerlen/ |website=Guide to District Heating |date=19 December 2019 |publisher=HeatNet_NWE EU project |access-date=13 August 2020}}</ref> In this case the distinguishing feature is unique access to an abandoned water-filled coal mine within the city boundary that provides a stable heat source for the system.

A fifth-generation network ("Balanced Energy Network", BEN) was installed in 2016 at two large buildings of the London South Bank University as a research and development project.<ref>{{cite web|title=Balanced Energy Network |url=https://www.benuk.net/index.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=About the BEN Project|url=http://www.lsbu.ac.uk/research/centres-groups/sites/ben-project/about|access-date=2019-02-17|archive-date=2019-02-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190218083313/http://www.lsbu.ac.uk/research/centres-groups/sites/ben-project/about|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Heat sources==
District heating networks exploit various energy sources, sometimes indirectly through multipurpose infrastructure such as [[cogeneration|combined heat and power]] plants (CHP, also called co-generation).

===Combustion of fossil or renewable fuels===
{{See also|Hydrogen fuel cell power plant}}

The most used energy source for district heating is the burning of [[hydrocarbons]]. As the supply of renewable fuels is insufficient, the fossil fuels coal and [[natural gas|gas]] are massively used for district heating.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.iea.org/reports/district-heating|title=District Heating – Analysis - IEA|date=November 2021|access-date=2022-05-21|author=Chiara Delmastro}}</ref> This burning of fossil hydrocarbons usually contributes to [[climate change]], as the use of systems to [[carbon capture and storage|capture and store the CO<sub>2</sub>]] instead of releasing it into the atmosphere is rare.

In the case of a cogeneration plant, the heat output is typically sized to meet half of the peak winter heat load, but over the year will provide 90% of the heat supplied. Much of the heat produced in summer will generally be wasted. The boiler capacity will be able to meet the entire heat demand unaided and can cover for breakdowns in the cogeneration plant. It is not economic to size the cogeneration plant alone to be able to meet the full heat load. In the [[New York City steam system]], that is around 2.5&nbsp;GW.<ref>{{cite web| title =Newsroom: Steam|publisher=ConEdison| url =http://www.coned.com/newsroom/energysystems_steam.asp| access-date =2007-07-20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Bevelhymer |first=Carl |title=Steam |publisher=Gotham Gazette |date=2003-11-10 |url=http://www.gothamgazette.com/article/issueoftheweek/20031110/200/674 |access-date=2007-07-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070813013416/http://www.gothamgazette.com/article/issueoftheweek/20031110/200/674 |archive-date=2007-08-13 }}</ref> Germany has the largest amount of CHP in Europe<!--20-30 GW-->.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.cogeneurope.eu/what-is-cogeneration_19.html | title = What is cogeneration? | publisher = COGEN Europe | date = 2015}}</ref>

A simple [[thermal power station]] can be 20–35% efficient,<ref name="energy.gov">{{cite web|url=http://fossil.energy.gov/programs/powersystems/turbines/turbines_howitworks.html |title=DOE – Fossil Energy: How Turbine Power Plants Work |publisher=Fossil.energy.gov |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110812012523/http://fossil.energy.gov/programs/powersystems/turbines/turbines_howitworks.html |archive-date=August 12, 2011 }}</ref> whereas a more advanced facility with the ability to recover waste heat can reach total energy efficiency of nearly 80%.<ref name="energy.gov"/> Some may approach 100% based on the [[lower heating value]] by condensing the flue gas as well.<ref name="Amager Bakke">{{cite web|url=https://stateofgreen.com/en/profiles/ramboll/solutions/waste-to-energy-chp-amager-bakke-copenhagen|title=Waste-to-Energy CHP Amager Bakke Copenhagen|access-date=2015-03-09|archive-date=2016-01-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160110191527/https://stateofgreen.com/en/profiles/ramboll/solutions/waste-to-energy-chp-amager-bakke-copenhagen|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Nuclear fission===
Around 40 nuclear power plants supply district heating, mostly in Russia, China and Eastern Europe.<ref name=power/> The heat produced by [[nuclear chain reaction]]s can be injected into district heating networks. This does not contaminate the district pipes with radioactive elements, as the heat is transferred to the network through [[heat exchanger]]s.<ref>{{cite news | last=Patel| first=Sonal| title =How an AP1000 Plant Is Changing the Nuclear Power Paradigm Through District Heating, Desalination| work=Power Magazine| date =November 1, 2021 | url =https://www.powermag.com/how-an-ap1000-plant-is-changing-the-nuclear-power-paradigm-through-district-heating-desalination/| access-date =November 20, 2021}}</ref> It is not technically necessary for the nuclear reactor to be very close to the district heating network, as heat can be transported over significant distances (exceeding 200&nbsp;km) with affordable losses, using [[insulated pipe]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.ijepes.2012.04.052 |title=Heat recovery from nuclear power plants |year=2012 |last1=Safa |first1=Henry |journal=International Journal of Electrical Power & Energy Systems |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=553–559 |bibcode=2012IJEPE..42..553S }}</ref>{{clarify|reason=insufficient explanation of heat and economy|date=November 2022}}

Since nuclear reactors do not significantly contribute to either [[air pollution]] or [[global warming]], they can be an advantageous alternative to the combustion of fossil hydrocarbons. However, only a small minority of the nuclear reactors currently in operation around the world are connected to a district heating network. These reactors are in Bulgaria, China, Hungary, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Switzerland and Ukraine.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.pnucene.2020.103518|title=Regress in nuclear district heating. The need for rethinking cogeneration |year=2020 |last1=Lipka |first1=Maciej |last2=Rajewski |first2=Adam |journal=Progress in Nuclear Energy |volume=130 |article-number=103518 |bibcode=2020PNuE..13003518L |s2cid=225166290 }}</ref><ref name=power>{{cite web |title=District Heating Supply from Nuclear Power Plants |url=https://www.powermag.com/district-heating-supply-from-nuclear-power-plants/ |website=POWER Magazine |date=1 February 2022}}</ref>

The [[Sibirskaya Nuclear Power Plant]] in [[USSR]] was the first nuclear [[Combined Heat And Power|CHP]] plant, supplying district heating to [[Seversk]] since 1961 and to a part of [[Tomsk]] since 1973, stopped in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Северское краеведение |url=http://lib.seversk.ru/kraeved/page/?doc=1467 |access-date=2025-08-14 |website=lib.seversk.ru}}</ref> The [[Ågesta Nuclear Power Plant]] in Sweden was an early example of nuclear cogeneration, providing small quantities of both heat and electricity to a suburb of the country's capital between 1964 and 1974. The [[Beznau Nuclear Power Plant]] in Switzerland has been generating electricity since 1969 and supplying district heating since 1984. The [[Haiyang Nuclear Power Plant]] in China started operating in 2018 and started supplying small scale heat to the Haiyang city area in 2020. By November 2022, the plant used 345 MW-thermal effect to heat 200,000 homes, replacing 12 coal heating plants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Largest nuclear heating project warms China's first carbon-free city |url=https://www.districtenergy.org/blogs/district-energy/2022/11/21/largest-nuclear-heating-project-warms-chinas-first |website=www.districtenergy.org |language=en |date=21 November 2022}}</ref>

Recent years have seen renewed interest in [[small modular reactors]] (SMRs) and their potential to supply district heating.<ref>{{cite news | title =Finnish firm launches SMR district heating project| work=World Nuclear News| date =February 24, 2020 | url =https://world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/Project-launched-to-develop-Finnish-SMR-for-distri| access-date =November 20, 2021}}</ref> Speaking on the [[Energy Impact Center]] (EIC) podcast ''[[Titans of Nuclear]]'', Christer Dahlgren, principal engineer at [[GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy]], noted that district heating could be the impetus for the construction of new nuclear power plants in the future.<ref>{{cite news | title =Christer Dahlgren| work=Titans of Nuclear| date =August 30, 2019 | url =https://www.titansofnuclear.com/experts/christerdahlgren| access-date =November 20, 2021}}</ref> EIC's own open-source SMR blueprint design, [[OPEN100]], could be incorporated into a district heating system.<ref>{{cite news | last=Proctor| first=Darrell| title =Tech Guru's Plan—Fight Climate Change with Nuclear Power| work=Power Magazine| date =February 25, 2020 | url =https://www.powermag.com/tech-gurus-plan-fight-climate-change-with-nuclear-power/| access-date =November 20, 2021}}</ref>

===Natural underground heat===
{{main|Geothermal heating}}
{{Expand section|date=May 2013}}

'''History'''

Geothermal district heating was used in [[Pompeii]], and in [[Chaudes-Aigues]] since the 14th century.<ref>{{cite conference |first=R. Gordon |last=Bloomquist |title=Geothermal District Energy System Analysis, Design, and Development |publisher=International Geothermal Association |conference=International Summer School |year=2001 |access-date=November 28, 2015 |quote=During Roman times, warm water was circulated through open trenches to provide heating for buildings and baths in Pompeii. |url=http://www.geothermal-energy.org/pdf/IGAstandard/ISS/2001Romania/bloomquist_dh.pdf |page=213(1) }}
*{{cite web |title=Geothermal District Energy System Analysis, Design, and Development |type=Abstract |website=Stanford University |url=https://pangea.stanford.edu/ERE/db/IGAstandard/record_detail.php?id=5313}}</ref>

'''Denmark'''

Denmark has one geothermal plant in operation in Thisted since 1984. Two other plants are now closed, located in Copenhagen (2005–2019), and Sønderborg (2013–2018). Both suffered issues with fine sand and blockages.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-04-19 |title=Geotermianlæg i drift |url=https://ens.dk/ansvarsomraader/geotermi/geotermianlaeg-i-drift |access-date=2024-05-02 |website=Energistyrelsen |language=da}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Hovedstadsområdets fjernvarmeselskaber dropper udvikling af geotermi |url=https://ing.dk/artikel/hovedstadsomraadets-fjernvarmeselskaber-dropper-udvikling-geotermi-226196 |last1=Madsen |first1=Jacob Lund |website=[[Ingeniøren]] |language=da |date=2019-05-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Det blev aldrig en succes: Nu nedlægger Sønderborg Varme geotermianlæg til 187 mio. kroner {{!}} jv.dk |url=https://jv.dk/soenderborg/det-blev-aldrig-en-succes-nu-nedlaegger-soenderborg-varme-geotermianlaeg-til-187-mio-kroner |website=jv.dk |language=da |date=2024-01-11}}</ref>

The country's first large-scale plant started in [[Skejby]] in [[Aarhus]] in 2025,<ref name=skejby>{{cite web |title=Aarhus-projektet dokumenterer, at geotermi virker |url=https://danskfjernvarme.dk/aktuelt/nyheder/2025/aarhus-projektet-dokumenterer-at-geotermi-virker |website=DanskFjernvarme |language=da |date=29 December 2025}}</ref> and by the end of 2030, it is expected to be able to cover approximately 20% of the district heating demand in Aarhus.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New rules pave the way for large-scale geothermal plant in Denmark |url=https://stateofgreen.com/en/news/new-rules-pave-the-way-for-large-scale-geothermal-plant-in-denmark/ |access-date=2024-05-02 |website=State of Green |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Iceland'''
{{main|Geothermal power in Iceland}};&nbsp;{{slink|District heating#National variation}}
Most of Iceland's population is heated by geothermal heat.

'''United States'''

Direct-use geothermal district heating systems, which tap geothermal reservoirs and distribute the hot water to multiple buildings for a variety of uses, have existed for over a century in the US but are uncommon.

In 1890, the first wells were drilled to access a hot water resource outside of Boise, Idaho. In 1892, after routing the water to homes and businesses in the area via a wooden pipeline, the first geothermal district heating system was created.

As of a 2007 study,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thorsteinsson |first1=Hildigunnur |title=U.S. Geothermal District Heating: Barriers and Enablers |url=http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/42932/251518357.pdf |access-date=25 July 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140809070925/http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/42932/251518357.pdf |archive-date=9 August 2014}}</ref> there were 22 geothermal district heating systems (GDHS) in the United States. As of 2010, two of those systems have shut down.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lund |first1=John |title=The United States of America Country Update 2010 |url=https://pangea.stanford.edu/ERE/pdf/IGAstandard/SGW/2010/lund.pdf |access-date=25 July 2014}}</ref> The table below describes the 20 GDHS currently{{when|date=August 2023}} operational in the US.

===Solar heat===
[[File:Marstal.powerplant.1.jpg|thumb| Central solar heating plant at [[Marstal]], Denmark. It covers more than half of Marstal's heat consumption.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Solar unterstützte Kraft-Würme-Kopplung mit saisonalem Wärmespeicher | date = 2013 | last1 = Pauschinger | first1 = Thomas | last2 = Schmidt | first2 = Thomas | journal = Euroheat & Power | issn = 0949-166X| volume = 42 | issue = 5 | pages = 38–41 | url = https://doczz.com.br/doc/780778/solar-unterst%C3%BCtzte-kraft-w%C3%A4rme-kopplung-mit-saisonalem}}</ref>]]
{{main|Central solar heating}}

Use of solar heat for district heating has been increasing in Denmark and Germany<ref>Schmidt T., Mangold D. (2013). [http://www.solar-district-heating.eu/LinkClick.aspx?fileticket=4VeN0WSc5Pk%3d&portalid=0 Large-scale thermal energy storage – Status quo and perspectives] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161018073544/http://solar-district-heating.eu/LinkClick.aspx?fileticket=4VeN0WSc5Pk%3d&portalid=0 |date=2016-10-18 }}. First international SDH Conference, Malmö, SE, 9–10th April 2013. Powerpoint.</ref> in recent years.<ref name=ing2015-10-23>{{cite web |url=http://ing.dk/artikel/fjernvarmevaerker-skifter-naturgassen-ud-med-sol-179659 |title=Fjernvarmeværker går fra naturgas til sol |first1=Sanne |last1=Wittrup |work=[[Ingeniøren]] |date=23 October 2015 |access-date=1 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160110191527/http://ing.dk/artikel/fjernvarmevaerker-skifter-naturgassen-ud-med-sol-179659 |archive-date=10 January 2016 }}</ref> The systems usually include inter[[seasonal thermal energy storage]] for a consistent heat output day to day and between summer and winter. Good examples are in [[Vojens]]<ref name=ing2015-06-14>{{cite web |url=http://ing.dk/artikel/verdens-stoerste-damvarmelager-indviet-i-vojens-176776 |title=Verdens største damvarmelager indviet i Vojens |first1=Sanne |last1=Wittrup |work=[[Ingeniøren]] |date=14 June 2015 |access-date=2015-11-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151019125824/http://ing.dk/artikel/verdens-stoerste-damvarmelager-indviet-i-vojens-176776 |archive-date=2015-10-19 }}</ref> at 50&nbsp;MW, [[Dronninglund]] at 27&nbsp;MW and Marstal at 13&nbsp;MW in Denmark.<ref>Holm L. European Sustainable Energy Week, Brussels. 18–22 June 2012. Powerpoint.</ref><ref>[http://www.solvarmedata.dk/index.asp?secid=228 Current data on Danish solar heat plants] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161223205042/http://www.solvarmedata.dk/index.asp?secid=228 |date=2016-12-23 }} (click Vojens in South-West Denmark, then "About the plant")</ref> These systems have been incrementally expanded to supply 10% to 40% of their villages' annual space heating needs. The solar-thermal panels are ground-mounted in fields.<ref>Dalenbäck, J-O (2012). [http://www.euroheat.org/Admin/Public/DWSDownload.aspx?File=%2fFiles%2fFiler%2fPresentations%2f20120618-22_EUSEW%2f120619_EUSEW_2+-+Pres-ZeroCity-Brussels-SDH-JOD-19june2012.pdf Large-Scale Solar Heating: State of the Art]{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. In Alberta, Canada the [[Drake Landing Solar Community]] has achieved a world record 97% annual solar fraction for heating needs, using solar-thermal panels on the garage roofs and thermal storage in a borehole cluster.<ref>Wong B., Thornton J. (2013). [http://www.geo-exchange.ca/en/UserAttachments/flex1304_5-%20SAIC-%20Bill%20Wong%202013%20-%20Integrating%20Solar%20and%20Heat%20Pumps.pdf Integrating Solar & Heat Pumps] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610063730/http://www.geo-exchange.ca/en/UserAttachments/flex1304_5-%20SAIC-%20Bill%20Wong%202013%20-%20Integrating%20Solar%20and%20Heat%20Pumps.pdf |date=2016-06-10 }}. Renewable Heat Workshop. (Powerpoint)</ref><ref>Natural Resources Canada, 2012. [http://www.nrcan.gc.ca/media-room/news-release/2012/6586 Canadian Solar Community Sets New World Record for Energy Efficiency and Innovation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130430221347/http://www.nrcan.gc.ca/media-room/news-release/2012/6586 |date=2013-04-30 }}. 5 Oct. 2012.</ref>

===Low-temperature natural or waste heat===
In Stockholm, the first heat pump was installed in 1977 to deliver district heating sourced from IBM servers. Today the installed capacity is about 660&nbsp;MW heat, using treated sewage water, sea water, district cooling, data centers and grocery stores as heat sources.<ref name="sciencedirect.com">{{cite journal | title = CHP and heat pumps to balance renewable power production: Lessons from the district heating network in Stockholm | journal = Energy | volume = 137 | pages = 670–678 | year =2017 | doi=10.1016/j.energy.2017.01.118 | author1 =Levihn, Fabian| bibcode = 2017Ene...137..670L }}</ref><ref name="bryant-2025">{{cite news | last1 = Bryant | first1 = Miranda | title = 'The heat you need at a reasonable price': how district heating can speed the switch to clean energy | date = 28 March 2025 | work = The Guardian | location = London, United Kingdom | issn = 0261-3077 | url = https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/mar/28/the-heat-you-need-at-a-reasonable-price-how-district-heating-can-speed-the-switch-to-clean-energy | access-date = 2025-03-29}}</ref> Another example is the [[Drammen Heat Pump|Drammen Fjernvarme District Heating project]] in Norway which produces 14&nbsp;MW from water at just 8&nbsp;°C, industrial heat pumps are demonstrated heat sources for district heating networks. Among the ways that industrial heat pumps can be used are:

# As the primary base load source where water from a low grade source of heat, e.g. a river, fjord, [[data center]], power station outfall, sewage treatment works outfall (all typically between 0&nbsp;˚C and 25&nbsp;˚C), is boosted up to the network temperature of typically 60&nbsp;˚C to 90&nbsp;˚C using heat pumps. These devices, although consuming electricity, will transfer a heat output three to six times larger than the amount of electricity consumed. An example of a district system using a heat pump to source heat from raw sewage is in Oslo, Norway that has a heat output of 18&nbsp;MW(thermal).<ref>Pedersen, S. & Stene, J. (2006). [http://www.heatpumpcentre.org/en/newsletter/previous/Documents/HPC-news_4_2006.htm 18 MW heat pump system in Norway utilises untreated sewage as heat source] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304034334/http://www.heatpumpcentre.org/en/newsletter/previous/Documents/HPC-news_4_2006.htm |date=2016-03-04 }}. IEA Heat Pump Centre Newsletter, 24:4, 37–38.</ref>
# As a means of recovering heat from the cooling loop of a power plant to increase either the level of flue gas heat recovery (as the district heating plant return pipe is now cooled by the heat pump) or by cooling the closed steam loop and artificially lowering the condensing pressure and thereby increasing the electricity generation efficiency.
# As a means of cooling flue gas scrubbing working fluid (typically water) from 60&nbsp;˚C post-injection to 20&nbsp;˚C pre-injection temperatures. Heat is recovered using a heat pump and can be sold and injected into the network side of the facility at a much higher temperature (e.g. about 80&nbsp;˚C).
# Where the network has reached capacity, large individual load users can be decoupled from the hot feed pipe, say 80&nbsp;˚C and coupled to the return pipe, at e.g. 40&nbsp;˚C. By adding a heat pump locally to this user, the 40&nbsp;˚C pipe is cooled further (the heat being delivered into the heat pump evaporator). The output from the heat pump is then a dedicated loop for the user at 40&nbsp;˚C to 70&nbsp;˚C. Therefore, the overall network capacity has changed as the total temperature difference of the loop has varied from 80 to 40&nbsp;˚C to 80&nbsp;˚C–x (x being a value lower than 40&nbsp;˚C).

Concerns have existed about the use of [[hydrofluorocarbon]]s as the working fluid (refrigerant) for large heat pumps. Whilst leakage is not usually measured, it is generally reported to be relatively low, such as 1% (compared to 25% for supermarket cooling systems). A 30-megawatt heatpump could therefore leak (annually) around 75&nbsp;kg of R134a or other working fluid.<ref name=":0" />

However, recent technical advances allow the use of natural heat pump refrigerants that have very low [[global warming potential]] (GWP). CO<sub>2</sub> refrigerant (R744, GWP=1) or ammonia (R717, GWP=0) also have the benefit, depending on operating conditions, of resulting in higher heat pump efficiency than conventional refrigerants. An example is a 14&nbsp;MW(thermal) district heating network in [[Drammen]], Norway, which is supplied by seawater-source heatpumps that use R717 refrigerant, and has been operating since 2011. 90&nbsp;°C water is delivered to the district loop (and returns at 65&nbsp;°C). Heat is extracted from seawater (from {{convert|60|ft|m|adj=on}} depth) that is 8 to 9&nbsp;°C all year round, giving an average [[coefficient of performance]] (COP) of about 3.15. In the process the seawater is chilled to 4&nbsp;°C; however, this resource is not used. In a district system where the chilled water could be used for air conditioning, the effective COP would be considerably higher.<ref name=":0">Hoffman, & Pearson, D. 2011. [http://www.ammonia21.com/web/assets/link/Hoffman7thApril2011London%20colour.pdf Ammonia heat pumps for district heating in Norway 7 – a case study] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203054940/http://www.ammonia21.com/web/assets/link/Hoffman7thApril2011London%20colour.pdf |date=2013-12-03 }}. Presented at Institute of Refrigeration, 7 April, London.</ref>

In the future, industrial heat pumps will be further de-carbonised by using, on one side, excess renewable electrical energy (otherwise spilled due to meeting of grid demand) from wind, solar, etc. and, on the other side, by making more of renewable heat sources (lake and ocean heat, geothermal, etc.). Furthermore, higher efficiency can be expected through operation on the high voltage network.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://setis.ec.europa.eu/system/files/JRCDistrictheatingandcooling.pdf |title=Combined Heat and Power and District Heating report. Joint Research Centre, Petten, under contract to European Commission, DG Energy 2013 |access-date=2013-12-02 |archive-date=2021-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428043116/http://setis.ec.europa.eu/system/files/JRCDistrictheatingandcooling.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Heat accumulators and storage==
[[File:Fernwärmespeicher Theiss.jpg|thumb|right|District heating accumulation tower from Theiss near [[Krems an der Donau]] in [[Lower Austria]] with a thermal capacity of {{convert|2|GW.h|TJ}}]]
Increasingly large [[Thermal energy storage|heat stores]] are being used with district heating networks to maximise efficiency and financial returns. This allows cogeneration units to be run at times of maximum electrical tariff, the electrical production having much higher rates of return than heat production, whilst storing the excess heat production. It also allows solar heat to be collected in summer and redistributed off season in very large but relatively low-cost in-ground insulated reservoirs or borehole systems. The expected heat loss at the 203,000m³ insulated pond in [[Vojens]] is about 8%.<ref name=ing2015-06-14/>

With European countries such as Germany and Denmark moving to very high levels (80% and 100% respectively by 2050) of renewable energy for all energy uses there will be increasing periods of excess production of renewable electrical energy. Heat pumps can take advantage of this surplus of cheap electricity to store heat for later use.<ref name=dafj2 /><ref>DYRELUND Anders, Ramboll, 2010. [http://www.ramboll.com/~/media/Files/RGR/Documents/Documents/Heat-Plan-Denmark-2010-final.ashx Heat Plan Denmark 2010]</ref> Such coupling of the electricity sector with the heating sector ([[Power-to-X]]) is regarded as a key factor for energy systems with high shares of renewable energy.<ref name="Lund 2017">{{cite journal |last1=Lund |first1=Henrik|display-authors=et al |date=2017 |title=Smart energy and smart energy systems |journal=[[Energy (journal)|Energy]] |volume=137 |pages=556–565 |doi=10.1016/j.energy.2017.05.123 |bibcode=2017Ene...137..556L |author1-link=Henrik Lund (academic)}}</ref>

==Heat distribution==
[[File:Heatpipe tunnel copenhagen 2009.jpg|thumb|Tunnel for heat pipes between [[Rigshospitalet]] and {{ill|Amagerværket|da}} in Denmark]]
[[File:Pre-installation insulated underground pipes for district heating.jpg|thumb|Insulated pipes to connect a new building to [[University of Warwick]]'s campus-wide combined heat and power system]]
[[File:2005-08-30-district-heating-pipeline.jpg|upright|thumb|District heating pipe in [[Tübingen]], Germany]]
[[File:Waerme Schulung CRC Wn 040.jpg|thumb|upright|[[District heating substation]] with a thermal power of 700&nbsp;kW which insulates the water circuit of the district heating system and the customer's central heating system]]
[[File:Fernwäremeübergabestation mit Warmwasser-Standspeicher.jpg|thumb|upright|Compact indoor unit of a single-family home with 20 kW heating power]]
After generation, the heat is distributed to the customer via a network of insulated pipes. District heating systems consist of feed and return lines. Usually the pipes are installed underground but there are also systems with overground pipes. The DH system's start-up and shut downs, as well as fluctuations on heat demand and ambient temperature, induce thermal and mechanical cycling on the pipes due to the thermal expansion. The axial expansion of the pipes is partially counteracted by frictional forces acting between the ground and the casing, with the [[shear stress]]es transferred through the PU foam bond. Therefore, the use of pre-[[insulated pipes]] has simplified the laying methods, employing cold laying instead of expansion facilities like compensators or U-bends, being so more cost effective.<ref>Christensen. Fatigue analysis of district heating systems. Netherlands Agency for Energy and the Environment 1999</ref> Pre-insulated pipes sandwich assembly composed of a steel heat service pipe, an insulating layer ([[polyurethane]] foam) and a [[polyethylene]] (PE) casing, which are bonded by the insulating material.<ref>EN 253:2019. District heating pipes. Bonded single pipe systems for directly buried hot water networks. Factory made pipe assembly of steel service pipe, polyurethane thermal insulation and a casing of polyethylene.</ref> While polyurethane has outstanding mechanical and thermal properties, the high toxicity of the [[diisocyanates]] required for its manufacturing has caused a restriction on their use.<ref>Commission Regulation (EU) 2020/1149 of 3 August 2020 amending Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) as regards diisocyanates: (EU) 2020/1149. In: Official Journal of the European Union; 2020.</ref> This has triggered research on alternative insulating foam fitting the application,<ref>{{cite thesis | last=Doyle | first=Lucía | title=A Circular Economy Approach to Multifunctional Sandwich Structures: Polymeric Foams for District Heating Pre-Insulated Pipes | year=2022 | publisher=HafenCity Universität Hamburg | doi=10.34712/142.35 | url=https://repos.hcu-hamburg.de/handle/hcu/833 | access-date=2023-01-23}}</ref> which include polyethylene terephthalate (PET)<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Doyle | first1=Lucía | last2=Weidlich | first2=Ingo | title=Sustainable insulation for sustainable DHC | journal=Energy Reports | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=7 | year=2021 | issn=2352-4847 | doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2021.08.161 | pages=150–157| s2cid=240180109 | doi-access=free | bibcode=2021EnRep...7..150D }}</ref> and polybutylene (PB-1).<ref>{{cite journal | last=Doyle | first=Lucía | title=Extrusion foaming behavior of polybutene-1. Toward single-material multifunctional sandwich structures | journal=Journal of Applied Polymer Science | publisher=Wiley | volume=139 | issue=12 | year=2021 | issn=0021-8995 | doi=10.1002/app.51816 | article-number=51816| s2cid=240464626 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Within the system heat storage units may be installed to even out peak load demands.

The common medium used for heat distribution is water or [[superheated water]], but steam is also used. The advantage of steam is that in addition to heating purposes it can be used in [[industrial processes]] due to its higher temperature. The disadvantage of steam is a higher heat loss due to the high temperature. Also, the [[thermal efficiency]] of cogeneration plants is significantly lower if the cooling medium is high-temperature steam, reducing [[electric power]] generation. Heat transfer oils are generally not used for district heating, although they have higher heat capacities than water, as they are expensive and have environmental issues.

At customer level the heat network is usually connected to the [[central heating]] system of the dwellings via [[heat exchanger]]s (heat substations): the working fluids of both networks (generally water or steam) do not mix. However, direct connection is used in the [[Odense]] system.{{cn|date=June 2026}}

Typical annual loss of thermal energy through distribution is around 10%, as seen in Norway's district heating network.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nve.no/global/energi/analyser/energi%20i%20norge%20folder/energy%20in%20norway%202009%20edition.pdf |title=Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110928144652/http://www.nve.no/global/energi/analyser/energi%20i%20norge%20folder/energy%20in%20norway%202009%20edition.pdf |archive-date=2011-09-28 }}</ref>


==Heat metering==
{{Main|Heat meter}}

The amount of heat provided to customers is often recorded with a [[heat meter]] to encourage conservation and maximize the number of customers which can be served, but such meters are expensive. Due to the expense of heat metering, an alternative approach is simply to meter the water – water meters are much cheaper than heat meters, and have the advantage of encouraging consumers to extract as much heat as possible, leading to a very low return temperature, which increases the efficiency of power generation.{{Citation needed|date = February 2016}}

Many systems were installed under a [[Socialism|socialist]] economy (such as in the former [[Eastern Bloc]]) which lacked heat metering and means to adjust the heat delivery to each apartment.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/02254fda-4966-11e4-8d68-00144feab7de|title=EU warms to the potential efficiencies of district heating|last=Oliver|first=Christian|date=October 22, 2014|work=Financial Times|access-date=2018-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|year=2011|institution=Mikkeli University of Applied Sciences|url=https://www.theseus.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/25777/DISTRICT_HEATING_SYSTEMS_IN_FINLAND_AND_RUSSIA.pdf|title=District Heating Systems in Finland and Russia|author=Kirill Eliseev}}</ref> This led to great inefficiencies – users had to simply open windows when too hot – wasting energy and reducing the numbers of connectable customers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2015/apr/13/warsaw-district-heating-system-poland-capital-cleaner-krakow|title=How Warsaw's district heating system keeps the capital cleaner than Kraków|last=Warsaw|first=Beth Gardiner in|date=2015-04-13|website=The Guardian|language=en|access-date=2018-10-07}}</ref>

==Size of systems==
District heating systems can vary in size. Some systems cover entire cities such as [[Stockholm]] or [[Flensburg]], using a network of large 1000&nbsp;mm diameter primary pipes linked to secondary pipes – e.g. 200&nbsp;mm diameter, which in turn link to tertiary pipes that might be of 25&nbsp;mm diameter which might connect to 10 to 50 houses.

Some district heating schemes might only be sized to meet the needs of a small village or area of a city in which case only the secondary and tertiary pipes will be needed.

Some schemes may be designed to serve only a limited number of dwellings, of about 20 to 50 houses, in which case only tertiary sized pipes are needed.

==Pros and cons==
District heating has various advantages compared to individual heating systems. Usually district heating is more energy efficient, due to simultaneous production of heat and electricity in combined heat and power generation plants. This has the added benefit of reducing [[greenhouse gas emissions]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Dunne|first=Eimear|title=Infographic explaining District Heating Systems|url=http://frontlineenergy.ie/district-energy-infographic/|work=Frontline Energy & Environmental|access-date=5 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140505123952/http://frontlineenergy.ie/district-energy-infographic/|archive-date=5 May 2014}}</ref> The larger combustion units also have a more advanced [[flue gas]] cleaning than single boiler systems. In the case of surplus heat from industries, district heating systems do not use additional fuel because they recover heat which would otherwise be dispersed to the environment.

District heating requires a long-term financial commitment that fits poorly with a focus on short-term returns on investment. Benefits to the community include avoided costs of energy through the use of surplus and wasted heat energy, and reduced investment in individual household or building heating equipment. District heating networks, heat-only boiler stations, and cogeneration plants require high initial capital expenditure and financing. Only if considered as long-term investments will these translate into profitable operations for the owners of district heating systems, or combined heat and power plant operators. District heating is less attractive for areas with low population densities, as the investment per household is considerably higher. Also it is less attractive in areas of many small buildings; e.g. detached houses than in areas with a fewer larger buildings; e.g. blocks of flats, because each connection to a single-family house is quite expensive.

==Ownership, monopoly issues and charging structures==
In many cases large combined heat and power district heating schemes are owned by a single entity. This was typically the case in the old Eastern bloc countries. However, for many schemes, the ownership of the cogeneration plant is separate from the heat using part.

Examples are Warsaw which has such split ownership with PGNiG Termika owning the cogeneration unit, the Veolia owning 85% of the heat distribution, the rest of the heat distribution is owned by municipality and workers. Similarly all the large CHP/CH schemes in Denmark are of split ownership.{{citation needed|date = March 2019}}

Sweden provides an alternative example where the heating market is deregulated. In Sweden it is most common that the ownership of the district heating network is not separated from the ownership of the cogeneration plants, the district cooling network or the centralized heat pumps. There are also examples where the competition has spawned parallel networks and interconnected networks where multiple utilities cooperate.{{citation needed|date = March 2019}}

In the United Kingdom there have been complaints that district heating companies have too much of a monopoly and are insufficiently regulated,<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-39736010 Green heating system accused of causing 'fuel poverty'] ''[[BBC]]''</ref> an issue the industry is aware of, and has taken steps to improve consumer experience through the use of customer charters as set out by the Heat Trust. Some customers are taking legal action against the supplier for misrepresentation and unfair trading, claiming district heating is not delivering the savings promised by many heat suppliers.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-39736010|title=Green scheme 'causing fuel poverty'|first1=Nicola|last1=Dowling|first2=Adrian|last2=Goldberg|date=30 April 2017|access-date=18 March 2018|work=BBC News}}</ref>

==National variation==
Since conditions from city to city differ, every district heating system is unique. In addition, nations have different access to primary energy carriers and so they have a different approach on how to address heating markets within their borders.

===Europe===
Since 1954, district heating has been promoted in Europe by Euroheat & Power. They have compiled an analysis of district heating and cooling markets in Europe within their [[Ecoheatcool]] project supported by the [[European Commission]]. A separate study, entitled Heat Roadmap Europe, has indicated that district heating can reduce the price of energy in the European Union between now and 2050.<ref>{{cite book|url=http://vbn.aau.dk/en/publications/heat-roadmap-europe-2050(306a5052-a882-4af9-a5da-87efa36efeaa).html|title=Heat Roadmap Europe 2: Second Pre-Study for the EU27|first1=David|last1=Connolly|first2=Brian Vad|last2=Mathiesen|first3=Poul Alberg|last3=Østergaard|first4=Bernd|last4=Möller|first5=Steffen|last5=Nielsen|first6=Henrik|last6=Lund|first7=Urban|last7=Persson|first8=Sven|last8=Werner|first9=Jan|last9=Grözinger|first10=Thomas|last10=Boermans|first11=Michelle|last11=Bosquet|first12=Daniel|last12=Trier|date=27 May 2013|publisher=Department of Development and Planning, Aalborg University|access-date=18 March 2018|via=vbn.aau.dk|isbn=9788791404481}}</ref> The legal framework in the member states of the [[European Union]] is currently influenced by the EU's [[CHP Directive]].

===Cogeneration in Europe===
The EU has actively incorporated cogeneration into its energy policy via the CHP Directive. In September 2008 at a hearing of the European Parliament's Urban Lodgment Intergroup, Energy Commissioner Andris Piebalgs is quoted as saying, "security of supply really starts with energy efficiency."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cogeneurope.eu/Downloadables/Publications/230908_Energy_Efficiency_Industrial_Forum_Security_of_Supply.pdf |title=Energy Efficiency Industrial Forum Position Paper: energy efficiency – a vital component of energy security }}{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Energy efficiency and cogeneration are recognized in the opening paragraphs of the European Union's Cogeneration Directive 2004/08/EC. This directive intends to support cogeneration and establish a method for calculating cogeneration abilities per country. The development of cogeneration has been very uneven over the years and has been dominated throughout the last decades by national circumstances.

As a whole, the European Union currently generates 11% of its electricity using cogeneration, saving Europe an estimated 35 Mtoe per annum.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cogeneurope.eu/news.htm |title=COGEN Europe News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090101121334/http://www.cogeneurope.eu/news.htm |archive-date=2009-01-01 }}</ref> However, there are large differences between the member states, with energy savings ranging from 2% to 60%. Europe has the three countries with the world's most intensive cogeneration economies: Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cogeneurope.eu/Downloadables/Publications/Cogeneration_Europe_Draft_paper_on_Security_of_Supply_in_EU_energy_policy.pdf |title=COGEN Europe: Cogeneration in the European Union's Energy Supply Security |date=16 October 2017 }}{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Other European countries are also making great efforts to increase their efficiency. Germany reports that over 50% of the country's total electricity demand could be provided through cogeneration. Germany set a target to double its electricity cogeneration from 12.5% of the country's electricity to 25% by 2020 and has passed supporting legislation accordingly in "Federal Ministry of Economics and Technology", (BMWi), Germany, August 2007. The UK is also actively supporting district heating. In the light of UK's goal to achieve an 80% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions by 2050, the government had set a target to source at least 15% of government electricity from CHP by 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/environment/climatechange/uk/energy/chp/index.htm |title=DEFRA Action in the UK – Combined Heat and Power |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612100647/http://www.defra.gov.uk/environment/climatechange/uk/energy/chp/index.htm |archive-date=2010-06-12 }}</ref> Other UK measures to encourage CHP growth are financial incentives, grant support, a greater regulatory framework, and government leadership and partnership.

According to the IEA 2008 modelling of cogeneration expansion for the G8 countries, expansion of cogeneration in France, Germany, Italy and the UK alone would effectively double the existing primary fuel savings by 2030. This would increase Europe's savings from today's 155&nbsp;TWh to 465&nbsp;TWh in 2030. It would also result in a 16% to 29% increase in each country's total cogenerated electricity by 2030.

Governments are being assisted in their CHP endeavors by organizations like [[COGEN Europe]] who serve as an information hub for the most recent updates within Europe's energy policy. COGEN is Europe's umbrella organization representing the interests of the cogeneration industry, users of the technology and promoting its benefits in the EU and the wider Europe. The association is backed by the key players in the industry including gas and electricity companies, ESCOs, equipment suppliers, consultancies, national promotion organisations, financial and other service companies.

A 2016 EU energy strategy suggests increased use of district heating.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/regdoc/rep/1/2016/EN/1-2016-51-EN-F1-1.PDF|title = Register of Commission Documents}}</ref>

====Austria====
[[File:Biomassekraftwerk mit Lager.jpg|thumb|right|The District Heating Power Plant Steyr is a renewable combined heat and power plant in which wood chips are used to generate power.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fernwaermesteyr.at/waerme_steyr/page/790213410858496064_790686873558106026~790686753835892434_790686753835892434,de.html|title=Bioenergie Steyr|first=Fernwärme|last=Steyr|website=www.fernwaermesteyr.at|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180318183603/http://www.fernwaermesteyr.at/waerme_steyr/page/790213410858496064_790686873558106026~790686753835892434_790686753835892434,de.html|archive-date=18 March 2018|df=dmy-all}}</ref>]]
[[File:Fernheizwerk Mödling von NordWest.jpg|thumb|Biomass fired district heating power plant in [[Mödling]], Austria]]
The largest district heating system in Austria is in [[Vienna]] (Fernwärme Wien) – with many smaller systems distributed over the whole country.

District heating in Vienna is run by Wien Energie. In the business year of 2004/2005 a total of 5,163&nbsp;GWh was sold, 1,602&nbsp;GWh to 251,224 private apartments and houses and 3,561&nbsp;GWh to 5211 major customers. The three large municipal waste [[incineration|incinerators]] provide 22% of the total in producing 116&nbsp;GWh electric power and 1,220&nbsp;GWh heat. Waste heat from municipal power plants and large industrial plants account for 72% of the total. The remaining 6% is produced by peak heating boilers from fossil fuel. A biomass-fired power plant has produced heat since 2006.

In the rest of Austria the newer district heating plants are constructed as biomass plants or as CHP-biomass plants like the [[w:de:Biomasseheizkraftwerk Mödling|biomass district heating of Mödling]] or the [[w:de:Biomasseheizkraftwerk Baden|biomass district heating of Baden]].

Most of the older fossil-fired district heating systems have a [[w:de:Fernwärmespeicher|district heating accumulator]], so that it is possible to produce the thermal district heating power only at that time where the electric power price is high.

==== Belgium ====
Belgium has district heating in multiple cities. The largest system is in the Flemish city [[Ghent]], the piping network of this power plant is 22&nbsp;km long. The system dates back to 1958.<ref>{{cite web|date=2016-11-03|title=Stadsverwarming in Gent voorziet 110 Luminus-klanten via warmtenet|url=https://lumiworld.luminus.be/up-to-date/stadsverwarming-in-gent-voorziet-luminusklanten-via-warmtenet/|access-date=2020-06-16|website=Lumiworld|language=nl-NL}}</ref>

====Bulgaria====
Bulgaria has district heating in around a dozen towns and cities. The largest system is in the capital [[Sofia]], where there are four power plants (two CHPs and two [[Heating plant|boiler station]]s) providing heat to the majority of the city. The system dates back to 1949.<ref>{{cite web |title=Основни етапи в развитието на Топлофикация София EАД |url=http://www.toplo.bg/za_nas/istoria |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120119073404/http://www.toplo.bg/za_nas/istoria |archive-date=19 January 2012 |access-date=15 January 2022 |website=www.toplo.bg}}</ref>

====Czech Republic====
The largest district heating system in the [[Czech Republic]] is in Prague owned and operated by Pražská teplárenská, serving 265,000 households and selling c. 13 PJ of heat annually. Most of the heat is actually produced as [[waste heat]] in 30&nbsp;km distant [[thermal power station]] in [[Mělník]]. There are many smaller central heating systems spread around the country<ref name=tscr>{{cite web|url=http://www.tscr.cz|title=Teplárenské sdružení ČR – sdružuje teplárny a podnikatele v teplárenství a energetice|first=Teplárenské sdružení České republiky -|last=www.tscr.cz|website=www.tscr.cz|access-date=18 March 2018}}</ref> including waste heat usage, [[municipal solid waste]] [[incineration]] and {{ill|heat plants|de|Heizkraftwerk}}.

====Denmark====
In Denmark district heating covers more than 64% of [[space heater|space heating]] and [[water heating]], mostly by imported biomass,<ref name=danskfjernvarme_stats /> but increasingly by low-price electricity using large heat pumps, large water heaters and heat storage.<ref name=dafj2>{{cite web |title=Danskernes fjernvarme produceres på el |url=https://danskfjernvarme.dk/aktuelt/nyheder/2025/danskernes-fjernvarme-produceres-paa-el |website=DanskFjernvarme |language=da |date=21 October 2025 |quote=power consumption 2.35 TWh in 2024 .. record number of hours with low or negative power price}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Fjernvarmen driver elektrificeringen i Danmark |url=https://danskfjernvarme.dk/aktuelt/nyheder/2025/fjernvarmen-driver-elektrificeringen-i-danmark |website=DanskFjernvarme |language=da |date=11 November 2025 |quote=35 TWh national power consumption}}</ref> In 2007, 80.5% of district heat was produced by [[combined heat and power]] plants. Cities such as Aalborg utilise a wide range of sources for waste heat reuse, including cement plants and even [[crematoria]].<ref>{{cite news | last1 = Coe | first1 = Joshua | title = How cremations are helping to heat homes in Denmark | date = 25 March 2026 | work = The World | location = Boston, USA| url = https://theworld.org/stories/2026/03/25/how-cremations-are-helping-to-heat-homes-in-denmark | access-date = 2026-03-25}}</ref> Heat recovered from waste incineration accounted for 20.4% of the total Danish district heat production.<ref>[https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20110310035158/http://www.ens.dk/graphics/UK_Facts_Figures/Statistics/yearly_statistics/2007/energy%20statistics%202007%20uk.pdf Danish Energy Statistics 2007] by the Danish Ministry of Energy (in Danish).</ref> In 2013, Denmark imported 158,000 ton waste for incineration.<ref>[http://www.danskfjernvarme.dk/nyheder/presseklip/151127klimaraad-affaldsimport-vil-belaste-dansk-co2regnskab Klimaråd: Affaldsimport vil belaste dansk CO<sub>2</sub>-regnskab] {{Webarchive|url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151128144041/http://www.danskfjernvarme.dk/nyheder/presseklip/151127klimaraad-affaldsimport-vil-belaste-dansk-co2regnskab |date=2015-11-28 }} 27 November 2015.</ref> Most major cities in Denmark have big district heating networks, including transmission networks operating with up to 125&nbsp;°C and 25 bar pressure and distribution networks operating with up to 95&nbsp;°C and between 6 and 10 bar pressure. The largest district heating system in Denmark is in the [[Copenhagen]] area operated by CTR I/S and VEKS I/S. In central Copenhagen, the CTR network serves 275,000 households (90–95% of the area's population) through a network of 54&nbsp;km double district heating distribution pipes providing a peak capacity of 663&nbsp;MW,<ref>[http://www.ctr.dk/images/publikationer/3folder2006.pdf Environmentally Friendly District Heating to Greater Copenhagen] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071129121423/http://www.ctr.dk/images/publikationer/3folder2006.pdf |date=November 29, 2007 }}, publication by [http://www.ctr.dk CTR I/S] (2006)</ref> some of which is combined with [[district cooling]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Gratis energi leverer både varme og køl i Tårnby |url=https://www.energy-supply.dk/article/view/674505/gratis_energi_leverer_bade_varme_og_kol_i_tarnby |website=Energy Supply DK |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191214022758/https://www.energy-supply.dk/article/view/674505/gratis_energi_leverer_bade_varme_og_kol_i_tarnby |archive-date=14 December 2019 |date=19 September 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> The consumer price of heat from CTR is approximately €49 per&nbsp;MWh plus taxes (2009).<ref>[http://www.ke.dk/portal/page/portal/Privat/Varme/Prisen_paa_fjernvarme?page=221 Prisen på Fjernvarme] {{webarchive|url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110719131304/http://www.ke.dk/portal/page/portal/Privat/Varme/Prisen_paa_fjernvarme?page=221 |date=July 19, 2011 }}, price list from the Danish homepage of a Copenhagen district heating provider [http://www.ke.dk Københavns Energi] {{webarchive|url= https://web.archive.org/web/20040611164451/http://www.ke.dk/ |date=June 11, 2004 }}</ref> Several towns have [[central solar heating]] with various types of thermal energy storage.

The Danish island of [[Samsø]] has three straw-fueled plants producing district heating.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dac.dk/en/dac-cities/sustainable-cities/all-cases/energy/samsoe-a-role-model-in-self-sufficiency/ |title=Network – DAC|website=dac.dk|access-date=18 March 2018}}</ref>

====Finland====
In Finland district heating accounts for about 50% of the total heating market,<ref>[http://www.energia.fi/en/districtheating/districtheating District heating in Finland] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722000506/http://www.energia.fi/en/districtheating/districtheating |date=July 22, 2011 }}</ref> 80% of which is produced by combined heat and power plants. Over 90% of apartment blocks, more than half of all terraced houses, and the bulk of public buildings and business premises are connected to a district heating network. [[Natural gas]] is mostly used in the south-east gas pipeline network, imported coal is used in areas close to ports, and [[peat]] is used in northern areas where peat is a local resource. Renewables, such as wood chips and other paper industry combustible by-products, are also used, as is the energy recovered by the incineration of [[municipal solid waste]]. Industrial units which generate heat as an industrial by-product may sell otherwise waste heat to the network rather than release it into the environment. Excess heat and power from [[pulp mill]] [[recovery boiler]]s is a significant source in mill towns. In some towns waste incineration can contribute as much as 8% of the district heating heat requirement. [[Availability]] is 99.98% and disruptions, when they do occur, usually reduce temperatures by only a few degrees.

In Helsinki, an underground [[datacenter]] next to the President's palace releases excess heat into neighboring homes,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=data-center-under-helsinki-to-warm-2010-03 |title=In Helsinki |publisher=Scientificamerican.com |access-date=2011-09-25}}</ref> producing enough heat to heat approximately 500 large houses.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.cnet.com/8301-11128_3-10405955-54.html |title=Underground data center to help heat Helsinki &#124; Green Tech – CNET News |publisher=News.cnet.com |date=2009-11-29 |access-date=2011-09-25}}</ref> A quarter of a million households around [[Espoo]] are scheduled to receive district heating from datacenters.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fortum and Microsoft announce world's largest collaboration to heat homes, services and businesses with sustainable waste heat from new data centre region |url=https://www.fortum.com/media/2022/03/fortum-and-microsoft-announce-worlds-largest-collaboration-heat-homes-services-and-businesses-sustainable-waste-heat-new-data-centre-region |website=Fortum |language=en |date=17 March 2022}}</ref>

====Germany====
In Germany district heating has a market share of around 14% in the residential buildings sector. The connected heat load is around 52,729&nbsp;MW. The heat comes mainly from cogeneration plants (83%). Heat-only boilers supply 16% and 1% is surplus heat from industry. The cogeneration plants use natural gas (42%), coal (39%), lignite (12%) and waste/others (7%) as fuel.<ref>[http://www.agfw.de/typo3conf/ext/naw_securedl/secure.php?u=0&file=fileadmin/dokumente/wir/Branchenreport_2006/ab2006gesamt_web.pdf&t=1187259422&hash=767cafb4adad1f785f119a86e2ea82c4 AGFW Branchenreport 2006] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927222112/http://www.agfw.de/typo3conf/ext/naw_securedl/secure.php?u=0&file=fileadmin%2Fdokumente%2Fwir%2FBranchenreport_2006%2Fab2006gesamt_web.pdf&t=1187259422&hash=767cafb4adad1f785f119a86e2ea82c4 |date=September 27, 2007 }}, by the German Heat and Power Association [http://www.agfw.de -AGFW-] (in German).</ref>

The largest district heating network is located in Berlin whereas the highest diffusion of district heating occurs in [[Flensburg]] with around 90% market share. In [[Munich]] about 70% of the electricity produced comes from district heating plants.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.swm.de/english/company/energy-generation/combined-heat-power.html|title=Combined heat and power|website=www.swm.de|access-date=18 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319004000/https://www.swm.de/english/company/energy-generation/combined-heat-power.html|archive-date=19 March 2018}}</ref>

District heating has rather little legal framework in Germany. There is no law on it as most elements of district heating are regulated in governmental or regional orders. There is no governmental support for district heating networks but a law to support cogeneration plants. As in the European Union the CHP Directive will come effective, this law probably needs some adjustment.

====Greece====
Greece has district heating mainly in the province of [[Western Macedonia]], Central Macedonia and the [[Peloponnese (region)|Peloponnese Province]]. The largest system is the city of [[Ptolemaida]], where there are five power plants (thermal power stations or TPS in particular) providing heat to the majority of the largest towns and cities of the area and some villages. The first small installation took place in Ptolemaida in 1960, offering heating to [[Proastio, Kozani|Proastio]] village of [[Eordaea]] using the TPS of Ptolemaida. Today District heating installations are also available in [[Kozani]], Ptolemaida, [[Amyntaio]], [[Philotas]], Serres and [[Megalopolis, Greece|Megalopolis]] using nearby power plants. In Serres the power plant is a Hi-Efficiency CHP Plant using natural gas, while coal is the primary fuel for all other district heating networks.

====Hungary====
According to the 2011 census there were 607,578 dwellings (15.5% of all) in Hungary with district heating, mostly [[Panelház|panel flats]] in urban areas.<ref>[http://www.ksh.hu/nepszamlalas/tablak_lakas Hungarian census 2011] table 1.2.10 (Hungarian)</ref> The largest district heating system located in [[Budapest]], the municipality-owned ''Főtáv Zrt.'' ("Metropolitan Teleheating Company") provides heat and piped hot water for 238,000 households and 7,000 companies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fotav.hu/fotav-zrt/cegunkrol/|title=Cégünkről|website=FŐTÁV – Budapesti Távhőszolgáltató Zrt.|access-date=18 March 2018}}</ref>

====Iceland====
[[Image:Borehole.jpg|upright|right|thumb|Geothermal borehole outside the Reykjavik Power Station.]]
{{main|Geothermal power in Iceland}}

93% of all housing in Iceland enjoy district heating services&nbsp;– 89.6% from [[geothermal energy]], Iceland is the country with the highest penetration of district heating.<ref>{{cite web |last=Iceland Energy Authority |title=Energy Statistics in Iceland 2020 |url=https://orkustofnun.is/gogn/os-onnur-rit/Orkutolur-2020-enska.pdf}}</ref> There are 117 local district heating systems supplying towns as well as rural areas with hot water&nbsp;– reaching almost all of the population. The average price is around US$0.027 per kWh of hot water.<ref>{{cite web |last=Iceland Energy Authority |first=Orkustofnun Data Repository OS-2021-T012-01 |date=2021 |title=Proportion of energy source in space heating based on heated space in Iceland 1952-2020 |url=https://orkustofnun.is/gogn/Talnaefni/OS-2021-T012-01.pdf}}</ref>

The [[Capital Region (Iceland)|Reykjavík Capital Area]] district heating system serves around 230,000 residents had a maximum thermal power output of 830 MW. In 2018, the average annual heating demand in the Reykjavik area was 473MW.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Reykjavík district heating I Projects I www.verkis.com |url=https://www.verkis.com/projects/utilities/district-heating-systems/nr/974 |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=www.verkis.com |language=en}}</ref> It is the largest district heating system in Iceland and is operated by [[Orkuveita Reykjavíkur|Veitur]]. Heat is supplied from the Hellisheiði (200MWth) and Nesjavellir (300MWth) CHP plants, as well as a few lower temperature fields inside Reykjavik. Heating demand has increased steadily as the population has grown, necessitating enlargement of thermal water production in the Hellisheiði CHP plant.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gretar Ívarsson |date=April 2019 |title=Hitaveita í Reykjavík – Vatnsvinnsla 2018 |url=https://eu-assets.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt5bf0023ca96cf071/bltbf89141dc99c4d9e/63a45186de61af37ca1576a9/hitaveita_i_reykjavik_-_vatnsvinnsla_2018.pdf}}</ref>

Iceland's second largest district heating system is on the [[Reykjanes peninsula]], with the [[Svartsengi power station|Svartsengi CHP plant]] providing heating to 21,000 homes including [[Keflavík|Keflavik]] and [[Grindavík|Grindavik]], with a thermal power output of 150 MW.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mannvit.com/GeothermalEnergy/DistrictHeating/DistrictHeatinginIceland/ |title=History of District Heating in Iceland |publisher=Mannvit.com |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007194242/http://www.mannvit.com/GeothermalEnergy/DistrictHeating/DistrictHeatinginIceland/ |archive-date=2011-10-07 }}</ref>

====Ireland====
