The [[Dublin Waste-to-Energy Facility]] will provide district heating for up to 50,000 homes in [[Poolbeg]] and surrounding areas.<ref>{{cite journal|title=An 'under the hood' look at Dublin's First 'waste-to-energy' plant|url=https://seanduke.com/2016/08/09/an-under-the-hood-look-at-dublins-first-waste-to-energy-plant/|journal=Science Spinning|author=Sean Duke|date=August 9, 2016|access-date=April 24, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170425025704/https://seanduke.com/2016/08/09/an-under-the-hood-look-at-dublins-first-waste-to-energy-plant/|archive-date=April 25, 2017}}</ref> Some existing residential developments in the [[Dublin Docklands|North Docklands]] have been constructed for conversion to district heating&nbsp;– currently using on-site gas boilers&nbsp;– and pipes are in place in the [[Liffey Service Tunnel]] to connect these to the incinerator or other waste heat sources in the area.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.dublincity.ie/ddhs |title = Dublin District Heating System &#124; Dublin City Council| date=28 June 2018 }}</ref>

[[Tralee]], County Kerry has a 1&nbsp;MW district heating system providing heat to an apartment complex, sheltered housing for the elderly, a library and over 100 individual houses. The system is fuelled by locally produced wood chip.<ref>{{cite web |date=2013 |title=Covenant of Mayors, Sustainable Energy Action Plan, 2012 - 2020 |url=http://www.kerrycoco.ie/en/allservices/environment/energy/thefile,8007,en.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506200928/http://www.kerrycoco.ie/en/allservices/environment/energy/thefile,8007,en.pdf |archive-date=2014-05-06 |access-date=2014-05-06 |website=Comhairle Contae Chiarraí / Kerry County Council}}</ref>

In [[Glenstal Abbey]], County Limerick there exists a pond-based 150&nbsp;kW heating system for a school.<ref>{{cite web |date=2012 |title=Geothermal Glenstal |url=http://www.glenstal.org/monastery/grounds/geothermal-glenstal/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120717101814/http://www.glenstal.org/monastery/grounds/geothermal-glenstal/ |archive-date=2012-07-17 |access-date=2012-07-02 |website=Glenstal Abbey Benedictine Community}}</ref>

A scheme to use waste heat from an [[Amazon Web Services]] datacentre in [[Tallaght]] is intended to heat 1200 units and municipal buildings<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.irishtimes.com/business/energy-and-resources/dublin-has-sufficient-waste-heat-to-meet-its-needs-forum-hears-1.3858743 | title=Dublin has sufficient waste heat to meet its needs, forum hears| newspaper=[[The Irish Times]]}}</ref>

====Italy====
[[File:Power plant at sunset.jpg|thumb|A cogeneration thermal power plant in [[Ferrera Erbognone]] ([[Province of Pavia|PV]]), Italy]]
In Italy, district heating is used in some cities ([[Bergamo]], [[Brescia]], [[Cremona]], [[Bolzano]], [[Verona]], [[Ferrara]], [[Imola]], [[Modena]],<ref>[https://www.gruppohera.it/clienti/casa/casa_teleriscaldamento/casa_teleriscaldamento_qualita_comm/32169.html Hera – Teleriscaldamento]</ref> [[Reggio Emilia]], [[Terlan]], [[Turin]], [[Parma]], [[Lodi, Lombardy|Lodi]], and now [[Milan]]). The district heating of Turin is the biggest of the country and it supplies 550.000 people (62% of the whole city population).

====Latvia====
In Latvia, district heating is used in major cities such as [[Riga]], [[Daugavpils]], [[Liepāja]], [[Jelgava]]. The first district heating system was constructed in Riga in 1952.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rs.lv/en/content/history |title=History of District Heating in Riga }}</ref> Each major city has a local company responsible for the generation, administration, and maintenance of the district heating system.

====Netherlands====
District heating is used in [[Rotterdam]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dLoFc26geBUC&q=district+heating+rotterdam&pg=PT102|title=Sustainable Development in the Process Industries: Cases and Impact|last1=Harmsen|first1=J.|last2=Powell|first2=Joseph B.|date=2011-11-30|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9781118209806|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G700CwAAQBAJ&q=district+heating+rotterdam&pg=PT61|title=Sustainable Urban Energy Policy: Heat and the city|last1=Hawkey|first1=David|last2=Webb|first2=Janette|last3=Lovell|first3=Heather|last4=McCrone|first4=David|last5=Tingey|first5=Margaret|last6=Winskel|first6=Mark|date=2015-12-14|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781317577065|language=en}}</ref> [[Amsterdam]], [[Utrecht]],<ref>{{cite web|last=Municipality of Utrecht|date=2021-12-23|title=Utrecht Energy Policy|url=https://omgevingsvisie.utrecht.nl/thematisch-beleid/energie/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918195351/https://omgevingsvisie.utrecht.nl/thematisch-beleid/energie/ |archive-date=2020-09-18 }}</ref> and [[Almere]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thermaflex.com/en/case-studies/almere-district-heating-network|title=Almere District Heating Network: Case Studies |website=Thermaflex|language=en|access-date=2019-10-14}}</ref> with more expected as the government has mandated a transition away from natural gas for all homes in the country by 2050.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.duurzaambedrijfsleven.nl/energie/30093/warmtenetten-amsterdam |date=5 Oct 2018 |title=Amsterdam stimuleert ontwikkeling duurzame warmtenetten |language=nl}}</ref>
The town of Heerlen has developed a grid using water in disused coalmines as a source and storage for heat and cold. This is a good example of a 5th generation heating and cooling grid<ref name=Mijnwater2013 /><ref name=Mijnwater2019 />

====North Macedonia====
District heating is only available in Skopje. Balkan Energy Group (BEG) operates three DH production plants, which cover majority of the network, and supply heat to around 60,000 households in Skopje, more than 80 buildings in the educational sector (schools and kindergartens) and more than 1,000 other consumers (mostly commercial).<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=District Energy in North Macedonia |url=https://www.euroheat.org/knowledge-hub/country-profiles/district-energy-north-macedonia/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001205620/https://www.euroheat.org/knowledge-hub/country-profiles/district-energy-north-macedonia/ |archive-date=2021-10-01 |access-date=2022-07-25 |website=Euroheat & Power}}</ref> The three BEG production plants use natural gas as a fuel source.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Energy and Water Services Regulatory Commission of the Republic of North Macedonia, Annual Report, 2018 |url=https://rise.esmap.org/data/files/library/north-macedonia/Energy%20Efficiency/North%20Macedonia_Energy%20and%20Water%20Services%20Regulatory%20Commission%20Annual%20Report%202018.pdf |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=RISE, Regulatory Indicators for Sustainable Energy |page=60}}</ref> There is also one cogeneration plant TE-TO AD Skopje producing heat delivered to the Skopje district heating system. The share of cogeneration in DH production was 47% in 2017. The distribution and supply of district heating is carried out by companies owned by BEG.<ref name=":2" />

====Norway====
In Norway district heating only constitutes approximately 2% of energy needs for heating. This is a very low number compared to similar countries. One of the main reasons district heating has a low penetration in Norway is access to cheap hydro-based electricity, and 80% of private electricity consumption goes to heat rooms and water. However, there is district heating in the major cities.

====Poland====
[[File:Wieluń CieplowniaMiejska3.jpg|thumb|upright|Coal heating plant in [[Wieluń]], Poland]]
In 2009, 40% of Polish households used district heating, most of them in urban areas.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stat.gov.pl/cps/rde/xbcr/gus/SE_zuzycie_energii_gosp_dom_2009.pdf|title=Zużycie energii w gospodarstwach domowych w 2009 r.|trans-title=Energy consumption in households in 2009|language=pl|date=2012-05-28|publisher=Główny Urząd Statystyczny|access-date=2013-01-25}}</ref> Heat is provided primarily by combined heat and power plants, most of which burn hard coal. The largest district heating system is in Warsaw, owned and operated by Veolia Warszawa, distributing approx. 34 PJ annually.

====Romania====
The largest district heating system in [[Romania]] is in [[Bucharest]]. Owned and operated by RADET, it distributes approximately 24 PJ annually, serving 570 000 households. This corresponds to 68% of Bucharest's total domestic heat requirements (RADET fulfills another 4% through single-building boiler systems, for a total of 72%).

====Russia====
[[File:C0253-GAST.jpg|thumbnail|right|The cancelled Russian {{ill|Gorky Nuclear Heating Plant|ru|Горьковская АСТ}} in [[Fedyakovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast]], Russia]]
In most Russian cities, district-level combined heat and power plants ({{lang|ru|ТЭЦ, теплоэлектроцентраль}}) produce more than 50% of the nation's electricity and simultaneously provide hot water for neighbouring city blocks. They mostly use coal- and [[Fuel gas|gas]]-powered [[steam turbine]]s for cogeneration of heat. Now, [[Combined cycle power plant|combined cycle gas turbine]]s designs are beginning to be widely used as well.

====Serbia====
In [[Serbia]], district heating is used throughout the main cities, particularly in the capital, [[Belgrade]]. The first district heating plant was built in 1961 as a means to provide effective heating to the newly built suburbs of [[New Belgrade|Novi Beograd]]. Since then, numerous plants have been built to heat the ever-growing city. They use natural gas as fuel, because it has less of an effect on the environment. The district heating system of Belgrade possesses 112 heat sources of 2,454&nbsp;MW capacity, over 500&nbsp;km of pipeline, and 4,365 connection stations, providing district heating to 240,000 apartments and 7,500 office/commercial buildings of total floor area exceeding 17,000,000 square meters.{{Citation needed|date = February 2016}}

====Slovenia====
[[File:TE Šoštanj (Šoštanj Power Plant in 2023).jpg|thumb|Slovenia - Šoštanj Power Plant - Cogeneration]]
The first district heating network in Slovenia and Yugoslavia began to be implemented on November 29, 1959, from the newly built network fed from the [[Velenje]] Thermal Power Plant for the needs of the new city center of Velenje. In Slovenia, coverage with district heating systems is 22%, or only 47 out of 210 municipalities have district heating systems. The largest coverage with the district heating system and the lowest price is in Velenje, where all city facilities are connected, so there are no local or individual fireplaces. The prices of MWh of district heat in Slovenia in 2010 ranged between EUR 25 and EUR 93. The largest district heating systems in Slovenia are in Velenje - Šalek Valley and [[Ljubljana]]. The total Slovenian installed production and distribution thermal power of all heating systems amounts to 1.7 GW.

====Slovakia====
Slovakia's centralised heating system covers more than 54% of the overall demand for heat. In 2015 approximately 1.8 million citizens, 35% of the total population of Slovakia, were served by district heating.<ref name="euroheat.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.euroheat.org/knowledge-hub/district-energy-slovakia/|title = District Energy in Slovakia|date = May 2017}}</ref> The infrastructure was built mainly during the 1960s and 1980s. In recent years large investments were made to increase the share of renewable energy sources and energy efficiency in district heating systems.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Energy Policies of IEA Countries. Slovak Republic 2018 Review |url=https://www.connaissancedesenergies.org/sites/default/files/pdf-actualites/energy_policies_of_iea_countries_slovak_republic_2018_review.pdf |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=[[International Energy Agency]] |page=144}}</ref>

The heat production comes mostly from natural gas and biomass sources, and 54% of the heat in district heating is generated through cogeneration.<ref name="euroheat.org"/>
The distribution system consists of 2800&nbsp;km of pipes. Warm and hot water are the most common heat carriers, but older high-pressure steam transport still accounts for around one-quarter of the primary distribution, which results in more losses in the system.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Energy Policies of IEA Countries. Slovak Republic 2018 Review |url=https://www.connaissancedesenergies.org/sites/default/files/pdf-actualites/energy_policies_of_iea_countries_slovak_republic_2018_review.pdf |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=[[International Energy Agency]] |page=138}}</ref>

In terms of the market structure, there were 338 heat suppliers licensed to produce and/or distribute heat in 2016, of which 87% were both producers and distributors. Most are small companies that operate in a single municipality, but some large companies such as Veolia are also present in the market. The state owns and operates large co-generation plants that produce district heat and electricity in six cities (Bratislava, Košice, Žilina, Trnava, Zvolen and Martin). Multiple companies can operate in one city, which is the case in larger cities. A large share of DH is produced by small natural gas heat boilers connected to blocks of buildings. In 2014, nearly 40% of the total DH generation was from natural gas boilers, other than co-generation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Energy Policies of IEA Countries. Slovak Republic 2018 Review |url=https://www.connaissancedesenergies.org/sites/default/files/pdf-actualites/energy_policies_of_iea_countries_slovak_republic_2018_review.pdf |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=[[International Energy Agency]] |page=137}}</ref>

====Sweden====
Sweden has a long tradition for using district heating (fjärrvärme) in urban areas. In 2015, about 60% of Sweden's houses (private and commercial) were heated by district heating, according to the Swedish association of district heating.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Statistik och pris - Svenske Fjärrvärme |url=http://www.svenskfjarrvarme.se/Statistik--Pris/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120418005915/http://www.svenskfjarrvarme.se/Statistik--Pris/ |archive-date=2012-04-18 |access-date=2022-07-26 |website=Energiföretagen}}</ref>
The city of [[Växjö]] reduced its {{CO2}} emissions from fossil fuels by 34% from 1993 to 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SESAC Site Växjö |url=https://smart-cities-marketplace.ec.europa.eu/projects-and-sites/projects/sesac/sesac-site-vaxjo |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=Smart Cities Marketplace}}</ref> This was to achieved largely by way of biomass fired district heating.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Växjö local energy |url=https://wwf.panda.org/wwf_news/?204516/Vxj-local-energy |access-date=2022-07-30 |website=[[World Wildlife Fund]] |language=en}}</ref> Another example is the plant of [[Enköping]], combining the use of short rotation plantations both for fuel as well as for phytoremediation.<ref>{{cite journal
 | title =Pulling effects of district heating plants on the adoption and spread of willow plantations for biomass: The power plant In Enköping (Sweden)
 | journal =Biomass and Bioenergy
 | volume =35
 | issue =7
 | pages =2986–2992
 | year =2011
 | doi =10.1016/j.biombioe.2011.03.040
 | author1=Mola-Yudego, B |author2=Pelkonen, P. | bibcode =2011BmBe...35.2986M
 }}</ref>

In 2024, 46% of the heat generated in Swedish district heating systems was produced with renewable [[bioenergy]] sources, as well as 22% in [[waste-to-energy]] plants, 7% was provided by heat pumps, 11% by [[flue-gas condensation]] and 8% by industrial [[waste heat recovery unit|waste heat recovery]]. 3% was generated from grid electricity. The remaining was produced by fossil fuels (2%) and [[peat]] (0.3%)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Miljövärdering av fjärrvärme - Energiföretagen Sverige |url=https://www.energiforetagen.se/statistik/fjarrvarmestatistik/miljovardering-av-fjarrvarme/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250630192154/https://www.energiforetagen.se/statistik/fjarrvarmestatistik/miljovardering-av-fjarrvarme/ |archive-date=2025-06-30 |access-date=2025-06-30 |website=Energiföretagen |language=sv}}</ref>

Because of the law banning traditional [[landfill]]s,<ref>{{cite journal |author=J.Wawrzynczyk |author2=M. Recktenwald |author3=O. Norrlöw |author4=E. Szwajcer Dey |title=The role of cation-binding agents and enzymes in solubilisation of sludge |journal=Water Research |date=March 2008 |volume=42 |issue=6, 7 |pages=1555–1562|url=http://www.bvsde.paho.org/bvsaar/cdlodos/pdf/theroleofcation519.pdf |access-date=16 April 2013 |doi=10.1016/j.watres.2007.11.004 |pmid=18054984 }}</ref> waste is commonly used as a fuel.

==== Ukraine ====
{{Expand section|date=February 2026}}
{{As of|2026}} district heating is mainly gas-fired and inefficient - there is a national strategy to improve it.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-01 |title=Reforming the district heating sector of Ukraine (ReWarm) {{!}} GIZ |url=https://www.giz.de/en/projects/reforming-district-heating-sector-ukraine-rewarm |access-date=2026-02-28 |website=www.giz.de |language=en}}</ref> Gas heats water which is circulated.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heinrichs |first=Pauline Sophie |date=2026-01-23 |title=Russian knowledge of Soviet-era energy systems has helped it to target Ukraine's heating and homes |url=http://theconversation.com/russian-knowledge-of-soviet-era-energy-systems-has-helped-it-to-target-ukraines-heating-and-homes-274052 |access-date=2026-02-28 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref> There is district heating in [[Kyiv]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Holmes |first=Oliver |last2=Swan |first2=Lucy |last3=Symons |first3=Harvey |last4=Watson |first4=Chris |last5=Clarke |first5=Seán |date=2026-02-14 |title=How a Soviet-era heating system exposes Ukraine to Russian attack – a visual guide |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/14/soviet-era-heating-system-ukraine-russia-visual-guide |access-date=2026-02-14 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The district heating is vulnerable to winter [[Russian strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure|Russian strikes]] which cause [[Ukrainian energy crisis|energy crises]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-24 |title=How Soviet urban planning is helping Russia freeze Ukraine |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c338jpk8r1vo |access-date=2026-02-28 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref>

====United Kingdom====
[[File:Pimlico accumulator tower 1.jpg|thumb|right|District heating accumulator tower and workshops on the [[Churchill Gardens]] Estate, [[Pimlico]], London. This plant once used waste heat piped from [[Battersea Power Station]] on the other side of the [[River Thames]]. (January 2006)]]
In the United Kingdom, district heating became popular after World War II, but on a restricted scale, to heat the large residential estates that replaced dwellings destroyed by the [[The Blitz|Blitz]]. In 2013 there were 1,765 district heating schemes, with 920 based in London alone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Summary evidence on District Heating Networks in the UK|url= https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/212565/summary_evidence_district_heating_networks_uk.pdf |publisher=DECC}}</ref> In total around 210,000 homes and 1,700 businesses are supplied by heat networks in the UK.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Future of Heating: Meeting the Challenge|url= https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/190149/16_04-DECC-The_Future_of_Heating_Accessible-10.pdf |publisher=DECC}}</ref>

The [[Pimlico District Heating Undertaking]] (PDHU) in London first became operational in 1950 and continues to expand to this day. The PDHU once relied on waste heat from the now-disused [[Battersea Power Station]] on the south side of the [[River Thames]]. It is still in operation; the water is now heated locally by a new energy centre which incorporates 3.1&nbsp;[[MWe]] / 4.0&nbsp;[[MWth]] of gas fired CHP engines and 3 × 8&nbsp;MW gas-fired boilers.

One of the United Kingdom's largest district heating schemes is EnviroEnergy in [[Nottingham]]. The plant, initially built by [[Boots (company)|Boots]], is now used to heat 4,600 homes, and a wide variety of business premises, including the [[Nottingham Royal Concert Hall|Concert Hall]], the [[Motorpoint Arena Nottingham|Nottingham Arena]], the Victoria Baths, the [[Broadmarsh|Broadmarsh Shopping Centre]], the [[Victoria Centre]], and others. The heat source is a [[waste-to-energy]] incinerator.

[[Sheffield]]'s district heating network was established in 1988 and is still expanding today. It saves an equivalent 21,000 plus tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> each year when compared to conventional sources of energy – electricity from the national grid and heat generated by individual boilers. There are currently over 140 buildings connected to the district heating network. These include city landmarks such as the [[Sheffield City Hall]], the [[Lyceum Theatre, Sheffield|Lyceum Theatre]], the [[University of Sheffield]], [[Sheffield Hallam University]], hospitals, shops, offices and leisure facilities plus 2,800 homes. More than 44&nbsp;km of underground pipes deliver energy which is generated at [[Sheffield Energy Recovery Facility]]. This converts 225,000 tonnes of waste into energy, producing up to 60&nbsp;MWe of thermal energy and up to 19&nbsp;MWe of electrical energy.

The [[Southampton District Energy Scheme]] was originally built to use just geothermal energy, but now also uses the heat from a gas-fired CHP generator. It supplies heating and [[district cooling]] to many large premises in the city, including the [[Westquay]] shopping centre, the De Vere Grand Harbour hotel, the [[Royal South Hants Hospital]], and several housing schemes. In the 1980s [[Southampton]] began to use combined heat and power district heating, taking advantage of geothermal heat "trapped" in the area. The geothermal heat provided by the well works in conjunction with the Combined Heat and Power scheme. Geothermal energy provides 15–20%, [[fuel oil]] 10%, and natural gas 70% of the total heat input for this scheme and the combined heat and power generators use conventional fuels to make electricity. "Waste heat" from this process is recovered for distribution through the 11&nbsp;km mains network.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Geothermie district heating scheme Southampton United Kingdom|url=http://www.energie-cites.org/db/southampton_140_en.pdf|access-date=2007-01-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927205633/http://www.energie-cites.org/db/southampton_140_en.pdf|archive-date=2007-09-27}} 080304 energie-cites.org</ref>

Scotland has several district heating systems. The first in the UK was installed at [[Aviemore]], and others followed at [[Lochgilphead]], [[Fort William, Scotland|Fort William]] and Forfar. [[Lerwick District Heating and Energy Recovery Plant|Lerwick District Heating Scheme]] in Shetland is of note because it is one of the few schemes where a completely new system was added to a previously existing small town.

[[Association for Decentralised Energy|ADE]] has an online map of district heating installations in the UK.<ref>{{cite web |title=District Heating Installation Map |url=https://www.theade.co.uk/resources/district-heating-installation-map |publisher=ADE}}</ref> ADE estimates that 54 percent of energy used to produce electricity is being wasted via conventional power production, which relates to £9.5 billion ($US12.5 billion) per year.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/articles/2017/11/what-a-waste-the-big-problem-of-heat-loss-in-uk-cities.html |title=What a Waste! The Big Problem of Heat Loss in UK Cities|work=www.renewableenergyworld.com |first= Kirsty |last=Lambert |date=9 November 2017 |access-date=12 November 2017}}</ref>

In the United Kingdom, the Heat Network Technical Assurance Scheme (HNTAS) is a regulatory framework being developed to establish minimum technical standards and an assurance process for heat networks. The scheme, underpinned by powers in the Energy Act 2023, is intended to require compliant heat networks to demonstrate that they meet mandated technical requirements throughout their lifecycle, covering design, installation, operation, and performance monitoring. HNTAS includes a structured assessment and certification system, with draft technical specifications and procedures published by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to support implementation. It is designed to improve the reliability, efficiency, and transparency of heat networks, and will apply to networks ranging from small communal systems to larger district heating schemes. DMS can advise.<ref name="HNTAS1">{{cite web |title=Heat Network Technical Assurance Scheme (HNTAS) |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-networks-regulation-technical-standards/heat-network-technical-assurance-scheme-hntas |publisher=GOV.UK}}</ref><ref name="HNTAS2">{{cite web |title=Heat networks regulation: technical standards |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-networks-regulation-technical-standards |publisher=GOV.UK}}</ref>

===North America===
In North America, district heating systems fall into two general categories. Those that are owned by and serve the buildings of a single entity are considered institutional systems. All others fall into the commercial category.

====Canada====
District Heating is becoming a growing industry in Canadian cities, with many new systems being built in the last ten years. Some of the major systems in Canada include:

* Calgary: [[ENMAX]] currently operates the Calgary Downtown District Energy Centre which provides heating to up to {{convert|10000000|sqft|m2}} of new and existing residential and commercial buildings. The District Energy Centre began operations in March 2010 providing heat to its first customer, the City of Calgary Municipal building.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.enmax.com/generation-wires/generation/district-energy-centre |title=ENMAX District Energy Centre |publisher=ENMAX.com |access-date=2015-09-25}}</ref>
* [[Edmonton]]: The community of [[Blatchford, Edmonton|Blatchford]], which is currently being developed on the grounds of Edmonton's former [[Edmonton City Centre Airport|City Centre Airport]], is launching a District Energy Sharing System (DESS) in phases.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=District Energy Sharing|url=https://blatchfordutility.ca/district-energy-sharing/|access-date=2020-09-24|website=Blatchford Renewable Energy Utility |publisher=City of Edmonton|language=en}}</ref> A geo-exchange field went online in 2019, and Blatchford's energy utility is in the planning and design phase for a sewage heat exchange system.<ref>{{cite news|last=Riebe|first=Natasha|date=November 1, 2019|title=Blatchford renewable energy utility ready to go|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/edmonton/edmonton-blatchford-1.5345452|access-date=September 24, 2020|website=CBC News}}</ref><ref name=":1" />
* [[Hamilton, Ontario|Hamilton]], ON has a district heating and cooling system in the downtown core, operated by HCE Energy Inc.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hamiltonce.com |title=HCE Energy Inc |publisher=hamiltonce.com |access-date=2015-12-18}}</ref>
* Montreal has a district heating and cooling system in the downtown core.
* [[Toronto]]:
** [[Enwave]] provides district heating and cooling within the downtown core of [[Toronto]], including deep lake cooling technology, which circulates cold water from Lake Ontario through heat exchangers to provide cooling for many buildings in the city.
** [[Creative Energy]] is constructing a combined-heat-and-power district energy system for the [[Mirvish Village]] development.
* [[Surrey, British Columbia|Surrey]]: Surrey City Energy owned by the city, provides district heating to the city's [[Whalley, Surrey|City Centre]] district.<ref>{{cite web|last=Reid|first=Amy|title=An exclusive look at Surrey's expanding district energy system|url=https://www.surreynowleader.com/news/video-an-exclusive-look-at-surreys-expanding-district-energy-system/|date=November 30, 2017|publisher=[[Surrey Now-Leader]]|access-date=January 28, 2018}}</ref>
* [[Vancouver]]:
** [[Creative Energy#Beatty Street, Vancouver|Creative Energy's Beatty Street facility]] has operated since 1968 and provides a central heating plant for the city's downtown core of [[Vancouver]]. In addition to heating 180 buildings, the Central Heat Distribution network also drives a [[steam clock]]. Work is currently underway to move the facility from natural gas to electric equipment.
** A large scale district heating system known as the Neighbourhood Energy Utility<ref>{{cite web|url=http://vancouver.ca/sustainability/building_neu.htm |title=Neighbourhood Energy Utility |publisher=Vancouver.ca |access-date=2011-09-25}}</ref> in the South East False Creek area is in initial operations with natural gas boilers and serves the 2010 Olympic Village. The untreated sewage heat recovery system began operations in January 2010, supplying 70% of annual energy demands, with retrofit work underway to move the facility off its remaining natural gas use.
* Windsor, Ontario has a district heating and cooling system in the downtown core.
* [[Drake Landing Solar Community]], AB, is small in size (52 homes) but notable for having the only central solar heating system in North America.
* London, Ontario and Charlottetown, PEI have district heating co-generation systems owned and operated by [[Veresen]].<ref name="vereseninc.com">{{cite web |title=District Energy |url=http://www.vereseninc.com/our-business/power/district-energy/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060457/http://www.vereseninc.com/our-business/power/district-energy/ |archive-date=2013-09-21 |access-date=2013-09-20 |website=[[Veresen]]}}</ref>
* [[Greater Sudbury|Sudbury, Ontario]] has a district heating cogeneration system in its downtown core, as well as a standalone cogeneration plant for the [[Sudbury Regional Hospital]]. In addition, Naneff Gardens, a new residential subdivision off Donnelly Drive in the city's [[Garson, Ontario|Garson]] neighbourhood, features a geothermal district heating system using technology developed by a local company, Renewable Resource Recovery Corporation.<ref>[http://www.northernlife.ca/news/localNews/2009/aug/geothermal100809.aspx "New geothermal technology could cut energy costs"]. ''[[Northern Life (newspaper)|Northern Life]]'', August 12, 2009.</ref>
* Ottawa, contains a significant district heating and cooling system serving the large number of federal government buildings in the city. The system loop contains nearly {{convert|1|e6usgal|m3|order=flip|abbr=unit|sigfig=1}} of chilled or heated water at any time.
* Cornwall, Ontario operates a district heating system which serves a number of city buildings and schools.
* [[Markham, Ontario]]: Markham District Energy operates several district heating sites:
** Warden Energy Centre (c. 2000), Clegg Energy Centre and Birchmount Energy Centre serving customers in the Markham Centre area
** Bur Oak Energy Centre (c. 2012) serving customers in the Cornell Centre area
Many Canadian universities operate central campus heating plants.

====United States====
[[File:Steam escaping at Florida A&M University.jpg|thumb|right|Steam escaping a district heating system at [[Florida A&M University]]]]
{{As of|2013}}, approximately 2,500 district heating and cooling systems existed in the United States, in one form or another, with the majority providing heat.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=HPACEngineering|title=Why Is District Energy Not More Prevalent in the U.S.?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180326040957/https://www.hpac.com/heating/why-district-energy-not-more-prevalent-us|url=https://www.hpac.com/heating/why-district-energy-not-more-prevalent-us|archive-date=March 26, 2018|date=June 7, 2013|publisher=Informa}}</ref>
* [[Consolidated Edison]] of [[New York (state)|New York]] (Con Ed) operates the New York City steam system, the largest commercial district heating system in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/coned.html |title=Con Ed Steam |publisher=Energy.rochester.edu |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070921191139/http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/coned.html |archive-date=2007-09-21 }}</ref> The system has operated continuously since March 3, 1882, and serves [[Manhattan Island]] from the Battery through 96th Street.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.coned.com/history/steam.asp |title=A Brief History of Con Edison |publisher=Con Edison |access-date=2014-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151114152015/http://www.coned.com/history/steam.asp |archive-date=2015-11-14 }}</ref> In addition to providing space- and water-heating, steam from the system is used in numerous restaurants for food preparation, for process heat in laundries and dry cleaners, for steam sterilization, and to power [[Absorption refrigerator|absorption chiller]]s for [[air conditioning]]. On July 18, 2007, one person was killed and numerous others injured when a [[2007 New York City steam explosion|steam pipe exploded]] on 41st Street at Lexington.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/6905738.stm | work=BBC News | title=Explosion rocks central New York | date=July 19, 2007 | access-date=May 1, 2010}}</ref> On August 19, 1989, three people were killed in an [[Gramercy Park asbestos steam explosion|explosion in Gramercy Park]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/07/19/nyregion/19explode.html?ex=1342584000&en=c9164269910ddad6&ei=5124&partner=permalink&exprod=permalink | work=The New York Times | title=Steam Blast Jolts Midtown, Killing One | first=James | last=Barron | date=July 19, 2007 | access-date=May 1, 2010}}</ref>
* [[Milwaukee]], [[Wisconsin]], has been using district heating for its [[central business district]] since the [[Valley Power Plant]] commenced operations in 1968.<ref>{{cite web |date=2013 |title=Valley Power Plant conversion |url=http://we-energies.com/home/projects/vapp.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130916040106/http://we-energies.com/home/projects/vapp.htm |archive-date=16 September 2013 |access-date=22 May 2022 |website=we-energies.com}}</ref> The air quality in the immediate vicinity of the plant, has been measured with significantly reduced ozone levels. The 2012 conversion of the plant, which changed the fuel input from coal to natural gas, is expected to further improve air quality at both the local César Chavez sensor as well as [[Antarctic]] sensors<ref>{{cite web|last=Content |first=Thomas |url=http://www.jsonline.com/business/we-energies-converting-valley-power-plant-j56hi5n-166616006.html |title=We Energies converting Valley power plant |publisher=Jsonline.com |date=2012-08-17 |access-date=2022-05-04}}</ref> The Wisconsin power plants double as breeding grounds for [[peregrine falcon]]s.<ref>{{cite web|author=WEC Energy Group |url=http://we-energies.com/environmental/protect_wildlife.htm |title=WEC Peregrine Falcons |publisher=We-energies.com |date= |access-date=2022-05-04}}</ref>
* Denver's district steam system is the oldest continuously operated commercial district heating system in the world. It began service November 5, 1880, and continues to serve 135 customers.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Jan Wagner| author2=Stephen P. Kutska| editor=Monica Westerlund| date=October 2008| title=DENVER'S 128-YEAR-OLD STEAM SYSTEM: "THE BEST IS YET TO COME"| journal=District Energy| volume=94| issue=4| pages=16–20
| issn=1077-6222| url=http://www.districtenergy-digital.org/districtenergy/2008Q4?pg=18#pg18}}</ref> The system is partially powered by the [[Xcel Energy]] Zuni Cogeneration Station, which was originally built in 1900.<ref>{{cite web |title=Zuni Station |url=http://www.xcelenergy.com/Colorado/Company/About_Energy_and_Rates/Power%20Generation/ColoradoPlants/Pages/ZuniStation.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628105705/http://www.xcelenergy.com/Colorado/Company/About_Energy_and_Rates/Power%20Generation/ColoradoPlants/Pages/ZuniStation.aspx |archive-date=28 June 2010 |access-date=20 July 2010 |website=Xcel Energy |quote=Plant Description: ... The facility also supplies steam for delivery to Xcel Energy's thermal energy customers in downtown Denver. ... Plant History: Zuni Station was originally built in 1900 and called the LaCombe Plant.}}</ref>
* [[NRG Energy]] operates district systems in the cities of San Francisco, [[Harrisburg, Pennsylvania|Harrisburg]], [[Minneapolis]], [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha]], [[Pittsburgh]], and [[San Diego]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nrgthermal.com |title=District energy &#124; combined heat and power plants &#124; NRG Thermal Corporation |publisher=Nrgthermal.com |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110925022823/http://www.nrgthermal.com/ |archive-date=2011-09-25 }}</ref>
* [[Seattle Steam Company]], a district system operated by Enwave, in Seattle. Enwave also operates district heat system in [[Chicago]], [[Houston]], [[Las Vegas]], [[Los Angeles]], [[New Orleans]], and [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] along with additional Canadian cities.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.enwave.com/locations.htm | access-date=2020-08-10| title=Locations - Enwave Energy Corporation}}</ref>
* Detroit Thermal operates a district system in [[Detroit]] that started operation at the [[Willis Avenue Station]] in 1903, originally operated by Detroit Edison.<ref>{{cite web|last=Oberholtzer|first=Michele|date=2018-02-01|title=What's the Source of the Steam Pouring Out of Detroit's Sidewalks?|url=https://www.hourdetroit.com/community/whats-the-source-of-the-steam-pouring-out-of-detroits-sidewalks/|access-date=2021-02-22|website=Hour Detroit Magazine|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.asme.org/wwwasmeorg/media/resourcefiles/aboutasme/who%20we%20are/engineering%20history/landmarks/105-detroit-edison-district-heating-system.pdf|title=Detroit Edison's District Heating System (1903) Beacon Street Plant|publisher=[[American Society of Mechanical Engineers]]}}</ref>
* Citizens Energy Group in [[Indianapolis]], [[Indiana]], operates the [[Perry K. Generating Station]], a [[gas-fired power plant]] that produces and distributes steam to about 160 downtown Indianapolis customers.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.--> |date=April 22, 2016 |url=https://www.ibj.com/articles/58240-citizens-seeks-rate-reduction-for-downtown-steam-customers |title=Citizens seeks rate reduction for downtown steam customers |newspaper=Indianapolis Business Journal |publisher=IBJ Media |access-date=August 13, 2022}}</ref>
* [[Lansing Board of Water & Light]], a municipal utility system in [[Lansing, Michigan]] operates a steam and chilled water system with the steam coming from the natural gas-fired REO Cogeneration Plant and the chilled water coming from the dedicated Roy E. Peffley Chilled Water Plant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Steam {{!}} lbwl.com |url=https://www.lbwl.com/customers/services/steam |access-date=2025-02-10 |website=www.lbwl.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Chilled Water {{!}} lbwl.com |url=https://www.lbwl.com/customers/services/chilled-water |access-date=2025-02-10 |website=www.lbwl.com |language=en}}</ref>
* Cleveland Thermal operates a district steam (since 1894) from the Canal Road plant near The Flats and district cooling system (since 1993) from Hamilton Avenue plant on the bluffs east of downtown.
* [[Veresen]] operates district heating/co-generation plants in [[Ripon, California]], and [[San Gabriel, California]].<ref name="fortchicago.com">{{cite web |last= |date=2010 |title=Fort Chicago's Power Business |url=http://www.fortchicago.com/our-businesses/power-business.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100811064633/http://www.fortchicago.com/our-businesses/power-business.html |archive-date=August 11, 2010 |website=Veresen, Fort Chicago Energy Partners}}</ref>
* Veolia Energy, a successor of the 1887 Boston Heating Company,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/ma/boston/bhc/ |title=Theodore Newton Vail and the Boston Heating Company, 1886–1890 |publisher=Energy.rochester.edu |access-date=2010-05-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090718051130/http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/ma/boston/bhc/ |archive-date=2009-07-18 }}</ref> operates a {{convert|26|mi|km|adj=on}} district system in [[Boston]] and [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]], and operates systems in Philadelphia PA, Baltimore MD, Kansas City MO, Tulsa OK, Houston TX and other cities.
* District Energy St. Paul operates the largest hot water district heating system in North America and generates the majority of its energy from an adjacent biomass-fueled combined heat and power plant. In March 2011, a 1&nbsp;MWh thermal solar array was integrated into the system, consisting of 144 20' x 8' solar panels installed on the roof of a customer building, RiverCentre.
* The California Department of General Services runs a central plant providing district heating to four million square feet in 23 state-owned buildings, including the State Capitol, using high-pressure steam boilers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://alerton.com/en-US/solutions/government/Case%20Studies/MK-CS-DGSCUP.pdf |title=SACRAMENTO CENTRAL UTILITY PLANT – CASE STUDY |publisher=Alerton.com |access-date=2013-10-25}}</ref>
* BPU of Jamestown NY operates a second generation water district heating system.  It was put into operation in 1984, runs from the BPU electrical plant and provides heat to the business district at Fahrenheit.

Historically, district heating was primarily used in urban areas of the US, but by 1985, it was mainly used in institutions.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/263/district-heating-and-cooling-in-the-united-states-prospects-and|title=District Heating and Cooling in the United States: Prospects and Issues|date=1985|publisher=National Research Council|isbn=9780309035378|language=en|doi=10.17226/263}}</ref> A handful of smaller municipalities in [[New England]] maintained municipal steam into the 21st century, in cities like [[Holyoke, Massachusetts]] and [[Concord, New Hampshire]], however the former would end service in 2010 and the latter in 2017, attributing aging infrastructure and capital expenses to their closures.<ref>{{cite news |last=Brooks |first=David |date=May 27, 2017 |title=Concord Steam: Last-of-its-kind power plant down to its final days |work=Concord Monitor |location=Concord, N.H. |url=https://www.concordmonitor.com/concord-steam-history-9673675 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190928221639/https://www.concordmonitor.com/concord-steam-history-9673675 |archive-date=September 28, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite report|title=City of Holyoke Energy Reduction Action Plan|archive-date=February 1, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170201122242/https://www.holyoke.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/Holyoke-Energy-Reduction-Plan-May-14-2010.pdf|url=https://www.holyoke.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/Holyoke-Energy-Reduction-Plan-May-14-2010.pdf|date=May 14, 2010}}
* {{cite report|title=Rules and Regulations of the Holyoke Gas & Electric Department|date=August 8, 2008|archive-date=October 28, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191028110523/https://www.hged.com/customers/payment-billing-rates/rates/electric-rates/Department_Rules_and_Regulations_eff.8-8-08.pdf|url=https://www.hged.com/customers/payment-billing-rates/rates/electric-rates/Department_Rules_and_Regulations_eff.8-8-08.pdf|pages=22–27}}
* {{cite news|newspaper=The Reminder |location=Springfield |url=http://archives.thereminder.com/localnews/Holyoke/holyokeappliesfor7/|last=Dobbs|first=G. Michael|date=January 19, 2010|title=Holyoke applies for $75 million energy grant}}
* {{cite news|title=New Steam Service to Start Monday|page=4|location=Springfield, Mass.|work=Springfield Republican|date=November 13, 1937}}</ref><ref>{{cite report|title=Holyoke Gas & Electric Department, 1902–2002, The First One Hundred Years|last=Moore|first=David|publisher=Holyoke Gas & Electric|url=https://www.hged.com/widgets/image-widgets/history-widget-folder/hge-history.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109220044/https://www.hged.com/widgets/image-widgets/history-widget-folder/hge-history.pdf|archive-date=2019-01-09|year=2002}}</ref> In 2019, Concord replaced a number of remaining pipes with more efficient ones for a smaller steam system heating only the [[New Hampshire State House|State House]] and [[New Hampshire State Library|State Library]], mainly due to historic preservation reasons rather than a broader energy plan.<ref>{{cite news|title=Replacing Concord Steam with new pipes continues to snarl downtown traffic|archive-date=April 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404150554/https://www.concordmonitor.com/steam-concord-install-update-24563773|url=https://www.concordmonitor.com/steam-concord-install-update-24563773|last=Brooks|first=David|work=Concord Monitor|location=Concord, N.H.|date=April 3, 2019}}</ref> [[File:BGSU Heating Plant Interior.jpg|thumb|The interior of the [[Bowling Green State University|BGSU]] Heating Plant]]
District heating is also used on many college campuses, often in combination with district cooling and electricity generation. Colleges using district heating include the [[University of Texas at Austin]]; [[Rice University]];<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sustainability.rice.edu/energy|title=Energy Consumption – Sustainability ===Asia===

====Japan====
87 district heating enterprises are operating in Japan, serving 148 districts.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.jdhc.or.jp/area/area01.html |title=平成21年4月現在支部別熱供給事業者: The Japan Heat Service Utilities Associations 2009 |publisher=Jdhc.or.jp |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007151412/http://www.jdhc.or.jp/area/area01.html |archive-date=2011-10-07 }}</ref>

Many companies operate district cogeneration facilities that provide steam and/or hot water to many of the office buildings. Also, most operators in the [[Greater Tokyo]] serve district cooling.

====China====
In southern [[China]] (south of the [[Qinling–Huaihe Line]]), there are nearly no district heating systems. In northern China, district heating systems are common.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Guan Jin |first1=James |title=District Energy in China |url=https://www.euroheat.org/knowledge-hub/district-energy-china/ |website=Euroheat&Power |access-date=21 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Jingjing |last2=Di Lucia |first2=Lorenzo |title=A transition perspective on alternatives to coal in Chinese district heating |journal=International Journal of Sustainable Energy Planning and Management |date=23 September 2015 |volume=6 |doi=10.5278/ijsepm.2015.6.5}} {{open access}}</ref> Most district heating systems are just for heating by burning [[Anthracite|hard coal]] instead of [[Cogeneration|CHP]]. Since [[air pollution in China]] has become quite serious, many cities gradually are now using natural gas rather than coal in district heating system. There is also some amount of geothermal heating<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tester |first1=Jeff |title=U.S. lagging in geothermal energy as China and others pull ahead |url=https://www.axios.com/us-lagging-in-geothermal-energy-as-china-and-others-pull-ahead-ea7ce800-df9b-431c-896c-8b1ab4bb9da2.html |website=Axios |date=17 July 2018 |access-date=21 February 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hallsson |first1=Hallur |title=The Icelandic geothermal model is changing China |url=https://icelandictimes.com/the-icelandic-geothermal-model-is-changing-china/ |website=Icelandic Times |access-date=21 February 2020 |date=1 October 2019}}</ref> and sea heat pump systems.<ref name="SeawaterHeatPumps">{{cite journal |author1=Chang Su |author2=Hatef Madani |author3= Hua Liu|author4= Ruzhu Wang |author5= Björn Palm |year=2020 |title=Seawater heat pumps in China, a spatial analysis |journal=Energy Conversion and Management |volume=203 |page=112440 |article-number=112240 |doi=10.1016/j.enconman.2019.112240|bibcode=2020ECM...20312240S |s2cid=209702976 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:kth:diva-266164 }}</ref>

In February 2019, China's [[State Power Investment Corporation]] (SPIC) signed a cooperation agreement with the [[Baishan]] municipal government in [[Jilin]] province for the Baishan Nuclear Energy Heating Demonstration Project, which would use a [[China National Nuclear Corporation]] [[DHR-400]] (District Heating Reactor 400 MWt).<ref name=nei-20190314>{{cite news |url=https://www.neimagazine.com/news/newschina-signs-agreement-for-nuclear-heating-demonstration-project-7039593 |title=China signs agreement for nuclear heating demonstration project |publisher=Nuclear Engineering International |date=14 March 2019 |access-date=18 March 2019}}</ref><ref name=wnn-20180907>{{cite news |url=http://www.world-nuclear-news.org/Articles/CNNC-completes-design-of-district-heating-reactor |title=CNNC completes design of district heating reactor |publisher=World Nuclear News |date=7 September 2018 |access-date=18 March 2019}}</ref> Building cost is 1.5 billion yuan ($230 million), taking three years to build.<ref name=reuters-20171210>{{cite news |url=https://uk.reuters.com/article/us-china-nuclear-heating/china-looks-to-nuclear-option-to-ease-winter-heating-woes-idUKKBN1E404J |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171210094952/https://uk.reuters.com/article/us-china-nuclear-heating/china-looks-to-nuclear-option-to-ease-winter-heating-woes-idUKKBN1E404J |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 10, 2017 |title=China looks to nuclear option to ease winter heating woes |last=Stanway |first=David |publisher=Reuters |date=10 December 2017 |access-date=18 March 2019}}</ref>

==== Turkey ====
[[Geothermal energy in Turkey]] provides some district heating,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-05-17 |title=Interview with Ufuk Sentürk – Chairman of JESDER, Turkey |url=https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/interview-with-ufuk-senturk-chairman-of-jesder-turkey/ |access-date=2022-08-01 |language=en-US}}</ref> and residential district heating and cooling requirements have been mapped.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sözen |first1=Adnan |last2=Menli̇k |first2=Tayfun |last3=Anvari̇-Moghaddam |first3=Amjad |date=2020-09-01 |title=Mapping of Turkey's District Heating/Cooling Requirements |journal=Politeknik Dergisi |language=en |volume=23 |issue=3 |pages=867–878 |doi=10.2339/politeknik.699047|s2cid=216520458 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Market penetration==
{{update|date=December 2022}}
Penetration of district heating (DH) into the heat market varies by country. Penetration is influenced by different factors, including environmental conditions, availability of heat sources, economics, and economic and legal framework. The [[European Commission]] aims to develop sustainable practices through implementation of district heating and cooling technology.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.adroitmarketresearch.com/industry-reports/district-heating-and-cooling-market |title=District Heating And Cooling Market Size by Type, End-Use Industry 2021-2028 |publisher=Adroitmarketresearch.com |date= |access-date=2022-05-04}}</ref>

In the year 2000 the percentage of houses supplied by district heat in some European countries was as follows:

In Iceland the prevailing positive influence on DH is availability of easily captured geothermal heat. In most Eastern European countries, energy planning included development of cogeneration and district heating. Negative influence in the Netherlands and UK can be attributed partially to milder climate, along with competition from natural gas.{{Citation needed|date=August 2022}} The tax on domestic gas prices in the UK is a third of that in France and a fifth of that in Germany.
