{{Sustainable energy}}
'''[[Green building]]''' is a technique that aims to create structures that are [[environmentally responsible]] and resource-efficient throughout their lifecycle – including siting, design, construction, operation, maintenance, renovation, and demolition.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.igreenbuild.com/cd_1967.aspx |title=GreenBuild.com |publisher=Igreenbuild.com |date=2005-12-06 |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323144116/http://www.igreenbuild.com/cd_1967.aspx |archive-date=2012-03-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
A 2009 report by the U.S. [[General Services Administration]] evaluated 12 sustainably designed GSA buildings and found they cost less to operate.

'''[[Wood products]]''' from responsible sources are a good choice for most green building projects – both new construction and renovations. Wood grows naturally using energy from the sun and is renewable, sustainable, and recyclable. It is an effective insulator and uses far less energy to produce than concrete or steel.<ref>[http://www.woodworks.org/woodBenefits/sustainableDesign/default.aspx WoodWorks Sustainable Design] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100818041504/http://www.woodworks.org/woodBenefits/sustainableDesign/default.aspx |date=August 18, 2010 }}</ref> Wood can also [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate climate change]] because wood products continue to store carbon absorbed by the tree during its growing cycle, and because substituting wood for fossil fuel-intensive materials such as steel and concrete result in ‘avoided’ [[greenhouse gas emissions]].

==Life cycle assessment==

A [[life cycle assessment]] can help avoid a narrow outlook on environmental, social, and economic concerns by assessing each and every impact associated with all the stages of a process from cradle to grave (i.e., from raw materials through materials processing, manufacture, distribution, use, repair and maintenance, and disposal or recycling).

A comprehensive review of scientific literature from Europe, North America, and Australia pertaining to life cycle assessment of wood products <ref>{{cite web |url=http://discover-decouvrir.cisti-icist.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/dcvr/ctrl?action=shwart&aix=3&aid=7314557 |title=Abstract Wooden building products in comparative LCA 2007 |publisher=Discover-decouvrir.cisti-icist.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca |date=2010-03-29 |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006135701/http://discover-decouvrir.cisti-icist.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/dcvr/ctrl?action=shwart&aix=3&aid=7314557 |archive-date=2011-10-06 |url-status=dead }}</ref> concluded, among other things;
* Fossil fuel consumption, the potential contributions to the greenhouse effect, and the quantities of solid waste tend to be minor for wood products compared to competing products.
* Wood products that have been installed and are used in an appropriate way tend to have a favorable environmental profile compared to functionally equivalent products out of other materials.

A study by the [[Canadian Wood Council]] compared the life cycle impacts of three {{convert|2400|sqft|m2|adj=on}} homes designed primarily in wood, steel, and concrete over the first 20 years of their lifespans. Relative to the wood design, the steel and concrete designs released more air pollution, produced more solid wastes, used more resources, required more energy, emitted more greenhouse gases, and discharged more water pollution.<ref>[http://www.cwc.ca/DesignWithWood/Sustainability/?Language=EN Canadian Wood Council] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110312112233/http://www.cwc.ca/DesignWithWood/Sustainability/?Language=EN |date=March 12, 2011 }}</ref>

When the complete life cycle is considered, including use and disposal, the great majority of the studies indicate that wood products have lower greenhouse gas emissions. In the few cases where wood products cause greater greenhouse gas emissions than their non-wood counterparts, the cause was inappropriate post-use disposal.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |title=FPInnovations 2010 A Synthesis of Research on Wood Products and Greenhouse Gas Impacts Page 6 |access-date=2013-02-21 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321215904/http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-21 }}</ref>

Tools are available that enable architects to judge the relative environmental merits of [[building material]]s. They include the ATHENA Impact Estimator for Buildings,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.athenasmi.org/tools/impactEstimator/index.html |title=ATHENA Institute Impact Estimator for Buildings |publisher=Athenasmi.org |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-date=2016-11-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161128201946/http://www.athenasmi.org/tools/impactEstimator/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> which is capable of modeling 95% of the building stock in North America, and the ATHENA® EcoCalculator for Assemblies<ref>[http://www.athenasmi.org/tools/ecoCalculator/index.html ATHENA Institute EcoCalculator for Assemblies] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101014164446/http://www.athenasmi.org/tools/ecoCalculator/index.html |date=October 14, 2010 }}</ref>  provides instant life cycle assessment results for common assemblies based on detailed assessments previously conducted using the Estimator.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.athenasmi.org/about/index.html |title=ATHENA Institute |publisher=Athenasmi.org |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-date=2017-08-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170818152228/http://www.athenasmi.org/about/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>  The EcoCalculator is available free from the non-profit [http://www.athenasmi.org Athena Sustainable Materials Institute] in order to encourage greater use of LCA by design and building professionals.

==Wood and climate change==
{{multiple image|perrow = 2|total_width=300
| image1 = GERENDAHÁZ HAJDÚBÖSZÖRMÉNY - panoramio.jpg
| image2 = Marxal, Kish (P1090377-HDR).jpg
| image3 = North Tracy Historic District-JSP1.JPG
| image4 = Vartomten, hovedbygning.jpg
| footer = Some examples of wooden buildings
}}
Trees absorb carbon dioxide and store it in biomass (wood, leaves, roots). When trees decompose or burn, much of the stored carbon is released back into the atmosphere, mainly as carbon dioxide, and some of the carbon remains in the forest debris and soils.<ref name="naturallywood1">{{cite web |url=http://naturallywood.com/uploadedFiles/General/Header/tackle-climate-change.pdf |title=Tackle Climate Change, Use Wood |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 }}{{Dead link|date=January 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Harvested wood is used for products such as structural lumber or furniture, the carbon is stored for decades or longer. A typical {{convert|2400|sqft|m2|adj=on}} home in North America contains 29 metric tons of carbon or the equivalent of offsetting the greenhouse gas emissions produced by driving a passenger car over five years (about 12,500 liters of gasoline.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fpinnovations.ca/ |title=FPInnovations Wood and Climate Change |publisher=Fpinnovations.ca |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>)
 
When wood replaces a fossil fuel for energy, or a construction material with a greater greenhouse gas footprint, this lowers greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name="naturallywood1"/>

Studies show that wood products are associated with far less greenhouse gas emissions over their lifetime than other major building materials. Substituting a cubic meter of blocks or brick with wood results in a significant saving of 0.75 to one tone of carbon dioxide.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/fileadmin/user_upload/rome2007/docs/Using_wood_products_to_mitigate_climate_change.pdf |title=Using Wood Products to Mitigate Climate Change Page 7 |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>
 
Increasing the use of wood products in construction and for other long-lived uses, plus the use of wood byproducts and wood waste as biomass replacement for fossil fuels, can contribute to atmospheric greenhouse gas stabilization. The sustainable management of forests for the production of wood products is a feasible and beneficial part of an overall strategy to mitigate climate change.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |title=FPInnovations 2010 A Synthesis of Research on Wood Products and Greenhouse Gas Impacts Page 8 |access-date=2013-02-21 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321215904/http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-21 }}</ref>

Securing the Future, a United Kingdom government strategy for sustainable development, stated: “Forestry practices can make a significant contribution by reducing greenhouse gas emissions through increasing the amount of carbon removed from the atmosphere by the national forest estate, by burning wood for fuel, and by using wood as a substitute for energy-intensive materials such as concrete and steel.”

==The role of wood in carbon balances==

[[FPInnovations]], a Canadian non-profit research organization, conducted a literature review of 66 scientific peer-reviewed articles regarding the net impact on atmospheric greenhouse gases due to wood product use within a life cycle perspective. It showed several ways wood product substitution affects greenhouse gas balances, including:

* Less fossil fuel consumption in manufacturing;
* Avoidance of industrial process carbon emissions from cement manufacturing when wood products replace cement-based products;
* Carbon storage in wood products and in the forest; and
* Avoided fossil fuel emissions when wood biofuels replace fossil fuels.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |title=FPInnovations 2010 A Synthesis of Research on Wood Products and Greenhouse Gas Impacts Page 3 |access-date=2013-02-21 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321215904/http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-21 }}</ref>

==Energy efficiency==

As high-performance buildings use less operating energy, the embodied energy required to extract, process, transport and install building materials may make up as much as 30% of the overall life cycle energy consumption. Studies such as the U.S. LCI Database Project show buildings built primarily with wood will have a lower embodied energy than those built primarily with brick, concrete or steel.

A recent case study of the Eugene Kruger Building in Quebec, Canada determined that the all-wood solution adopted for this 8,000-square-metre academic building resulted in a 40% reduction in embodied energy compared to steel and concrete alternatives.

A 2002 study compared production energy values for building components (e.g. walls, floors, roofs) made predominantly of wood, steel and concrete, and found that wood construction has a range of energy use from 185 to 280 Gigajoules (GJ), concrete from 265 to 521 GJ, and steel from 457 to 649 GJ. Wood construction will generally use less energy than other materials, although the high end of the range of wood construction energy overlaps with the low end of the range of concrete construction.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |title=FPInnovations 2010 A Synthesis of Research on Wood Products and Greenhouse Gas Impacts Page 42 |access-date=2013-02-21 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321215904/http://www.forintek.ca/public/pdf/Public_Information/technical_rpt/TR19%20Complete%20Pub-web.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-21 }}</ref>

The passive design uses natural processes – convection, absorption, radiation, and conduction – to minimize energy consumption and improve thermal comfort. Researchers in Europe have identified wood as a suitable material for the development of passive buildings due to its unique combination of properties, including thermal resistance, natural finish, structural integrity, and lightweight and weatherproof qualities. Passive design is beginning to be incorporated in small buildings in North America through the use of structural wood panels.
 
Due to its cellular structure and many tiny air pockets, wood is a better insulator than steel and concrete in most climates – 400 times better than steel and 10 times better than concrete. More insulation is needed for steel and concrete to achieve the same thermal performance.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://naturallywood.com/uploadedFiles/General/Green_Building/Module-3_Energy_Conservation.pdf |title=Naturally:wood Green Building Toolkit Module 3 Energy Conservation |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120722140227/http://www.naturallywood.com/sites/default/files/Module-3-Energy-Conservation.pdf |archive-date=2012-07-22 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

A 2002 study prepared by the [[National Association of Home Builders]] Research Center Inc.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.p2pays.org/ref/15/14083.pdf |title=NAHB Research Center Inc. Steel vs. Wood: Long-Term Thermal Performance Comparison 2002 |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> compared long-term energy use in two nearly identical side-by-side homes, one framed with conventional dimensional lumber and the second framed with cold-formed steel. It found the steel-framed house used 3.9% more natural gas in the winter and 10.7% more electricity in the summer.

==Health and well-being==

Solid wood products, particularly flooring, are often specified in environments where occupants are known to have allergies to dust or other particulates.

Wood itself is considered to be hypo-allergenic and its smooth surfaces prevent the buildup of particles common in soft finishes like carpet. The use of wood products can also improve air quality by absorbing or releasing moisture in the air to moderate humidity.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.naturallywood.com/resources |title=Naturally:wood Green Building with Wood Toolkit |publisher=Naturallywood.com |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>
A study at the University of British Columbia and FPInnovations <ref>{{cite thesis|url=http://circle.ubc.ca/handle/2429/28644 |title=Wood in the Human Environment: Restorative Properties of Wood in the Build Indoor Environment Fell, David Robert |year=2010 |publisher=Circle.ubc.ca |doi=10.14288/1.0071305 |access-date=2013-02-21|last1=Fell |first1=David Robert }}</ref> found that the visual presence of wood in a room lowers [[sympathetic nervous system]] (SNS) activation in occupants, further establishing the positive link between wood and human health. SNS activation is the way human bodies prepare themselves to deal with stress. It increases blood pressure and heart rate while inhibiting digestion, recovery and repair functions in order to deal with immediate threats. While necessary in the short term, prolonged periods in an SNS-activated state have a negative effect on the body's physiological and psychological health.

The study supports wood's value as a tool in [[evidence-based design]] (EBD) – a growing field that seeks to promote health and other positive outcomes such as increased productivity and well-being based on scientifically credible evidence. So far, EBD has focused largely on healthcare and, in particular, patient recovery.

==Reducing waste==
[[File:Wood-pallet-building.jpg|thumb|right|Wooden [[pallet]]s used on a building's exterior to filter sunlight]]
Green building seeks to avoid wasting energy, water and materials during construction. Design and building professionals can reduce [[construction waste]] through design optimization, using right-sized framing members, for example, or pre-manufactured and engineered components.

The wood industry reduces waste in a similar way by optimizing sawmill operations and by using wood chips and sawdust to produce paper and composite products, or as fuel for renewable bioenergy. North American wood producers use 98 percent of every tree harvested and brought to a mill.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://woodworks.org/files/PDF/publications/Green_Bldg.pdf |title=Wood and Green Building |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>

Rather than demolishing structures at the end of their useful life, they can be deconstructed to reclaim useful building materials rather than dumping them in the landfill.<ref>[http://www.jgpress.com/inbusiness/archives/_free/000648.html In Business magazine Green Builders Get Big Help from Deconstruction] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121092246/http://www.jgpress.com/inbusiness/archives/_free/000648.html |date=November 21, 2008 }}</ref>
 
When used properly, wood, concrete and steel can last for decades or centuries. In North America, most structures are demolished because of external forces such as zoning changes and rising land values. Designing for flexibility and adaptability secures the greatest value for the [[embodied energy]] in building materials.

Wood is versatile and flexible, making it the easiest construction material for renovations. Wood buildings can be redesigned to suit changing needs, whether this involves adding a new room or moving a window or door.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.naturallywood.com/why-wood |title=Naturally:wood |publisher=Naturallywood.com |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> Wood structures are typically easy to adapt to new uses because the material is so light and easy to work with. Few homeowner or professional remodelers have the skill and equipment needed to alter steel-frame structures.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cwc.ca/Resources/Tips/#Q18 |title=Canadian Wood Council |publisher=Cwc.ca |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>

Structural wood members can typically be reclaimed and reused for the same or similar purpose with only minor modifications or wastage, or remilled and fashioned into alternate products such as window and door frames.
To reduce the amount of wood that goes to landfill, the {{CO2}} Neutral Alliance (a coalition of government, NGOs and the forest industry) created the website dontwastewood.com. The site includes resources for regulators, municipalities, developers, contractors, owner/operators and individuals/homeowners looking for information on wood recycling.

==Responsible sourcing==

Wood is a responsible environmental choice for construction as long as it comes from forests that are managed sustainably. [[Illegal logging]] and the international trade in illegally logged timber is a major problem for many timber-producing countries in the developing world. It causes environmental damage, costs governments billions of dollars in lost revenue, promotes corruption, undermines the rule of law and good governance and funds armed conflict. Consumer countries can use their buying power by ensuring the wood products they buy are from known and legal sources.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.illegal-logging.info/ |title=Illegal-Logging.info |publisher=Illegal-Logging.info |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>

Deforestation, which is the permanent removal of forests where the land is converted to other uses such as agriculture or housing, is also a significant problem in developing countries, and globally accounts for 17% of the world's greenhouse gas emissions.

The forests most vulnerable to destruction are in tropical regions of the world, where the rate of deforestation was estimated at {{convert|32000000|acre|km2}} a year from 1990 to 2005. According to the State of the World's Forests Report, 2007, “the world lost about 3 percent of its forest area from 1990 to 2005; but, in North America, the total forest area remained virtually constant.” When forest land is converted for other uses, a portion of the deforestation can be offset by afforestation—such as the planting of trees on land that has been bare of trees for a long time.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bcclimatechange.org/ |title=Tackle Climate Change – Use Wood book |access-date=2011-05-05 |archive-date=2011-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110426103912/http://www.bcclimatechange.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/009/a0773e/a0773e00.HTM |title=State of the World's Forests, 2007 |publisher=Fao.org |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref>

Voluntary third-party forest certification is a credible tool for communicating the environmental and social performance of forest operations.<ref name="metafore1">{{cite web |author=GreenBlue |url=http://www.metafore.org/index.php?p=About+Certification&s=153 |title=Metafore |publisher=Metafore |date=2012-05-22 |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-date=2009-04-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090405013048/http://www.metafore.org/index.php?p=About+Certification&s=153 |url-status=dead }}</ref> With forest certification, an independent organization develops standards of good forest management, and independent auditors issue certificates to forest operations that comply with those standards. This certification verifies that forests are well-managed – as defined by a particular standard – and ensures that certified wood and paper products come from legal and responsible sources.<ref name="metafore1"/>

==Green building rating systems==

A 2010 study by the Light House Sustainable Building Centre in British Columbia, Canada examined the ways in which the world's major voluntary green building rating systems incorporate wood. It found that rating systems for single-family homes in North America were the most inclusive of wood products and rating systems for commercial buildings and buildings outside of North America were the least inclusive.<ref>[http://continuingeducation.construction.com/article.php?L=221&C=694McGraw Hill Construction How Wood Products Stack Up in Green Building Systems]{{Dead link|date=June 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Systems studied included [[BREEAM]] (United Kingdom), Built Green (United States and Canada), CASBEE (Japan), [[Green Globes]] (United States), [[Green Star (Australia)|Green Star]] (Australia), [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED]] (launched in United States and used in countries such as Canada, China, India and Mexico), [[Living Building Challenge]] (United States and Canada), the [[NAHB – National Green Building Program]] (United States), and the SB Tool (Canada and UK).

In most cases, the rating systems offer credits/point for the use of wood in the following areas: certified wood; recycled /reused /salvaged materials; and local sourcing of materials. In some cases, building techniques and skills (such as advanced framing) and waste minimization are recognized, and most demand that all wood adhesives, resins, engineered and composite products contain no added [[urea formaldehyde]] and have strict limits on VOC ([[volatile organic compound]]) content.

==LEED certified wood credit==
{{see also|Certified wood}}

In December 2010, the [[U.S. Green Building Council]] failed to get enough yes votes from members for a proposed rewrite of the certified wood policy in its [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design]] (LEED) rating system. Since its inception, LEED has only accepted wood certified to Forest Stewardship Council standards.<ref>{{cite web|author=&ndash; Tristan Roberts |url=http://www.buildinggreen.com/auth/article.cfm/2010/12/7/Not-Enough-Votes-for-LEED-Certified-Wood-Benchmark/ |title=Environmental Building News |publisher=Buildinggreen.com |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> 
The two largest third-party forest certification standards in the United States – the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) <ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fscus.org/green_building/index.php |title=Forest Stewardship Council |publisher=Fscus.org |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> and the Sustainable Forestry Initiative (SFI) <ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sfiprogram.org/leed/index.php |title=Sustainable Forestry Initiative |publisher=Sfiprogram.org |date= |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> – opposed the proposed benchmarks. FSC questioned their rigor and SFI claimed the process was overly detailed and complex.

A number of organizations, including the [[National Association of State Foresters]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stateforesters.org/node/886 |title=National Association of State Foresters Resolution 2008-6: Green Building and the Role of Wood Products |publisher=Stateforesters.org |date=2008-10-01 |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> the Canadian Institute of Forestry,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cif-ifc.org/uploads//Website_Assets/USGB_media_release_April_19_2010.pdf |title=Canadian Institute of Forestry |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321061607/http://www.cif-ifc.org/uploads//Website_Assets/USGB_media_release_April_19_2010.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-21 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the Society of American Foresters<ref>{{cite web|last=Goergen |first=Michael T. |url=http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/opinion/2011509983_guest03green.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110630020750/http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/opinion/2011509983_guest03green.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 30, 2011 |title=Michael Goergen, Society of American Foresters Column in Seattle Times |publisher=The Seattle Times |date=2010-04-02 |access-date=2013-02-21}}</ref> called for LEED to recognize all credible certification programs to encourage the use of wood as a green building material.

In its 2008-2009 Forest Products Annual Review, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe/Food and Agriculture Organization stated that green building initiatives (GBI) can be a mixed blessing for wood products. “GBI standards giving exclusive recognition to particular
forest-certification brands may help drive demand for these brands at the expense of wider appreciation of the environmental merits of wood.” <ref>{{cite web |url=http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/Final_FPAMR2009.pdf |title=2008-2009 UNECE-FAO Forest Products Annual Review Page 123 |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717023154/http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/Final_FPAMR2009.pdf |archive-date=2010-07-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In its 2009–2010 review, the UNECE/FAO reported growing convergence between certification systems: "Over the years, many of the issues that previously divided the (certification) systems have become much less distinct. The largest certification systems now generally have the same structural programmatic requirements."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/Final_FPAMR2009.pdf |title=2008-2009 UNECE-FAO Forest Products Annual Review Page 121 |date= |access-date=2013-02-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717023154/http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/Final_FPAMR2009.pdf |archive-date=2010-07-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Green building in Canada
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
[[File:CIRS Building UBC.jpg|thumb|360x360px|Centre for Interactive Research on Sustainability, University of British Columbia. LEED Platinum Certified Building. Completed in 2011. 2260 West Mall, Vancouver, Canada]]
'''[[Green building]] in [[Canada]]''' refers to the design, construction, and operation of Canadian buildings with a focus on [[sustainability]], [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]], and reduced [[environmental impact]]  on the Canadian environment.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-08-11 |title=Green buildings |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/green-buildings |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

The practice has developed in response to concerns about [[climate change]], [[resource consumption]], and [[urban development]] in Canada.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2024-07-08 |title=The Canada Green Buildings Strategy: Transforming Canada's buildings sector for a net-zero and resilient future |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/canada-green-buildings-strategy-transforming-canada-s-buildings-sector-net-zero-resilient-future |access-date=2025-02-25 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

Various initiatives, including policies, regulations and third-party certification systems such as [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED)]] and the [[Canada Green Building Council|Canadian Green Building Council (CaGBC)]] influence the adoption of green building practices across the country.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Two Million Green Homes |url=https://www.cagbc.org/news-resources/research-and-reports/two-million-green-homes/ |access-date=2025-02-25 |website=Canada Green Building Council (CAGBC) |language=en-CA}}</ref>

The [[Government of Canada|Canadian government]], along with provincial and municipal authorities, has implemented various evolving strategies like advancements in materials, energy systems, and building technologies to support [[Sustainability in construction|sustainable construction]], including financial incentives, updated [[building code]]s, and [[Air pollution|emissions reduction]] targets. <ref name=":72">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-08-11 |title=Green building programs and funding |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/green-building-programs-funding |access-date=2025-02-25 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=O’Neill |first1=Kirstie |last2=Affolderbach |first2=Julia |date=2024-05-27 |title=Assembling place-based transitions: capitalist logics of green building in Vancouver, Canada |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02723638.2023.2243132 |journal=Urban Geography |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=840–862 |doi=10.1080/02723638.2023.2243132 |issn=0272-3638}}</ref>

This article provides an overview of green building in Canada, including its policies, [[Professional certification|certification programs]], notable projects, ongoing challenges, [[Affordability of housing in Canada|affordability]], and design strategies.

== Background ==
The development of [[green building]] practices in Canada has been shaped by evolving [[Environmentalism|environmental awareness]], advancements in [[building science]], and government initiatives.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last=Boake |first=Terri |title=Moving Towards Green: A Brief History of the Beginnings of Sustainable Design in Canada |url=https://www.academia.edu/3437942 |journal=[[University of Waterloo School of Architecture]]}}</ref> Early discussions on sustainability in [[construction]] were influenced by broader [[environmental movement]]s and research on [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] and climate-responsive design.<ref name=":11" /> Over time, the focus on reducing [[energy consumption]] and minimizing environmental impact led to the introduction of [[Policy|policies]] and programs aimed at improving [[building performance]].<ref name=":11" />

In response to rising energy costs and environmental concerns, Canada introduced initiatives such as the [[R-2000 program|R-2000]] Home Program in the late 1980s to promote energy-efficient residential construction.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Mayo |first1=Tim |last2=Sinha |first2=Robin |date=1997-07-01 |title=R-2000 and Advanced Houses: The Canadian Experience |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/109719639702100108 |journal=Journal of Thermal Insulation and Building Envelopes |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=91–111 |doi=10.1177/109719639702100108 |issn=1065-2744|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Throughout the following decades, additional programs expanded to address [[Commercial property|commercial buildings]], [[indoor air quality]], and the use of [[Sustainable materials management|sustainable materials]]. These efforts contributed to the development of national standards and policies supporting energy efficiency and [[Air pollution|emissions reduction]] in the building sector.

In March 2006, Canada's first green building point of service, Light House Sustainable Building Centre, opened on [[Granville Island]] in the heart of Vancouver, BC. A destination for the public and professionals alike, the Light House resource centre is funded by Canadian government departments and businesses to help implement green building practices and to recognize the economic value of green building as a new regional economy.

== Government Policies and Initiatives ==

=== Federal Strategies ===
The Government of Canada has implemented several strategies to promote green building practices and transition towards a net-zero emissions future. These initiatives aim to enhance energy efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and improve the resilience of the building sector.

==== Canada Green Building Strategy ====
The [https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/canada-green-buildings-strategy-transforming-canada-s-buildings-sector-net-zero-resilient-future '''Canada Green Buildings Strategy'''] (CGBS) is a federal initiative aimed at making homes and buildings across the country more [[Efficient energy use|energy-efficient]], affordable, and resilient to [[climate change]].<ref name=":102">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2024-07-08 |title=The Canada Green Buildings Strategy: Transforming Canada's buildings sector for a net-zero and resilient future |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/canada-green-buildings-strategy-transforming-canada-s-buildings-sector-net-zero-resilient-future |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> The strategy focuses on three main areas consisting of accelerating retrofits, building green from the start, and shaping the future of the buildings sector.<ref name=":102"/> It promotes the use of cleaner energy sources for heating and cooling, encourages sustainable construction materials, and supports measures to protect buildings from extreme weather.<ref name=":102"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-08-11 |title=Green building programs and funding |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/building-energy-efficiency/green-building-programs-funding |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> The goal is to improve energy efficiency while addressing housing affordability and economic growth.<ref name=":102"/>

==== Key Programs ====
The federal government has introduced several programs to support greener buildings. The Canada [https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/canada-greener-homes-grant Greener Homes Grant] and [https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/canada-greener-homes-loan Canada Greener Homes Loan] help homeowners make energy-efficient upgrades.<ref name=":92">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2021-03-17 |title=Canada Greener Homes Grant |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/canada-greener-homes-grant |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref name=":102"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-04-28 |title=Canada Greener Homes Loan |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/canada-greener-homes-loan |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> The [https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/oil-heat-pump-affordability-program Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program] provides support for switching to cleaner heating systems.<ref name=":72"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-11-18 |title=Oil to Heat Pump Affordability program |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/canada-greener-homes-initiative/oil-heat-pump-affordability-program |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> The Green and Inclusive Community Buildings Program funds energy-efficient retrofits for public buildings, while the Greening Government Strategy focuses on making federal buildings more sustainable.<ref name=":102" /> These initiatives involve collaboration with provinces, municipalities, Indigenous communities, and private sector partners to drive progress toward a low-carbon, climate-resilient future.<ref name=":102" />

=== Provincial and Municipal ===

==== Green Municipal Fund ====
[https://greenmunicipalfund.ca/about-green-municipal-fund '''The Green Municipal Fund (GMF)'''] is a program administered by the [[Federation of Canadian Municipalities]] (FCM) that provides financial support for environmental projects undertaken by municipal governments in Canada.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2017-01-13 |title=NRCan 2017-18 Departmental Plan - Green Municipal Fund (GMF) |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/corporate/planning-reporting/departmental-plan/nrcan-2017-18-departmental-plan/green-municipal-fund-gmf |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref name=":32">{{Cite web |last=Barreca |first=Alena |date=2020-09-04 |title=Green Municipal Fund: Environmental Funding for Canadian Municipalities |url=https://funding.ryan.com/blog/government-funding/green-municipal-fund-overview/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Ryan |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":42">{{Cite web |title=About the Green Municipal Fund {{!}} Green Municipal Fund |url=https://greenmunicipalfund.ca/about-green-municipal-fund |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=greenmunicipalfund.ca}}</ref> Funded by the Government of Canada, the program offers grants, loans, and loan guarantees to assist municipalities in initiatives that focus on improving air, water, and [[soil quality]], as well as reducing greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name=":32"/><ref name=":42"/> The GMF supports projects at various stages, including planning, feasibility studies, pilot initiatives, and full-scale capital projects.<ref name=":42"/>

Eligibility for GMF funding includes [[municipal government]]s, municipally owned corporations, [[Nonprofit corporation|non-profit]] affordable housing providers, and municipal partners such as private sector entities, [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous]] communities, and [[non-governmental organization]]s.<ref name=":32"/><ref name=":42"/> The application process differs depending on each of the 2 primary funding streams, with Community Efficiency Financing (CEF) projects requiring a two-stage process and Sustainable Affordable Housing (SAH) projects allowing continuous application intake.<ref name=":32" /> The GMF is structured to provide financial and technical support to municipalities working toward sustainability and environmental resilience.<ref name=":82">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2017-01-13 |title=NRCan 2017-18 Departmental Plan - Green Municipal Fund (GMF) |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/corporate/planning-reporting/departmental-plan/nrcan-2017-18-departmental-plan/green-municipal-fund-gmf |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref name=":42" />

==== R-2000 & EnerGuide ====
[https://natural-resources.canada.ca/corporate Natural Resources Canada (NRCan)] implemented the voluntary [[R-2000 program|'''R-2000 Home Program''']] 1982 service organizations and certified professionals across the country to enhance [[Building code|construction building codes]] to increase energy efficiency and promote sustainability.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Mayo |first1=Tim |last2=Sinha |first2=Robin |date=1997-07-01 |title=R-2000 and Advanced Houses: The Canadian Experience |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/109719639702100108 |journal=Journal of Thermal Insulation and Building Envelopes |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=91–111 |doi=10.1177/109719639702100108 |issn=1065-2744|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2018-02-02 |title=R-2000: environmentally friendly homes |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/r-2000-environmentally-friendly-homes |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>  Homes meeting the standard must comply with energy performance requirements that go beyond conventional building codes, with a focus on air quality, insulation, and efficiency in heating and cooling systems.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2018-02-05 |title=Details of the R-2000 Standard |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/details-r-2000-standard |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Trends |first=Canadian Home |date=2011-01-12 |title=What exactly is an R-2000* certified home and what are the benefits of building one? |url=https://canadianhometrends.com/what-exactly-is-an-r-2000-certified-home-and-what-are-the-benefits-of-building-one/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Home Trends Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=R-2000 AND ENERGUIDE |url=https://chbanl.ca/r-2000-and-energuide/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Canadian Home Builders’ Association of Newfoundland and Labrador |language=en-CA}}</ref> The program has been updated several times to reflect changes in building science and technology.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Mayo |first1=Tim |last2=Sinha |first2=Robin |date=1997-07-01 |title=R-2000 and Advanced Houses: The Canadian Experience |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/109719639702100108 |journal=Journal of Thermal Insulation and Building Envelopes |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=91–111 |doi=10.1177/109719639702100108 |issn=1065-2744|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":22">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2018-02-02 |title=R-2000: environmentally friendly homes |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/r-2000-environmentally-friendly-homes |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref> In 1995, technical requirements were advised to lower energy consumption targets and introduce indoor air quality and environmental considerations.<ref name=":13" /> Further updates, such as those in 2012, incorporate stricter energy efficiency measures and additional performance criteria like and not limited to enhanced air tightness, improved ventilation systems, stringent insulation requirements, advanced window performance.<ref name=":22" /><ref name=":52">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2018-02-05 |title=Details of the R-2000 Standard |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/details-r-2000-standard |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

A feature that functions alongside  the R-2000 home program to assess its efficiency is the [[EnerGuide]] rating service.<ref name=":62">{{Cite web |title=R-2000 AND ENERGUIDE |url=https://chbanl.ca/r-2000-and-energuide/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Canadian Home Builders’ Association of Newfoundland and Labrador |language=en-CA}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=R-2000 AND ENERGUIDE |url=https://chbanl.ca/r-2000-and-energuide/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Canadian Home Builders’ Association of Newfoundland and Labrador |language=en-CA}}</ref> This service is available across Canada, allows home builders and home buyers to measure and rate the performance of their homes, and confirm that those specifications have been met.<ref name=":62" /><ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Finn |first=Noah |date=2012-01-03 |title=EnerGuide: Understanding Home Energy Ratings {{!}} Alleguard Foam Solutions |url=https://alleguard.com/insights/energuide-understanding-home-energy-ratings/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Alleguard |language=en-US}}</ref>

Regional initiatives based on R-2000 include [[Energy Star]] for New Homes, Built Green, Novoclimat, GreenHome, [[Power Smart]] for New Homes, and GreenHouse.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Certification |url=https://www.builtgreen.net/certification |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=www.builtgreen.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2016-07-07 |title=Energy efficiency housing initiatives |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-housing-initiatives |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Groupe ecoPlus {{!}} Novoclimat Program |url=https://www.servicesecoplus.ca/en/energy-efficiency-audits-for-houses/novoclimat-program/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Services ecoPlus |language=en-CA}}</ref><ref name=":92"/>

== Green Architecture and Design Practices In Canada ==

=== Sustainable Building Materials ===
Sustainable building materials are increasingly used in Canadian architecture to reduce environmental impact and improve energy efficiency.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Raemy |first=Fabian |date=2024-03-06 |title=16 Sustainable Building Materials For Your Next Construction Project |url=https://greenbuildingcanada.ca/sustainable-building-materials/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=greenbuildingcanada.ca |language=en-CA}}</ref> These materials are selected based on factors such as low embodied carbon, recyclability, energy performance, and local availability.<ref name=":10" /> Common materials include reclaimed wood, recycled steel, hempcrete, cork, bamboo, and high-efficiency insulation products, which help minimize resource extraction and landfill waste.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Startritehomes |date=2025-02-23 |title=Top Environmentally Friendly Building Materials for Energy-Efficient Homes in Canada |url=https://www.startritehomes.com/post/top-environmentally-friendly-building-materials-for-energy-efficient-homes-in-canada |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=StartRiteHomes |language=en}}</ref>

[[Adaptive reuse]] of existing buildings is also a growing practice in Canadian green architecture, as it conserves materials, reduces demolition waste, and preserves the [[embodied energy]] in older structures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berthold |first1=Étienne |last2=Pawliw |first2=Kim |last3=Righi |first3=Sarah |date=2025-05-13 |title=Built Religious Heritage, Circular Economy, and Life-Cycle Assessment: A Case Study of a Convent Property in the Province of Quebec, Canada |journal=Energies |language=en |volume=18 |issue=10 |pages=2512 |doi=10.3390/en18102512 |doi-access=free |issn=1996-1073 }}</ref>

Designers are also exploring newer alternatives such as wood-based panels, [[magnesium oxide]] boards, and bio-based products to support healthier indoor air quality and building durability.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trusscore |title=The Ultimate Guide to Sustainable Building Materials in 2024 |url=https://trusscore.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-sustainable-building-materials-in-2024.html |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=Trusscore |language=en}}</ref> The growth of sustainable construction practices is being driven by shifting consumer expectations, regulatory changes, and increased awareness of climate-related risks.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-12 |title=Envisioning the Future: Sustainable Construction Practices in Canada |url=https://www.executrade.com/news/post/envisioning-the-future-sustainable-construction-practices-in-canada |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.executrade.com |language=en}}</ref> Canadian firms are also responding to trends like prefabrication and modular design, which support waste reduction and improved material efficiency.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-01 |title=Canada Sustainable Building Materials Trends |url=https://constructive-voices.com/canada-sustainable-building-materials-trends/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Smith-Edgell |first=Aidan |date=2023-10-31 |title=Mapping Canada's New Greenprint with Sustainable Building Materials - RBC Thought Leadership |url=https://thoughtleadership.rbc.com/mapping-canadas-new-greenprint-with-sustainable-building-materials/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241207170311/https://thoughtleadership.rbc.com/mapping-canadas-new-greenprint-with-sustainable-building-materials/ |archive-date=2024-12-07 |access-date=2025-05-02 |work=RBC Thought Leadership |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Passive Design Strategies ===
Passive design strategies are increasingly used in Canadian architecture to enhance building performance and reduce [[energy consumption]] by leveraging climate-responsive features.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-13 |title=Passive Design: Natural Heating and Cooling for Sustainable Living - CMI Group Inc. |url=https://www.cmigroupinc.ca/passive-design/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |language=en-US}}</ref> Architects often orient buildings to maximize [[solar gain]] in winter and minimize overheating in summer through shading and window placement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Building Orientation for Optimum Energy |url=https://www.nachi.org/building-orientation-optimum-energy.htm |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.nachi.org |language=en}}</ref> High-performance insulation, airtight construction, and [[thermal mass]] are integrated into designs to maintain indoor comfort without heavy reliance on mechanical systems.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2014-03-06 |title=Keeping The Heat In - Section 8: Upgrading windows and exterior doors |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/home-energy-efficiency/keeping-heat-section-8-upgrading-windows-exterior-doors |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

In coastal or temperate regions, passive ventilation and natural cooling techniques are used to address humidity and airflow concerns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Passive Design Architecture Examples Around the World (2025) |url=https://www.novatr.com/blog/passive-design-architecture-examples |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.novatr.com |language=en-in}}</ref> These strategies are large factor to net-zero energy building design in Canada, where the goal is to minimize energy demand and meet the remaining energy needs through renewable sources such as [[Solar panel|solar panels.]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Net Zero Projects and Programs |url=https://www.chba.ca/net-zero-projects-and-programs/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=Canadian Home Builders' Association |language=en-US}}</ref> Architects incorporating passive design principles aim to align with national and provincial standards promoting energy-efficient and low-carbon construction across diverse Canadian climates.<ref name=":14" />

== Canadian Green Building Certification Programs ==

=== [https://www.cagbc.org/our-work/certification/leed/ LEED Canada] ===
[[Canada Green Building Council|The Canada Green Building Council]] (CaGBC), established in 2002, obtained a license from the U.S. Green Building Council in 2003 to adapt [[LEED]] for use in Canada.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=USGBC |url=https://www.usgbc.org/resources/leed-motion-canada |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.usgbc.org |language=en}}</ref> This adaptation built on earlier Canadian efforts such as BREEAM-Canada, introduced in 1996 by the [[CSA Group|Canadian Standards Association]], which helped shape the early structure and credit categories of the original LEED system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History Of Green Building Rating Systems In Canada|url=https://www.canadianconsultingengineer.com/features/history-of-green-building-rating-systems-in-canada/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=[[Canadian Consulting Engineer]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

LEED certification in Canada evaluates buildings based on several criteria, including [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]], [[water conservation]], indoor environmental quality, and sustainable materials.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Employment and Social Development |date=2010-04-01 |title=Leadership In Energy And Environmental Design (Leed) And Green Globes Design Buildings |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/news/archive/2010/04/leadership-energy-environmental-design-leed-green-globes-design-buildings.html |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> Projects are awarded certification at one of four levels—Certified, Silver, Gold, or Platinum—based on the number of points achieved within the rating system.<ref name=":4" /> Certification is available for a variety of building types, such as new construction, existing buildings, commercial interiors, and residential homes.

The CaGBC continues to oversee LEED certification in Canada and maintains resources and guidance tailored to local building codes and climate considerations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=LEED |url=https://www.cagbc.org/our-work/certification/leed/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=Canada Green Building Council (CAGBC) |language=en-CA}}</ref> Canada remains one of the most active countries outside the United States for LEED-certified space.<ref name=":3" />

=== [https://bomabest.org/ BOMA BEST] ===
BOMA BEST (Building Environmental Standards) is a national certification program administered by BOMA Canada that evaluates the environmental performance and management of existing buildings in Canada.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=BOMA BEST - Sustainable & Smart Building Certification Program |url=https://bomabest.org/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=BOMA BEST - English |language=en-US}}</ref> Introduced in 2005 as a replacement for the Go Green and Go Green Plus programs, the initiative provides a framework for assessing sustainability practices across multiple building types, including offices, retail spaces, industrial sites, and multi-unit residential buildings.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |date=2023-12-21 |title=A guide to Canadian green building standards and certifications |url=https://www.bdc.ca/en/articles-tools/sustainability/climate-action-centre/articles/leed-energy-star-boma-best-more-guide-to-canadian-green-building-standards-certifications |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=BDC.ca |language=en}}</ref>

The program certifies buildings at five levels—Baseline, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum—based on a building’s compliance with best practices and performance across categories such as energy, water, waste, emissions, and occupant well-being.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Five Levels of Certification |url=https://bomabestfieldguide.org/user-manual/about-levels-of-certification/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=BOMA Field Guide - English |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2023, BOMA Canada launched BOMA BEST Sustainable 4.0 and BOMA BEST Smart, reflecting updated priorities such as decarbonization, health, and digital integration.<ref name=":7" />

As of 2024, thousands of buildings across Canada have received BOMA BEST certification, making it one of the country’s most widely used environmental assessment programs for existing buildings.<ref name=":9" />

=== BREEAM ===
'''[[BREEAM]]''' (Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method) is one of the world's oldest green building certification systems, originally developed in the United Kingdom in 1990 by the [[Building Research Establishment]] (BRE).<ref>{{Cite web |title=About BREEAM |url=https://breeam.com/about |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=BREEAM |language=en-GB}}</ref> Although it is not a Canadian-specific program, BREEAM has influenced the development of Canadian standards and has been used selectively for projects in Canada, particularly for clients with global portfolios or in partnership with international developers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=courtney.senior |date=2023-12-12 |title=Green Building Certification in Canada: A Comprehensive Guide |url=https://connectedsensors.com/blog/green-building-certification/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |language=en-US}}</ref>

BREEAM evaluates buildings across several sustainability categories, including energy, water, materials, pollution, waste, and management practices.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The BREEAM Rating System explained |url=https://www.cim.io/blog/the-breeam-rating-system-explained |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.cim.io |language=en}}</ref> The system assigns ratings ranging from Pass to Outstanding, based on a point-based assessment tailored to building type and project goals. While not as widely adopted in Canada as LEED or BOMA BEST, BREEAM remains a globally recognized benchmark that supports the design and operation of high-performing green buildings.<ref>{{Cite web |last=College |first=Brighton |date=2024-02-18 |title=Canadian Green Building Certifications Explained {{!}} Brighton |url=https://brightoncollege.com/blog/canadian-green-building-certifications-explained/ |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=Brighton College |language=en-CA}}</ref>

==Notable green buildings==
* [[VanDusen Botanical Garden|VanDusen Botanical Garden Visitor Centre]]
* Beamish-Munro Hall at [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] features sustainable construction methods such as high fly-ash concrete, triple-glazed windows, dimmable fluorescent lights and a grid-tied photovoltaic array.
* Gene H. Kruger Pavilion<ref>[https://www.ulaval.ca/en/node/245 "Gene-H.-Kruger Building | Université Laval]". ''www.ulaval.ca''. Retrieved 2025-02-25.</ref> at [[Laval University]] uses largely nonpolluting, nontoxic, recycled and [[renewable material]]s as well as advanced bioclimatic concepts that reduce energy consumption by 25% compared with a concrete building of the same dimensions. The structure of the building is made entirely out of wood products, thus further reducing the environmental impact of the building.
* The [[Greenstone Building]], which houses federal government offices in [[Yellowknife]], capital of the [[Northwest Territories]], became the first LEED Gold certified building in [[Northern Canada]] in 2007.<ref name="Daily Commercial News story">{{cite news|title=Yellowknife's Greenstone Government of Canada building receives LEED Gold standard|url=http://dailycommercialnews.com/Projects/News/2007/8/Yellowknifes-Greenstone-Government-of-Canada-building-receives-LEED-Gold-standard-DCN024198W/|newspaper=[[Daily Commercial News]]|date=August 30, 2007|accessdate=September 9, 2015}}</ref>
* The [[City of Calgary Water Centre]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.calgary.ca/watercentre |title=Water Centre |access-date=2009-11-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100109123346/http://www.calgary.ca/watercentre/ |archive-date=2010-01-09 |url-status=dead }}</ref> officially opened June 4, 2008 at the Manchester Centre with a minimum Green Building Council of Canada’s Gold LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) level certification. The {{convert|183000|sqft|m2|adj=on}} [[office]] building is 95 per cent day lit, conserves energy and water and fosters a productive, healthy environment for visitors and employees alike.
* Rodeo Fine Homes<ref>[https://www.thestar.com/article/586211 Rodeo Fine Homes]</ref> development in Newmarket, Ontario is first in Canada to be built entirely to LEED platinum eco-standard. The 34 homes in the EcoLogic development by Rodeo Fine Homes will use at least 50 per cent less water, have 35 per cent fewer discharge flows and generate 60 per cent less solid waste, greenhouse gas production and energy consumption than conventional homes. Local suppliers are featured, such as [[Forest Stewardship Council]] certified lumber from Kott Lumber in Stouffville and Mississauga cabinet manufacturer Aya produced the urea formaldehyde-free EVO [[cabinetry]].

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Green home

{{Short description|Type of house designed to be environmentally sustainable}}
{{AI-generated|date=August 2025}}
[[File:2009-07-22 Green home at 930 W Markham Ave 4.jpg|thumb|An example of a green home design that is energy-efficient and has a sloped roof to divert rainwater for collection]]
{{Climate change and society|Economics/Finance}}
[[File:Green Mokotow Housing, Warsaw.jpg|thumb|Green housing located in Warsaw, Poland.]]
A '''green home''' is a type of [[house]] designed to be [[Sustainability|environmentally sustainable]]. Green homes focus on the efficient use of "[[Low-energy house|energy]], [[Water conservation|water]], and [[Sustainable architecture|building materials]]".<ref>{{cite book |title=Good green homes |last=Roberts |first=Jennifer |year=2003 |publisher=Gibbs Smith |isbn= 9781423612056|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x6puyqEok3YC&q=%22Green+home%22 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref> A green home may use sustainably sourced, environmentally friendly, and/or recycled building materials. This includes materials like [[Reclaimed lumber|reclaimed wood]], [[Scrap|recycled metal]], and low [[Volatile Organic Compound|VOC (volatile organic compound)]] paints. Additionally, green homes often prioritize [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] by incorporating features, such as high-performance [[Building insulation|insulation]], energy-efficient [[Major appliance|appliances]], and [[Home automation|smart home]] technologies that monitor and optimize energy usage. [[Water conservation]] is another important aspect, with green homes often featuring water-saving fixtures, [[rainwater harvesting]] systems, and [[Greywater|grey water]] recycling systems to reduce water waste. It may include [[sustainable energy]] sources such as [[Solar energy|solar]] or [[Geothermal energy|geothermal]], and be sited to take maximum advantage of natural features such as sunlight and tree cover to improve [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]]. 

==Elements==
No government standards define what constitutes a green remodel, beyond non-profit certification. In general, a green home is a house that is built or remodeled in order to conserve "energy or water; improve [[indoor air quality]]; use sustainable, recycled or used materials; and produce less waste in the process." This may include buying more [[Efficient energy use|energy-efficient]] [[Home appliance|appliances]] or employing building materials that are more efficient in managing temperature.<ref>{{cite news |title=Green home remodeling still a gray area |author=Jennifer Alsever |newspaper=[[NBC News]] |date=June 5, 2007
|url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/18560189 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131226233438/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/18560189/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 26, 2013 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref>

A green home often incorporates design elements that maximize [[Daylighting (architecture)|natural lighting]] and ventilation, reducing the need for artificial lighting and HVAC systems. Additionally, sustainable landscaping practices, such as [[Natural landscaping|native plantings]] and [[rainwater harvesting]] systems, can further enhance the eco-friendliness of the property. Integration of renewable energy sources like [[Solar panel|solar panels]] can also contribute to the overall sustainability of the home, reducing reliance on non-renewable energy sources and decreasing [[greenhouse gas emissions]]. In essence, a green home strives to minimize its environmental impact throughout its lifecycle, from construction to daily operation and eventual disposal or repurposing of materials.

==History==

=== United States ===
In the United States, the [[green building]] movement began in the 1970s, after the [[price of oil]] began to increase sharply. In response, researchers began to look into more energy efficient systems. 
Nevertheless, individuals required persistence to navigate the bewildering array of incomplete and imperfect information that was the wilderness frontier of what is now known as green building. In 1999, Richard and Katherine Homan began building Dallas, Texas' first comprehensive green home.
<ref>
East Kessler neighbor honored for ‘first comprehensive green home’ in Dallas
[https://oakcliff.advocatemag.com/2012/02/east-kessler-neighbor-honored-for-first-comprehensive-green-home-in-dallas/ Accessed Jun 28, 2022]
</ref>
It took until 2012 for the city to issue a proclamation for having the city's first comprehensive green home.

Many organizations were founded in the 1990s to promote green buildings. Some organizations worked to improve consumer knowledge so that they could have more green homes. The [[International Code Council]] and the [[National Association of Home Builders]] began working in 2006 to create a "voluntary green home building standard".<ref>{{cite book |title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to Green Building and Remodeling |last=Queen |first=Bill |author2=Lori Hall Steele |author3=John Barrows |author4=Lisa Iannucci  |year=2009 |publisher=Penguin |isbn= 9781440658518|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YB4ADAMeqIAC&q=%22Green+home%22&pg=PT24 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref>

The [[Energy Policy Act of 2005|Energy Policy Act]] was enacted in 2005, which allowed tax reductions for homeowners who could show the use of energy efficient changes to their homes, such as [[solar panel]]s and other solar-powered devices.<ref>{{cite news |title=Groundbreaking Green Home Tax Breaks |author=Matt Woolsey |newspaper=[[Forbes]] |date=March 7, 2007 |url=https://www.forbes.com/2007/03/06/tax-green-credit-forbeslife-cx_mw_0307greencredits.html |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref>

== Certifications ==
Various types of certifications certify a home as a green home. 

=== United States ===
'''[[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED]]:''' The [[U.S. Green Building Council]] has a green certification titled [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design]].<ref>{{cite news |author=Janet Frankston |date=April 10, 2004 |title=Some buyers will pay more for 'green' home |url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/chicagotribune/access/614276091.html?dids=614276091:614276091&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Apr+10%2C+2004&author=Janet+Frankston%2C+Atlanta+Journal&pub=Chicago+Tribune&desc=Some+buyers+will+pay+more+for+%27green%27+home&pqatl=google |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130201003256/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/chicagotribune/access/614276091.html?dids=614276091:614276091&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Apr+10,+2004&author=Janet+Frankston,+Atlanta+Journal&pub=Chicago+Tribune&desc=Some+buyers+will+pay+more+for+'green'+home&pqatl=google |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 1, 2013 |access-date=November 27, 2010 |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] }}</ref> The factors that it considers include "the site location, use of energy and water, incorporation of healthier building and insulation materials, recycling, use of renewable energy, and protection of natural resources".<ref>{{cite book |last=Streep |first=Meryl |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hM_Z7iynmSQC&q=%22Green+home%22&pg=PA289 |title=Green guide: the complete reference for consuming wisely |publisher=National Geographic Books |year=2008 |isbn=9781426202766 |page=290 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref> LEED offers a specific certification track for residential buildings, known as LEED for Homes. This program assesses the environmental performance of single-family homes, multifamily buildings, and mixed-use developments, considering factors such as location, water efficiency, materials selection, and indoor air quality.<ref>Green Building Council. "LEED for Homes: Reference Guide for Green Building Design and Construction." USGBC, 2021.</ref>

'''Model Green Home Building Guidelines:''' The US [[National Association of Home Builders]] independently created its Model Green Home Building Guidelines as a type of certification, along with programs for utilities.<ref>{{cite book |last=Yudelson |first=Jerry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4s8OMWoO00QC&q=%22Green+home%22&pg=PA133 |title=The green building revolution |author2=S. Richard Fedrizzi |publisher=Island Press |year=2008 |isbn=9781597267632 |page=60 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Dennis |first=Lori |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PdDxCc5aUKAC&q=%22Green+home%22&pg=PT16 |title=Green Interior Design |publisher=Random House, Inc. |year=2010 |isbn=9781581157741 |access-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref>

'''[[ENERGY STAR]]:''' In the United States, the ENERGY STAR program, administered by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)]], certifies homes that meet stringent energy efficiency standards. ENERGY STAR-certified homes are designed to use less energy for heating, cooling, and water heating, resulting in lower utility bills and reduced greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>Environmental Protection Agency. "Energy Star Home Advisor: A Guide to Energy-Efficient Homes." EPA, 2020.</ref>

'''Passive House:''' The [[Passive_house#Passive_House_standards_in_the_US_-_Passive_House_Standard_and_PHIUS+|Passive House Institute and Passive House Institute US (PHIUS+)]] standards focus on designing and constructing ultra-low energy buildings that require very little energy for heating or cooling. Passive House certification requires rigorous adherence to specific energy performance criteria, including airtightness, high-quality insulation, and mechanical ventilation with heat recovery.<ref>Miller, David. "The Passive House: A Complete Guide to Passive House Design and Construction." Routledge, 2018.</ref>

=== International ===
'''[[Living Building Challenge]]:''' This certification program, administered by the International Living Future Institute, goes beyond traditional green building standards by emphasizing regenerative design principles. Buildings certified under the Living Building Challenge must meet strict criteria related to energy, water, materials, equity, and beauty, and must demonstrate net-positive impacts on the environment and community.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

'''[[BREEAM|BREEAM (Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method)]]:''' Originating in the United Kingdom, BREEAM is a widely recognized green building certification system used internationally. It assesses the environmental performance of buildings based on criteria such as energy and water use, materials selection, waste management, and ecological impact.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Karolinski |first=Brian |date=2024 |title=Certificated Green Home in Varna, Bulgaria |url=https://www.greenhomebg.com/ |access-date=December 10, 2024 |website=GreenHomebg.com}}</ref>

=== Australia ===
'''[[Green Star (Australia)|Green Star]]:''' Green Star is an Australian sustainability rating system for buildings and communities, developed by the Green Building Council of Australia. It evaluates the environmental attributes of buildings across categories such as energy efficiency, indoor environmental quality, transport, and innovation.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

=== India ===
'''IGBC-Certified Green Home''' The Indian Green Building Council (IGBC), part of the [[Confederation of Indian Industry]] was formed in the year 2001. The council offers a wide array of services that include developing new green building rating programmes, certification services and green building training programs.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

'''Climate Smart Homes'''

Climate Smart Homes is Housing initiative developed by ''B.H.R.T. Infra Private Limited'' These homes are designed for sustainable living, countering the challenges posed by climate change on housing and residents, such as heatwaves and cold waves, while promoting energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. India's first Climate Smart Home is located in Ludhiana, Punjab on a 20-by-50-foot east-facing plot, with a total built-up area of 2,500 square feet. The design incorporates Vastu Shastra principles and is specifically tailored to India's Composite Climatic Zone, utilizing government data on weather patterns and temperature trends.
[[File:B.H.R.T. Infra Climate Smart Home.jpg|thumb|Climate smart home built by B.H.R.T. Infra]]


'''Features'''

Climate Smart Homes incorporate various design features intended to adapt to India's diverse climate zones and mitigate the impacts of extreme weather. Key characteristics include:

# '''Climatic Zone Adaptation''': Tailored to India's geographical and climatic diversity, these homes factor in site-specific conditions and anticipated climatic changes.
# '''Thermal Protection''': The homes utilize construction materials with low thermal conductivity, featuring walls and roofs with U-values of 0.175 W/m<sup>2</sup>K and 0.235 W/m<sup>2</sup>K, respectively, to reduce energy consumption and thermal stress.
# '''UV Ray Mitigation''': Orientation-specific designs are used to block ultraviolet rays, contributing to healthier indoor environments.
# '''Natural Ventilation and Daylight''': Techniques such as cross ventilation, stack ventilation, and strategic window placement enhance airflow and natural lighting, reducing dependence on mechanical systems.

'''Health and Environmental Benefits'''

The initiative aims to address both human health and environmental sustainability. Key benefits include:

* Improved indoor comfort during extreme temperatures through thermally efficient roofs and walls.
* Enhanced natural lighting to support Vitamin D synthesis and reduce reliance on artificial lighting.

* Water-efficient systems that conserve resources while promoting sustainability.

'''Impacts on Health'''

Climate Smart Homes are designed to mitigate health risks associated with extreme weather. These include:

* Reducing heat-related conditions such as dehydration and heatstroke.
* Minimizing cardiovascular and respiratory stress during extreme weather.
* Alleviating mental health challenges associated with climatic stress through improved living conditions.

'''Broader Context'''

The Climate Smart Homes initiative aligns with national programs such as ''Make in India'' and ''Atmanirbhar Bharat'', and contributes to India's Vision 2047 and global climate goals. The project is led by Taniksh Gaur Verma, who has certifications in climate change from the United Nations. The initiative seeks to promote sustainable and resilient housing for all sectors of society.

== Global examples ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2024}}
'''Earthship Biotecture (Taos, New Mexico, USA):''' [[Earthship|Earthships]] are a unique type of sustainable home pioneered by architect Michael Reynolds. These homes are built using recycled materials such as tires, bottles, and cans, and they utilize passive solar heating, natural ventilation, and rainwater harvesting systems to achieve off-grid living. The thick walls made of rammed earth or tires provide excellent thermal mass, helping to regulate indoor temperatures year-round. Earthships often incorporate greenhouse spaces for food production, further enhancing their self-sufficiency and sustainability.

'''The Zero Carbon House (Birmingham, UK):''' The Zero Carbon House, also known as the 'Balsall Heath House,' is an innovative example of sustainable retrofitting. Originally a Victorian terraced house, with [[wythe|double-wythe]] solid-brick walls (i.e. no [[cavity wall]]s), it was transformed into a zero-carbon dwelling through extensive renovation and the integration of energy-efficient technologies. The house features high levels of insulation, triple-glazed windows, airtight construction with mechanical ventilation heat recovery, and rooftop solar panels for renewable energy generation. It also incorporates passive design principles to minimize energy demand while maximizing comfort for occupants — achieving a fifth of the heat demand of 3 kWh/m<sup>2</sup>.year against a Passivhaus standard of 15 kWh/m<sup>2</sup>.year. The Zero Carbon House serves as a model for reducing carbon emissions in existing urban housing stock.<ref>UK Green Building Council [https://ukgbc.org/resources/zero-carbon-house-birmingham/]</ref><ref>Zero Carbon House Birmingham [https://zerocarbonhousebirmingham.org.uk/]</ref>

'''The [[Bosco Verticale|Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest)]] (Milan, Italy):''' The Bosco Verticale is a pair of residential towers designed by Stefano Boeri Architects. What makes these buildings unique is their extensive greenery, with thousands of trees and shrubs planted on balconies at every level. The vegetation helps to absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, filter pollutants, and regulate indoor temperatures, reducing the buildings' environmental impact and enhancing urban biodiversity. The Bosco Verticale demonstrates how high-density urban living can be combined with nature to create sustainable and aesthetically pleasing living spaces.
