{{Climate change and society|Economics/Finance}}

[[File:Passive house in La Crosse.jpg|thumb|Passive house developed by [[Western Technical College]] in [[La Crosse, Wisconsin]]<ref>{{cite web | title=24th St. Passive House by Intep | url=https://www.intep.us/24th-street-passive-house |website=Intep.us |access-date=2026-06-23 }}</ref>]]

'''Passive house''' or '''{{lang|de|Passivhaus}}''' is a voluntary building performance standard designed to have high [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] and [[thermal comfort]] while substantially reduces a building’s [[carbon footprint]].<ref name="NYT-2010.09.25">{{cite news |last=Zeller |first=Tom Jr. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/26/business/energy-environment/26smart.html?_r=1&ref=earth&pagewanted=all |title=Beyond Fossil Fuels: Can We Build in a Brighter Shade of Green? |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 26, 2010 |page=BU1}}</ref> Buildings certified to the standard are [[Low-energy house|ultra-low energy]] and typically require very little energy for [[space heating]] or cooling.<ref name="NYT-2010.09.25b">{{cite news |last1=Gröndahl |first1=Mika |last2=Gates |first2=Guilbert |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2010/09/26/business/smart.html?ref=energy-environment |title=The Secrets of a Passive House |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 25, 2010 |access-date=September 27, 2010}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite web |url=https://passiv.de/en/02_informations/02_passive-house-requirements/02_passive-house-requirements.htm |title=Passive House requirements |publisher=Passive House Institute |access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref> The approach is used for housing and for non-residential buildings such as offices, schools, kindergartens and healthcare facilities. Energy efficiency is integral to [[architectural design]] rather than an add-on.<ref name="plainiotis">{{cite book |title=Design for Sustainability |first1=Yan |last1=Ji |first2=Stellios |last2=Plainiotis |year=2006 |location=Beijing |publisher=China Architecture and Building Press |isbn=978-7-112-08390-9}}</ref> Although most common in new construction, the principles are also applied in deep renovations.

{{As of|2025|1|post=,}} projects certified by the Passive House Institute (PHI) comprise over 47,400 units with about {{convert|4.32|e6m²|e6sqft|abbr=unit}} of treated floor area (TFA) worldwide; the public PHI database lists nearly 6,000 projects.<ref>{{cite web |title=Passive House building certification data: over 4 million m² worldwide |url=https://passivehousecal.org/passive-house-building-certification-data-over-4-million-square-meters-worldwide-passive-house-institute/ |publisher=Passive House California |date=February 15, 2025 |access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref> In [[North America]], the Passive House Institute US (PHIUS) reported over 500 certified projects in total and around {{convert|1.6|e6sqft|m²|abbr=unit}} certified in 2024 alone, with {{convert|4.4|e6sqft|m²|abbr=unit}} design-certified that year.<ref>{{cite web |title=2024 Annual Report |url=https://www.phius.org/sites/default/files/2025-04/2024%20Annual%20Report%20v2.pdf |publisher=Passive House Institute US |date=April 2025 |access-date=2025-09-26 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The World We Want: Taking Stock and Looking Ahead (2025) |url=https://www.phius.org/world-we-want-taking-stock-and-looking-ahead |publisher=Passive House Institute US |date=January 10, 2025 |access-date=2025-09-26 }}</ref> While early adoption concentrated in [[List of countries and territories where German is an official language|German-speaking countries]] and [[Scandinavia]], certified projects are now documented across diverse climate zones, including hot-humid and tropical regions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Passive House in the Global South |url=https://passipedia.org/basics/passive_houses_in_different_climates/passive_house_in_the_global_south |website=Passipedia |date=August 13, 2025 |access-date=2025-09-26 }}</ref>

==History==
{{multiple image
 | width=150
 | image1=Bo Adamson.jpg
 | caption1=Bo Adamson, co-originator of the passive house concept
 | image2=Wolfgang Feist.jpg
 | caption2=Wolfgang Feist, co-originator and founder of the [[Passivhaus-Institut]] (PHI) in Germany
}}

The term ''passive house'' was originally used in the 1970s for buildings emphasizing passive solar strategies. Since the 1990s, the term has instead referred to buildings that meeting specific quantified PHI certification criteria (space conditioning, primary energy, airtightness and comfort requirements).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ürge-Vorsatz |first1=Diana |last2=Khosla |first2=Radhika |last3=Bernhardt |first3=Rob |last4=Chan |first4=Yi Chieh |last5=Vérez |first5=David |last6=Hu |first6=Shan |last7=Cabeza |first7=Luisa F. |date=2020-10-17 |title=Advances Toward a Net-Zero Global Building Sector |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=227–269 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-012420-045843 |hdl=10459.1/69710 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The standard originated from a 1988 discussion between Bo Adamson (Lund University) and Wolfgang Feist (then at the Institute for Housing and Environment, [[Darmstadt]]), followed by research supported by the state of [[Hesse]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.iwu.de/1/home/ |title=Institute for Housing and the Environment |access-date=2017-12-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171212084308/http://www.iwu.de/1/home/ |archive-date=2017-12-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Feist |first=Wolfgang |date=September 2006 |title=15th Anniversary of the Darmstadt-Kranichstein Passive House |url=http://www.passivhaustagung.de/Kran/First_Passive_House_Kranichstein_en.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714052350/http://www.passivhaustagung.de/Kran/First_Passive_House_Kranichstein_en.html |archive-date=2014-07-14 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref> Passive solar strategies are not required, although they often form part of the approach to meet the certification criteria.

North American “superinsulation” pioneers of the 1970s (e.g., the [[Saskatchewan Conservation House]] and the Leger House) provided important technical precedents, including [[Heat recovery ventilation|heat-recovery ventilation]] and airtightness testing.<ref>{{Cite web|date=March 27, 2018 |title=How Saskatchewan Pioneered Energy-Efficient Housing and Influenced Building Standards |url=https://www.src.sk.ca/blog/how-saskatchewan-pioneered-energy-efficient-houses-and-influenced-building-standards |website=Saskatchewan Research Council}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=September 22, 2010|title=History of Super-insulated Housing in North America|url=https://bcbec.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/5-History-of-Superinsulation-Compatibility-Mode.pdf|website=British Columbia Building Envelope Council}}</ref>

=== Examples ===
Four terraced houses in [[Darmstadt-Kranichstein]] (1990–1991) are widely cited as the first built to what became the Passive House standard.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273766969_The_world's_first_Passive_House_Darmstadt-Kranichstein_Germany|title=The world’s first Passive House, Darmstadt-Kranichstein, Germany|website=Researchgate.net|format=PDF|access-date=June 23, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=The world's first Passive House, Darmstadt-Kranichstein, Germany|website=Passipedia.org| url=https://passipedia.org/examples/residential_buildings/multi-family_buildings/central_europe/the_world_s_first_passive_house_darmstadt-kranichstein_germany }}</ref>[[File:Schiestlhaus Jul2007.jpg|thumb|right|The {{ill|Schiestlhaus|de}} (Austria, 2005), first high-alpine passive house]]
[[File:Passivhaus Darmstadt Kranichstein Fruehling 2006.JPG|thumb|A passive house building in [[Darmstadt]], Germany]]
The [[Passivhaus-Institut]] (PHI) was founded in 1996 in Darmstadt to develop, promote and certify buildings under to the standard. By 2010 it was estimated that over 25,000 Passive House buildings existed worldwide.<ref name="NYT-2010.09.25" /><ref name='NYT'>{{cite news |first=Elisabeth 
|last=Rosenthal |title=Houses With No Furnace but Plenty of Heat |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/27/world/europe/27house.html?ref=world&pagewanted=all|newspaper=The New York Times |date=December 26, 2008 |access-date=December 27, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.passivhaustagung.de/elfte/english/01_start_home.html |title=11th International Conference on Passive Houses, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081231014027/http://www.passivhaustagung.de/elfte/english/01_start_home.html |archive-date=2008-12-31 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref>

The standard has since been applied to-large scale developments. [[Gaobeidian]], [[China]], hosts what is reported as the world’s largest Passive House development (Railway City), with several hundred thousand m² of certified area built in phases since 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.treehugger.com/green-architecture/chinese-city-has-largest-passive-house-project-world.html|title=Chinese city has the largest Passive House project in the world|website=Treehugger|date=October 24, 2019|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Gaobeidian Railway City|url=https://loopdesignawards.com/project/gaobeidian-railway-city/|website=Loop Design Awards|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref> The {{convert|88|m|ft|adj=on}} tower in [[Bilbao]], [[Spain]] (2018), is the world's tallest certified Passive House building.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bolueta in Bilbao, Spain, is now the tallest Passive House building in the world|url=https://prismpub.com/bolueta-in-bilbao-spain-is-now-the-tallest-passive-house-building-in-the-world/|website=Prismpub.com|date=October 31, 2018|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Tallest passive building (Passivhaus)|url=https://guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/633179-tallest-passive-building-passivhaus|website=Guinnessworldrecords.com|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref>

In the UK health sector, the Passivhaus-certified Foleshill Health Centre (Coventry, opened 2021) demonstrated substantial energy savings in operation and a replicable delivery model for NHS facilities.<ref>{{cite web|title=Foleshill Health Centre (project profile)|url=https://www.passivhaustrust.org.uk/projects/detail/?cId=122|website=Passivhaus Trust|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Low energy use confirmed at Foleshill Health Centre|url=https://communityhealthpartnerships.co.uk/case-studies/low-energy-use-confirmed-at-foleshill-health-centre/|website=Community Health Partnerships|date=April 27, 2023|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref>

In the United States, Katrin Klingenberg’s 2003 “Smith House” ([[Urbana, Illinois|Urbana, IL]]) contributed to the development of the movement that led to the creation of PHIUS (2007). PHIUS has since certified hundreds of projects; New York City’s Park Avenue Green (2019) was recognized as North America’s largest Passive House affordable housing project at the time.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phius.org/about/mission-history |title=Mission & History |website=Passive House Institute US |access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Park Avenue Green is the largest Passive House building in North America|url=https://www.brightpower.com/projects/park-ave-green/|website=Bright Power|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=North America's largest Passive House affordable housing complex|url=https://archinect.com/news/article/150200885/north-america-s-largest-passive-house-affordable-housing-complex|website=Archinect.com|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref>

More recent examples within the United States can be seen in projects such as the Gallatin Passive House built in 2020 by North River Architecture and Planning in Gallatin, New York.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gallatin passive house {{!}} Phius |url=https://www.phius.org/certified-project-database/gallatin-passive-house |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.phius.org |language=en}}</ref> The Sonoran Desert Passive in Tucson, Arizona which was designed by Brubaker Architects and received its final certification in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sonoran Desert Passive {{!}} Phius |url=https://www.phius.org/certified-project-database/sonoran-desert-passive |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.phius.org |language=en}}</ref> Another example of a passive addition (rather than completely new build or renovation) can be found in the Theresa Passive House designed by Studio Ferme, in Austin, Texas; the project completed construction in 2020 and received it's final certification in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Theresa Passive House {{!}} Phius |url=https://www.phius.org/certified-project-database/theresa-passive-house |access-date=2026-10-13 |website=www.phius.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Standards==
[[File:Passivhaus thermogram gedaemmt ungedaemmt.png|thumb|Thermogram: Passive house (right) vs. conventional building (left)]]

While techniques such as [[superinsulation]] predate the standard, Passive House (PHI) specifies quantitative performance criteria and quality assurance. Key requirements include:<ref name="auto"/>
* Annual space heating (and, in suitable climates, cooling) demand ≤ {{convert|15|kWh/m2/a|abbr=on}} '''or''' peak heat load ≤ {{convert|10|W/m2|abbr=on}}, as calculated with the Passive House Planning Package (PHPP), using local climate data.
* Airtightness: ''n''<sub>50</sub> ≤ 0.6 h⁻¹ at ±50 Pa, measured via a blower-door test.
* Efficient mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (typically ≥75% sensible efficiency).
* Whole-building primary energy/renewable energy limits as defined by PHI (see PHI documentation).

===Passive House Standards in North America===
Two related but distinct Passive House certification systems are used in North America:
* '''PHI''' (Darmstadt): the original international Passive House standard and certification system using PHPP and PHI quality assurance.<ref>{{cite web | title=About| publisher=Passive House Canada | date=5 August 2026<!--from page source-->| url=https://www.passivehousecanada.com/about-passive-house-canada/}}</ref>
* '''PHIUS+''' (Chicago): climate-specific performance targets (CORE/ZERO/REVIVE families) with on-site QA/QC by accredited raters and verifiers; criteria are optimized for carbon and cost within each North American climate zone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Phius Standards|url=https://www.phius.org/standards|website=PHIUS|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=About Phius Alliance Canada | publisher=Phius | url=https://www.phius.org/canada-about | access-date=22 August 2026}}</ref>
The two programs use different energy models and protocols and certify independently.<ref>{{cite web | title=PHI and Phius: What's the Difference? | url=https://passivehousenetwork.org/phi-and-phius/?srsltid=AfmBOoq_mz3qM_6XKYNQm7tx1ZkDkYEgCjl19dh5ZIWNW5PPo-YLe34w|website=Passivehousenetwork.org }}</ref>

==Construction costs==
Passive House building costs vary by market, building type, and the experience of the construction team. Reported cost premiums for Passive House construction over conventional construction have ranged from ~5–10% in Germany, the UK and the US, with reductions noted as supply chains mature.

The specific drivers of building cost and complexity vary, but relative to basic Code-compliant construction, Passive Houses typically include superinsulation of the envelope, requiring greater thickness and complexity of the wall assembly in particular, and particular attention to air, water, and vapour barriers, including at all penetrations. They also include very high performance window and exterior door systems.

Cost premiums are partially offset by downsized or eliminated conventional heating/cooling systems, and lower operating costs over the building life cycle.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.passivehouse-international.org/index.php?page_id=79 |title=The Passive House – sustainable, affordable, comfortable, versatile |website=International Passive House Association |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2013/dec/08/live-in-passive-house-passivhaus |title=How can I live in a passive house? |first=Lucy |last=Siegle |date=December 8, 2013 |newspaper=The Guardian |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref> Delivery at cost parity with standard code buildings has been demonstrated in some German multifamily projects (e.g., Vauban, Freiburg).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.passivhaus-vauban.de/passivhaus.en.html |title=What is a Passive House? |first=Andreas |last=Delleske |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref> High-latitude locations (>60°N) can face higher envelope and glazing costs to meet targets.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Henk_Kaan.pdf |title=Passive Houses in High Latitudes |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130302154535/http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Henk_Kaan.pdf |archive-date=2013-03-02 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref>

Passive House features can also be incorporated into existing buildings through retrofits, although such projects can turn out to be expensive. In the UK an architect incurred a total cost to adapt a small four-bedroom 1960s house of about £80,000, over ten years to spread the cost, without including additional costs for architectural work. The windows cost about £30,000; making the house airtight about £5,000. On a hot day, the temperature inside was about 10°C (18°F) cooler than outside. In winter a single radiator was enough to heat the whole house, with a reduction of 88% in required energy. However, in a heatwave with hot nights, unusual in the UK, the temperature during the day rose to about the night-time ambient temperature.<ref name=tanaka>{{cite news| last=Tanaka | first=Miho | title=Could these alternative homes be the future in a hotter Britain? | publisher=BBC News | date=21 August 2026 | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg5l3z7p922o}}</ref> While retrofitting to full passive house standard is expensive, it has been suggested that "even doing the 50% best is massive in terms of energy bills".<ref name=tanaka/>

==Design and construction==
[[File:Passive house scheme 1.svg|thumb|Passive house combines envelope performance, airtightness and efficient services.]]

Core practices include:
* '''Passive solar design and urban/landscape integration''' – compact massing, appropriate solar gains, shading, and mitigation of overheating; strategies are adapted to climate, especially in hot-humid regions.<ref>{{cite web|title=Passive House in the Global South|url=https://passipedia.org/basics/passive_houses_in_different_climates/passive_house_in_the_global_south|website=Passipedia|date=2025-08-13|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref>
* '''Superinsulation''' and '''thermal-bridge-free''' detailing (typical opaque U-values ~0.10–0.15 W/m²·K).<ref name="Swanson">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/slideshow/2010/09/26/business/energy-environment/Passive.html |last=Swanson |first=Herb |title=Energy Efficiency, a Step Further |newspaper=The New York Times |date=September 26, 2010 |access-date=2010-09-29}}</ref>
* '''High-performance windows''' (triple/quad glazing, low-e coatings, inert-gas fills, warm-edge spacers; whole-window U-values often ≤0.80 W/m²·K).<ref>{{cite web | title=Passivhaus Institut | url=https://passiv.de/en/02_informations/02_passive-house-requirements/02_passive-house-requirements.htm|website=Passiv.de }}</ref>
* '''Airtightness''' to ''n''<sub>50</sub> ≤0.6 h⁻¹, verified by blower-door testing; intermediate tests during construction are recommended.<ref>{{cite web|title=Passive House requirements|url=https://passiv.de/en/02_informations/02_passive-house-requirements/02_passive-house-requirements.htm|website=Passiv.de|access-date=2025-09-26}}</ref>
* '''Balanced mechanical ventilation with heat recovery''' (typically ≥75% efficiency) for IAQ and energy recovery; earth-tubes may be used with careful moisture control where appropriate.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Holladay|first=Martin|title=Belgian Passivhaus is Rendered Uninhabitable by Bad Indoor Air|journal=Green Building Advisor|date=June 1, 2012|url=http://www.greenbuildingadvisor.com/blogs/dept/musings/belgian-passivhaus-rendered-uninhabitable-bad-indoor-air|access-date=2012-06-14}}</ref>
* '''Low-load space conditioning''' – many climates allow heating via tempered ventilation air with small duct heaters or heat-pump coils; peak loads are limited by envelope performance.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.passivhaustagung.de/zehnte/englisch/texte/PEP-Info1_Passive_Houses_Kronsberg.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070116113351/http://www.passivhaustagung.de/zehnte/englisch/texte/PEP-Info1_Passive_Houses_Kronsberg.pdf |archive-date=2007-01-16 |title=Passive House Estate in Hannover-Kronsberg |page=72 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref>

==Performance and occupant behaviour==
Concerns are sometimes raised that occupants must restrict behaviours (e.g., opening windows), but sensitivity analyses indicate performance is generally robust to typical occupant variation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blight |first1=T. S. |last2=Coley |first2=D. A. |year=2013 |title=Sensitivity analysis of the effect of occupant behaviour on the energy consumption of passive house dwellings |journal=Energy and Buildings |volume=66 |pages=183–192|doi=10.1016/j.enbuild.2013.06.030 |bibcode=2013EneBu..66..183B }}</ref>

==International comparisons==
* '''United States''' – Space-heating intensity around {{convert|1|BTU/ft2|kJ/m2}} per [[heating degree day]] is typical for PHI Passive House, compared to ~5–15 for code-built homes (2003 MEE Code), representing 75–95% savings. Waldsee BioHaus (Minnesota) follows the German standard and reported ~85% lower energy use than comparable [[LEED]] homes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waldseebiohaus.typepad.com/biohaus/design.html |title=Design & Architecture |website=Waldsee BioHaus Environmental Living Center |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref>
* '''United Kingdom''' – New houses to Passive House standard used ~77% less space-heating energy than homes built under circa-2006 Building Regulations.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Energy_Saving_Potential_2.pdf |title=Energy Saving Potential of Passive Houses in the UK |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160603104908/http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Energy_Saving_Potential_2.pdf |archive-date=2016-06-03 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref> It was estimated that in 2026 about 1% of new-build housing was built to voluntary passive house standards, a figure expected to increase.<ref name=tanaka/>
* '''Ireland''' – Typical Passive House dwellings consumed ~85% less space-heating energy and cut related CO₂ by ~94% versus 2002 Regulations baselines.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Irena_Kondratenko.pdf |title=Passive Houses in Ireland |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160603105008/http://erg.ucd.ie/pep/pdf/Irena_Kondratenko.pdf |archive-date=2016-06-03 |access-date=2017-12-11}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Passive survivability
======================================================================

'''Passive survivability''' refers to a building's ability to maintain critical life-support conditions in the event of extended loss of power, heating fuel, or water.<ref name=":1" /> This idea proposes that designers should incorporate ways for a building to continue sheltering inhabitants for an extended period of time during and after a disaster situation, whether it be a storm that causes a power outage, a [[drought]] which limits water supply, or any other possible event.

The term was coined by BuildingGreen President and EBN Executive editor Alex Wilson in 2005 after the wake of [[Hurricane Katrina]].<ref>Quinion, Michael. "World Wide Words: Passive Survivability." World Wide Words. 5 Aug. 2003. Web. 2 Dec. 2014.<http://www.worldwidewords.org/turnsofphrase/tp-pas1.htm>[http://www.worldwidewords.org/turnsofphrase/tp-pas1.htm]</ref> Passive survivability is suggested to become a standard in the design criteria for houses, apartment buildings, and especially buildings used as emergency shelters. While many of the strategies considered to achieve the goals of passive survivability are not new concepts and have been widely used in [[green building]] over the decades, the distinction comes from the motivation for moving towards resilient and safe buildings.<ref name=":1" />

==Current issues==
The increase in duration, frequency, and intensity of extreme weather events due to climate change exacerbates the challenges that passive survivability tries to address.<ref name=":1" /> Climates that did not previously need cooling are now seeing warmer temperatures and a need for [[air conditioning]]. [[Sea level rise]] and storm surge increases the risk of flooding in coastal locations, while precipitation-based flooding is an issue in low-lying areas. In order for buildings to provide livable conditions at all times, potential threats must be realized.

===Power outages===
In much of the developed world, there is a heavy reliance on a [[Power grid|grid]] for power and gas. These grids are the main source of energy for many societies, and while they generally do not get interrupted, they are constantly prone to events that may cause disruption, such as [[natural disaster]]s. In California, there have even been intentional power outages as a preventative measure in response to wildfires caused by power lines.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/california-wildfires-and-intentional-power-outages-call-for-more-resilient-power-systems/|title=California wildfires and intentional power outages call for more resilient power systems|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=October 30, 2019|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> When a power outage occurs, most mechanical heating and cooling can no longer operate. The aim of passive survivability is to be prepared for when such an event may occur, and maintain safe indoor temperatures. While [[Emergency power system|back-up generators]] can provide some power during an outage, it is often not enough for heating and cooling needs or adequate lighting.<ref name=":1" />

=== Extreme temperature ===
Heat is the leading cause of weather-related death in the US.<ref name=":2" /> [[Heat wave]]s coinciding with power outages puts many lives at risk due to the inability of a building to keep temperatures down. Even without a power outage, lack of access to air conditioning or lack of funds to pay for electricity also highlights the need for passive ways to maintain a livable thermal environment.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Nahlik|first1=Matthew J.|last2=Chester|first2=Mikhail V.|last3=Pincetl|first3=Stephanie S.|last4=Eisenman|first4=David|last5=Sivaraman|first5=Deepak|last6=English|first6=Paul|date=September 2017|title=Building Thermal Performance, Extreme Heat, and Climate Change|journal=Journal of Infrastructure Systems|language=en|volume=23|issue=3|pages=04016043|doi=10.1061/(ASCE)IS.1943-555X.0000349|issn=1076-0342|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8fp1c9t9|hdl=2286/R.I.55247|s2cid=52060479 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> One of the issues that passive survivability looks at is considering the many ways to keep [[thermal resistance]] of a building skin to prevent a room from becoming overbearing in the event of having a lack of access to standard temperature regulating systems.

In the winter months, power outages or lack of a fuel source for heat pose a threat when there are [[cold front]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.buildinggreen.com/op-ed/passive-survivability|title=Passive Survivability|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=December 1, 2005|website=Building Green|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> Leaky construction and poor insulation result in rapid heat loss, causing indoor temperatures to fall.

=== Drought ===
During a [[drought]], the limited water supply means a community must get by using less, which may mean mandatory restrictions on water use. Extended dry spells can instigate [[wildfire]]s, which add a heightened level of devastation.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/fundamentals-of-resilient-design-8-water-in-a-drought-prone-era/|title=Fundamentals of Resilient Design #8: Water in a Drought-Prone Era|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=September 14, 2012|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> Drying clay soil can cause critical water mains to burst and damage homes and infrastructure.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/05/us/05ttdrought.html|title=Drought Effects Extend Far Beyond Water Restrictions|last=Auber|first=Ari|date=2011-08-04|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-12-08|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Droughts can also cause power-outages in areas where thermo-electric power plants are the main source of electricity.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/making-the-case-for-resilient-design/|title=Fundamentals of Resilient Design #1: Making the Case|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=August 24, 2012|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> Water-efficient appliances and landscaping is crucial in water-scarce locations.

=== Natural disasters ===
Natural disasters such as [[Tropical cyclone|hurricanes]], [[earthquake]]s, [[tornado]]es, and other storm events can result in destruction of infrastructure that provides key electricity, water, and energy sources.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.buildinggreen.com/feature/passive-survivability-new-design-criterion-buildings|title=Passive Survivability: A New Design Criterion for Buildings|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=May 3, 2006|website=Building Green|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> Flooding after extreme precipitation is a major threat to buildings and utilities. The resulting electricity or water shortages can pose more of a threat than the event itself, often lasting longer than the initial disaster.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/dramatically-better-building-envelopes/|title=Fundamentals of Resilient Design #4: Dramatically Better Building Envelopes|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=August 27, 2012|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref>

=== Terrorist threats ===
[[Terrorism|Terrorist]] threats and [[cyberterrorism]] can also cause an interruption in power supply. Attacks on central plants or major distribution segments, or hacking of a utility grid's control system are possible threats that could cut off electricity, water, or fuel.<ref name=":0" />

== Passive design strategies ==
There are many passive strategies that require no electricity but instead can provide heating, cooling, and lighting for a building through proper design. In envelope-dominated buildings, the climate and surroundings have a greater effect on the interior of the structure due to a high surface area to volume ratio and minimal internal heat sources.<ref name=":03">{{Cite book|title=Heating, cooling, lighting : sustainable design methods for architects|last=Lechner, Norbert|isbn=978-1-118-84945-3|edition=Fourth|location=Hoboken, New Jersey|oclc=867852750|date = 2014-09-23}}</ref> Internally dominated buildings, such as the typical office building, are more affected by internal heat sources like equipment and people, however the [[building envelope]] still plays an important role, especially during a power outage.

While the distinction between the two types of buildings can sometimes be unclear, all buildings have a [[balance point temperature]] that is a result of building design and function. Balance point temperature is the outdoor temperature under which a building requires heating.<ref name=":03"/> An internally dominated structure will have a lower balance point temperature because of more internal heat sources, which means a longer overheated period and shorter under-heated period. Achieving a livable thermal environment during a power outage is dependent on the balance point temperature, as well as the interaction with the surrounding environment. A key aspect of all design for passive survivability is climate-responsive design. Passive strategies should be chosen based on climate and local conditions, in addition to building function.

=== Thermal envelope ===
When a building has leaky construction or poor [[Building insulation|insulation]], desired heat is lost in the winter and conditioned air is lost in the summer.<ref name=":03"/> This loss is accounted for by pumping more mechanical heating or cooling into the building to make up the difference. Since this strategy is obsolete during a power outage, the building should be able to maintain internal temperatures for longer periods of time. To avoid heat loss by [[Infiltration (HVAC)|infiltration]], the thermal envelope should be constructed with minimal breaks and joints, and cracks around windows and doors should be sealed. The air tightness of a building can be tested using a blower-door test.

Heat is also lost by transmission through the many surfaces in a room, including walls, windows, floors, ceilings, and doors. The area and [[thermal resistance]] of the surface, as well as the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors, determines the rate of heat loss.<ref name=":03"/> Continuous insulation with high [[R-value (insulation)|R-values]] reduces heat loss by transmission in walls and ceilings. Double and triple-pane windows with special coatings reduce loss through windows.<ref name=":3" /> The practice of [[superinsulation]] greatly reduces heat loss through high levels of thermal resistance and air tightness.

=== Passive solar ===
[[File:Illust passive solar d1.gif|alt=Diagram of a building showing passive solar heating design strategies.|thumb|This building is designed to maintain its internal temperature by working with the sun, using the indicated features.]]
The ability to passively heat a building is beneficial during the colder winter months to help keep temperature levels up. [[Passive solar building design|Passive solar]] systems collect and distribute energy from the sun without the use of mechanical equipment such as fans or pumps. Passive solar heating consists of equator-facing glazing (south-facing in the northern hemisphere) to collect solar energy and [[thermal mass]] to store the heat.<ref name=":03"/> A direct-gain system allows [[Shortwave radiation|short-wave radiation]] from the sun to enter a room through the window, where the floor and wall surfaces then act as thermal mass to absorb the heat, and the long-wave radiation is trapped inside due to the [[greenhouse effect]].<ref name=":03"/> Proper glazing to thermal mass ratios should be used to prevent overheating and provide adequate heating.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/passive-solar-heating-a-key-to-resilience/|title=Fundamentals of Resilient Design #5: Passive Solar Heating|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=August 30, 2012|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> A [[Trombe wall]] or indirect gain system places the thermal mass right inside the glazing to collect heat during the day for night-time use due to time-lag of mass.<ref name=":03"/> This method is useful if daylighting is not required, or can be used in combination with direct-gain. A third technique is a sunspace or isolated gain system, which collects solar energy in a separate space attached to the building, and which can double as a living area for most of the year.<ref name=":03"/>

=== Heat avoidance ===
Heat avoidance strategies can be used to reduce cooling needs during the overheated periods of the year. This is achieved largely though shading devices and building orientation. In the northern hemisphere, windows should primarily be placed on southern facades which receive the most sun during the winter, while windows on east and west facades should be avoided due to difficulty to shade and high [[Solar irradiance|solar radiation]] during the summer.<ref name=":03"/> Fixed [[Overhang (architecture)|overhangs]] can be designed that block the sun during the overheated periods and allow the sun during the under-heated periods. Movable shading devices are most appropriate due to their ability to respond to the environment and building needs.<ref name=":03" /> Using light colors on roofs and walls is another effective strategy to reduce heat gain by reflecting the sun.

=== Natural ventilation ===
[[Natural ventilation]] can be used to increase [[thermal comfort]] during warmer periods. There are two main types of natural ventilation: comfort ventilation and night-flush cooling. Comfort ventilation brings in outside air to move over skin and increase the skin's evaporative cooling, creating a more comfortable thermal environment.<ref name=":03" /> The temperature does not necessarily decrease unless the outdoor temperature is lower than the indoor temperature, however the air movement increases comfort. This technique is especially useful in humid climates. When the wind is not blowing, a [[solar chimney]] can increase ventilation flow by using the sun to increase buoyancy of air.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.resilientdesign.org/natural-cooling-and-resilience/|title=Fundamentals of Resilient Design #6: Natural Cooling|last=Wilson|first=Alex|date=Sep 3, 2012|website=Resilient Design Institute|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref>

Night-flush cooling utilizes the cool nighttime air to flush the warm air out of the building and lower the indoor temperature. The cooled structure then acts as a [[heat sink]] during the day, when bringing the warm outdoor air in is avoided. Night-flush cooling is most effective in locations that have large [[Diurnal temperature variation|diurnal temperature ranges]], such as in hot and dry climates.<ref name=":03" /> With both techniques, providing operable windows alone does not result in adequate natural ventilation; the building must be designed for proper airflow.

=== Daylighting ===
When the power goes out, rooms at the center of a building typically receive little to no light. Designing a building to take advantage of natural [[daylight]] instead of relying on [[electric light]]ing will make it more resilient to power outages and other events. [[Daylighting (architecture)|Daylighting]] and passive solar gain often go hand in hand, but in the summer there is a desire for “cool” daylight. Daylighting design should therefore provide adequate lighting without adding undesired heat. Direct sunlight and reflected light from the sky have different levels of radiation.<ref name=":03" /> The daylighting design should reflect the needs of the building in both its climate and function, and different methods can achieve that. Southern and northern windows are generally best for daylighting, and [[Clerestory|clerestories]] or monitors on the roof can bring daylight into the center of a building.<ref name=":03" /> Placing windows higher up on a wall will bring the light further into the room, and other methods like [[Architectural light shelf|light shelves]] can bring light deeper into a building by reflecting light off the ceiling.<ref name=":03" />

==Other design strategies==

The over arching goal of passive survivability is to try to reduce discomfort or suffering in the event of having a key source cut off to a building. There are several different solutions to any one design problem. While many of the solutions that are presented by advocates of passive survivability are ones that have been universally accepted by passive design and other standard sustainability practices, it is important to examine these measures and apply the appropriate strategies to developing and existing buildings in order to minimize the risk of displeasure or death.<ref>Wilson, Alex. "Mandate Passive Survivability in Building Codes." Mandate Passive Survivability in Building Codes. Finehomebuilding.com, 14 May 2008. Web. 3 Dec. 2014.<http://www.finehomebuilding.com/how-to/departments/cross-section/mandate-passive-survivability-in-building-codes.aspx>. [http://www.finehomebuilding.com/how-to/departments/cross-section/mandate-passive-survivability-in-building-codes.aspx]</ref>

=== Back-up Power ===
[[File:Altach-Veranstaltungszentrum KOM-photovoltaic system-01ASD.jpg|alt=Solar PV panels on the roof of a building.|thumb|Photovoltaic solar panels on the roof of a building, providing on-site electrical power.]]
Buildings should be designed to maintain survivable thermal conditions without air conditioning or supplemental heat. Providing [[Emergency power system|back-up generators]] and adequate fuel to maintain the critical functions of a building during outages are conventional solutions to power-supply interruptions. However, unless they are very large, generators support only basic needs for a short amount of time and may not power systems such as air conditioning, lighting, or even heating or ventilation during extended outages. Back-up generators are also expensive both to buy and maintain. Storing significant quantities of fuel on-site to power generators during extended outages has inherent environmental and safety risks, particularly during storms.

Renewable energy systems can provide power during an extreme event. For example, [[Photovoltaics|photovoltaic]] (or solar electric) power systems, when coupled with on-site battery storage can provide electricity when the grid loses power. Other fuel sources like wood can provide heat if buildings are equipped with wood-burning stoves or fireplaces.

=== Water ===
Emergency water supply systems such as rooftop [[rainwater harvesting]] systems can provide water for toilet flushing, bathing, and other building needs in the event of water supply interruptions. [[Rainwater tank|Rain barrels]] or larger cisterns store water from runoff that can often use a gravity-feed to obtain the water for use. Installing [[composting toilet]]s and waterless [[urinal]]s ensure those facilities can continue to function regardless of the circumstance, while reducing water consumptions on a daily basis. Having backup sources of potable water on-site is also a necessity in the case of water interruption.<ref name=":4" />

== Passive survivability in rating systems ==

=== Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design ===
[[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design]] (LEED) is a widely used green building certification in the United States. As of LEED version 4, there is a pilot credit called “Passive Survivability and Backup Power During Disruptions” under LEED BD+C: New Construction.<ref name=":04">{{Cite web|url=http://www.usgbc.org/credits/passivesurvivability|title=Passive Survivability and Back-up Power During Disruptions {{!}} U.S. Green Building Council|website=www.usgbc.org|language=en|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> The credit is worth up to two points, with one point awarded for providing for passive survivability and thermal safety, and one point awarded for providing backup power for critical loads. For the passive survivability point, the building must maintain thermally safe conditions during a four-day power outage during both peak summer and peak winter conditions.<ref name=":04" /> LEED lists three paths to compliance for thermal safety, two of which consist of thermal modelling, and the remaining path being [[Passive house|Passive House]] certification.

=== Passive house certification ===
[[File:Passive house scheme 1.svg|alt=Diagram of building showing passive house design strategies.|thumb|A passive house uses the indicated design features to achieve an extremely low energy consumption.]]
While passive survivability is not mentioned by name in the two major [[passive house]] standards, Passive House Institute and Passive House Institute US (PHIUS), the passive strategies that make these buildings so [[Efficient energy use|energy efficient]] are the same strategies outlined for passive survivability. Buildings that achieve passive house certification are hitting some of the main criteria for passive survivability, including airtight construction and [[superinsulation]].<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=https://www.phius.org/what-is-passive-building/passive-house-principles|title=The Principles: Passive House Institute U.S.|website=www.phius.org|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> Many buildings will also have on-site [[photovoltaics]] to offset energy consumption. These buildings that rely very little on energy will be more resilient in power outages and extreme weather.<ref name=":12" />

=== RELi ===
RELi is a building and community rating system completely based on resilient design. It has been adopted by the US [[Green building council|Green Building Council]], the same body that developed LEED.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gbci.org/reli|title=RELi {{!}} GBCI|website=www.gbci.org|date=11 November 2019|access-date=2019-12-10}}</ref> The Hazard Adaptation and Mitigation category has several credits related to passive survivability. One required credit is “Fundamental Emergency Operations: Thermal Safety During Emergencies” which requires indoor temperatures to be at or below outdoor temperatures in the summer, and above 50&nbsp;°F in the winter for up to four days.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://c3livingdesign.org/?page_id=11817|title=RELi Action List + Credit Catalogue|last=|first=|date=2017|website=The C3 Living Design Project|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another way to comply is to provide a thermal safe zone with adequate space for all building occupants. There is an optional poly-credit, “Advanced Emergency Operations: Back-Up Power, Operations, Thermal Safety & Operating Water,” that incorporates other passive survivability measures such as water storage.<ref name=":5" /> Another poly-credit, “Passive Thermal Safety, Thermal Comfort, & Lighting Design Strategies,” outlines more passive strategies including [[passive cooling]], [[Passive solar building design|passive heating]], and [[Daylighting (architecture)|daylighting]].<ref name=":5" />
