===India===
India's first net zero building is [[Indira Paryavaran Bhawan]], located in [[New Delhi]], inaugurated in 2014. Features include [[passive solar building design]] and other green technologies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pib.nic.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?relid=104214|title=Prime Minister Inaugurates 'Indira Paryavaran Bhawan'. Bhawan is India's First on Site Net Zero Building|date=25 February 2014|publisher=Press Information Bureau, Government of India|access-date=23 May 2014}}</ref> High-efficiency solar panels are proposed. It cools air from toilet exhaust using a [[thermal wheel]] in order to reduce load on its [[chiller]] system. It has many water conservation features.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.moef.nic.in/ipb/home1.htm|title=Welcome to Indira Paryavaran Bhawan|date=March 24, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324090535/http://www.moef.nic.in/ipb/home1.htm|archive-date=2019-03-24}}</ref>

===Iran===
In 2011, ''Payesh'' Energy House (PEH) or ''Khaneh Payesh Niroo'' by a collaboration of Fajr-e-Toseah Consultant Engineering Company<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fajr-t.com/en/index.html |title=Fajr-e-Tosea Consulting Engineers Co. |work=fajr-t.com |year=2014 |access-date=25 June 2014 |archive-date=12 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141112150726/http://fajr-t.com/en/index.html }}</ref> and Vancouver Green Homes Ltd] under management of Payesh Energy Group (EPG) launched the first Net-Zero passive house in Iran. This concept makes the design and construction of PEH a sample model and standardized process for mass production by MAPSA.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mapsa.co.ir/index.php/newtechmapsa/minisystemsmapsa|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130730171044/http://www.mapsa.co.ir/index.php/newtechmapsa/minisystemsmapsa|title=گروه ششم: زیر سیستمها|first=مدیر|last=سایت|archive-date=July 30, 2013|website=www.mapsa.co.ir}}</ref>

Also, an example of the new generation of zero energy office buildings is the 24-story OIIC<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oiic-ir.com/Default.aspx?tabid=53 |title=Oil Industry Investment Company |work=oiic-ir.com |year=2014 |access-date=25 June 2014 |archive-date=14 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140614013538/http://www.oiic-ir.com/Default.aspx?tabid=53 }}</ref> Office Tower, which is started in 2011, as the OIIC Company headquarters. It uses both modest energy efficiency, and a big distributed renewable energy generation from both solar and wind. It is managed by Rahgostar Naft Company in [[Tehran, Iran]]. The tower is receiving economic support from government subsidies that are now funding many significant fossil-fuel-free efforts.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oiic-ir.com/%D8%B4%D8%B1%DA%A9%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%B9%D9%87/%D8%B4%D8%B1%DA%A9%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%87%DA%AF%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%86%D9%81%D8%AA/tabid/230/Default.aspx |title=شرکت ره گستر نفت |publisher=Oiic-ir.com |access-date=25 June 2014 |archive-date=27 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140927230542/http://www.oiic-ir.com/%D8%B4%D8%B1%DA%A9%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%B9%D9%87/%D8%B4%D8%B1%DA%A9%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%87%DA%AF%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%86%D9%81%D8%AA/tabid/230/Default.aspx }}</ref>

===Ireland===
In 2005, a private company launched the world's first standardised passive house in Ireland, this concept makes the design and construction of passive house a standardised process.
Conventional low energy construction techniques have been refined and modelled on the PHPP (Passive House Design Package) to create the standardised passive house.
Building offsite allows high precision techniques to be utilised and reduces the possibility of errors in construction.

In 2009 the same company started a project to use 23,000 liters of water in a seasonal storage tank, heated up by [[Evacuated tube#Evacuated tube collectors|evacuated solar tubes]] throughout the year, with the aim to provide the house with enough heat throughout the winter months thus eliminating the need for any electrical heat to keep the house comfortably warm. The system is monitored and documented by a research team from [[Ulster University|The University of Ulster]] and the results will be included in part of a [[PhD]] thesis.

In 2012 Cork Institute of Technology started renovation work on its 1974 building stock to develop a net zero energy building retrofit.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.zero2020energy.com |title=zero2020energyhtml |publisher=Zero2020energy.com |access-date=25 June 2014}}</ref> The exemplar project will become Ireland's first zero energy testbed offering a post-occupancy evaluation of actual building performance against design benchmarks.

===Jamaica===
The first zero energy building in Jamaica and the Caribbean opened at the Mona Campus of the University of the West Indies (UWI) in 2017.<ref name="Project Green Building">{{cite web|date=27 October 2017|title=Caribbean's First Net Zero Building Opens at University|url=https://www.proudgreenbuilding.com/news/caribbeans-first-net-zero-building-opens-at-university/|publisher=Project Green Building|access-date=5 November 2020|archive-date=12 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200812151951/https://www.proudgreenbuilding.com/news/caribbeans-first-net-zero-building-opens-at-university/}}</ref> The 2300 square foot building was designed to inspire more sustainable and energy efficient buildings in the area.<ref name="Project Green Building" />

===Japan===
After the [[April 2011 Fukushima earthquake]] followed by the up with [[Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster]], Japan experienced severe power crisis that led to the awareness of the importance of energy conservation.

In 2012 [[Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry]], [[Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism]] and [[Ministry of the Environment (Japan)]] summarized the road map for Low-carbon Society which contains the goal of ZEH and ZEB to be standard of new construction in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://standard-project.net/smarthouse/zeh.html|title=ゼロエネルギー住宅(ZEH)とは|website=Standard Project}}</ref>

The Mitsubishi Electric Corporation is underway with the construction of Japan's first zero energy office building, set to be completed in October, 2020 (as of September 2020).<ref name="Smart Energy International">{{cite web|date=9 August 2019|title=Mitsubishi Electric Receives Net Zero Energy Building Certification|url=https://www.smart-energy.com/renewable-energy/mitsubishi-electric-receives-net-zero-energy-building-certification/|publisher=Smart Energy International|access-date=5 November 2020|archive-date=30 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130052943/https://www.smart-energy.com/renewable-energy/mitsubishi-electric-receives-net-zero-energy-building-certification/}}</ref> The SUSTIE ZEB test facility is located in Kamakura, Japan, to develop ZEB technology.<ref name="Smart Energy International" /> With the net zero certification, the facility projects to reduce energy consumption by 103%.<ref>{{cite web|date=October 2020|title=Mitsubishi Electric's Net Zero Energy Building Test Facility to Be Completed on Oct. 14|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200930005315/en/Mitsubishi-Electric%E2%80%99s-Net-Zero-Energy-Building-Test-Facility-to-Be-Completed-on-Oct.-14|publisher=Businesswire}}</ref>

Japan has made it a goal that all new houses be net zero energy by 2030.<ref>{{cite web|date=6 August 2015|title=The Present and Future of Net Zero Energy Houses in Japan|url=https://resources.realestate.co.jp/buy/the-present-and-future-of-net-zero-energy-houses-in-japan/|publisher=Real Estate Japan}}</ref> The developing company Sekisui House introduced their first net zero home in 2013, and is now planning Japan's first zero energy condominium in Nagoya City, it is a three-story building with 12 units.<ref name="Sekisui House News Release-2016">{{cite web|date=20 December 2016|title=Japan's First Zero Energy Apartment Building Coming In 2019|url=https://japanpropertycentral.com/2016/12/japans-first-zero-energy-apartment-building-coming-in-2019/|publisher=Sekisui House News Release}}</ref> There are solar panels on the roof and fuel cells for each unit to provide backup power.<ref name="Sekisui House News Release-2016"/>

=== Korea (Republic of) ===
[[File:Energy X DY-Building.jpg|thumb|EnergyX DY-Building ([[:ko:에너지엑스 DY빌딩|에너지엑스 DY빌딩]]), the first commercial Net-Zero Energy Building (NZEB, or ZEB grade 1) and the first Plus Energy Building (+ZEB, or ZEB grade plus) in Korea, was opened and introduced in 2023.]]
South Korea's Mandatory ZEB requirements, which have been previously applied to buildings with a GFA of 1,000 m2+ in 2021 will expand to buildings with a GFA of 500 m2+ in 2022, until being applicable to all public buildings starting in 2024. For private buildings, ZEB certification will be mandated for building permits with a GFA of over 100,000 m2 from 2023. After 2025, zero-energy construction for private buildings will be expanded to GFAs over 1,000 m2. The goal of the policy is to convert all public sector buildings to ZEB grade 3 (an energy independence rate of 60% ~ 80%), and all private buildings to ZEB grade 5 (an energy independence rate of 20% ~ 40%) by 2030.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=Crystal |date=November 2022 |title=Regulations from 2023 on carbon emissions for new buildings to drive ESG adoption |url=https://pdf.savills.asia/asia-pacific-research/asia-pacific-research/acr---ko-esg-2h-2022.pdf |journal=Savills Research |volume=Korea ESG |page=3 |via=Savills Korea}}</ref>

EnergyX DY-Building (에너지엑스 DY빌딩), the first commercial Net-Zero Energy Building (NZEB, or ZEB grade 1) and the first [[Energy-plus building|Plus Energy Building]] (+ZEB, or ZEB grade plus) in Korea was opened and introduced in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-26 |title=에너지엑스, 국내 첫 상업용 플러스 제로에너지빌딩 건설 |url=https://news.koreadaily.com/2023/05/25/economy/economygeneral/20230525180015767.html |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=news.koreadaily.com |language=ko}}</ref> The energy technology and sustainable architectural platform company EnergyX developed, designed, and engineered the building with its proprietary technologies and services.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-25 |title=건축 플랫폼 에너지엑스, 제로에너지 포럼 및 준공식 개최 |url=http://www.nextdaily.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=223066 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=넥스트데일리 |language=ko |last1=기자 |first1=이호 }}</ref> EnergyX DY-Building received the ZEB certification with an energy independence rate (or energy self-sufficiency rate) of 121.7%.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-13 |title=에너지엑스, 에너지자립률 121.7%... 국내 최초 플러스 제로에너지빌딩 준공 |url=http://www.industrynews.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=51208 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=인더스트리뉴스 |language=ko}}</ref>

===Malaysia===
In October 2007, the [[Malaysia]] Energy Centre (PTM) successfully completed the development and construction of the PTM Zero Energy Office (ZEO) Building. The building has been designed to be a super-energy-efficient building using only 286&nbsp;kWh/day. The renewable energy – photovoltaic combination is expected to result in a net zero energy requirement from the grid. The building is currently undergoing a fine tuning process by the local energy management team. Findings are expected to be published in a year.<ref>[http://www.ptm.org.my/PTM_Building PTM Zero Energy Office Building Project.] August 2006.</ref>

In 2016, the Sustainable Energy Development Authority Malaysia (SEDA Malaysia) started a voluntary initiative called Low Carbon Building Facilitation Program. The purpose is to support the current low carbon cities program in Malaysia. Under the program, several project demonstration managed to reduce energy and carbon beyond 50% savings and some managed to save more than 75%. Continuous improvement of super energy efficient buildings with significant implementation of on-site renewable energy managed to make a few of them become nearly Zero Energy (nZEB) as well as Net-Zero Energy Building (NZEB). In March 2018, SEDA Malaysia has started the Zero Energy Building Facilitation Program.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Steve Lojuntin |date=2018-03-11 |title=Zero Energy Building in Malaysia by SEDA Malaysia |url=https://www.slideshare.net/mobile/asetip/zero-energy-building-in-malaysia-by-seda-malaysia |journal=SEDA Malaysia}}</ref>

Malaysia also has its own sustainable building tool special for Low Carbon and zero energy building, called GreenPASS that been developed by the Construction Industry Development Board Malaysia (CIDB) in 2012, and currently being administered and promoted by SEDA Malaysia. GreenPASS official is called the Construction Industry Standard (CIS) 20:2012.

===Netherlands===
In September 2006, the Dutch headquarters of the [[World Wildlife Fund]] (WWF) in [[Zeist]] was opened. This earth-friendly building gives back more energy than it uses. All materials in the building were tested against strict requirements laid down by the WWF and the architect.<ref>{{cite web | title = huisvesting | url = http://www.wnf.nl/nl/overwnf/huisvesting/ | access-date = 2011-03-17 | archive-date = 2011-03-03 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110303132450/http://www.wnf.nl/nl/overwnf/huisvesting/ }}</ref>

===Norway===
In February 2009, the Research Council of [[Norway]] assigned The Faculty of Architecture and Fine Art at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology to host the Research Centre on Zero Emission Buildings (ZEB), which is one of eight new national Centres for Environment-friendly Energy Research (FME). The main objective of the FME-centres is to contribute to the development of good technologies for environmentally friendly energy and to raise the level of Norwegian expertise in this area. In addition, they should help to generate new industrial activity and new jobs. Over the next eight years, the FME-Centre ZEB will develop competitive products and solutions for existing and new buildings that will lead to market penetration of zero emission buildings related to their production, operation and demolition.

===Singapore===

Singapore unveiled a prominent development at the National University of Singapore that is a net-zero energy building. The building, called SDE4, is located within a group of three buildings in its School of Design and Environment (SDE).<ref>{{cite journal |title=Singapore: NUS launches Singapores first new-build net-zero energy building |journal=MENA Report |date=2019 }}</ref> The design of the building achieved a Green Mark Platinum certification as it produces as much energy as it consumes with its solar panel covered rooftop and hybrid cooling system along with many integrated systems to achieve optimum energy efficiency. This development was the first new-build zero-energy building to come to fruition in Singapore, and the first zero-energy building at the NUS. The first retrofitted zero energy building to be developed in Singapore was a building at the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) academy by the Minister for National Development Mah Bow Tan at the inaugural Singapore Green Building Week on October 26, 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2009-10-26 |title=Singapore's first 'Zero Energy Building' launched |url=https://www.lushhomemedia.com/singapores-first-zero-energy-building-launched/ |access-date=2022-08-05 |website=LushHomeMedia |language=en-US}}</ref> Singapore's Green Building Week (SGBW) promotes sustainable development and celebrates the achievements of successfully designed sustainable buildings.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-09-05 |title=Speech by Minister Lawrence Wong at the Singapore Green Building Week Opening Ceremony 2018 |url=https://www.mnd.gov.sg/newsroom/speeches/view/speech-by-minister-lawrence-wong-at-the-singapore-green-building-week-opening-ceremony-2018 |access-date=2022-08-05 |website=Ministry of National Development}}</ref>

A net-zero energy building unveiled more recently is the SMU Connexion (SMUC). It is the first net-zero energy building in the city that also utilizes mass engineered timber (MET). It is designed to meet the [[Building and Construction Authority]] (BCA) Green Mark Platinum certification and has been in operation since January 2020.

===United Kingdom===
{{Update section|date=May 2019}}
{{Further|Energy efficiency in British housing}}
In December 2006, the government announced that by 2016 all new homes in England will be zero energy buildings. To encourage this, an exemption from [[Stamp Duty Land Tax]] is planned. In [[Wales]] the plan is for the standard to be met earlier in 2011, although it is looking more likely that the actual implementation date will be 2012. However, as a result of a unilateral change of policy published at the time of the March 2011 budget, a more limited policy is now planned which, it is estimated, will only mitigate two thirds of the emissions of a new home.<ref>[http://www.wwf.org.uk/wwf_articles.cfm?unewsid=4801 Why we've resigned from the Zero Carbon Taskforce] WWF UK, published 2011-04-04, accessed 2014-02-10</ref><ref>[http://www.sbmsearch.com/uploads/articles/pdf/255.pdf Government's U turn on Zero Carbon is anti-green and anti-growth] [[UK Green Building Council]], published 11-03-23, accessed 2014-02-10</ref>
* [[BedZED]] development
* Hockerton Housing Project

In January 2019 the Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government simply defined 'Zero Energy' as 'just meets current building standards' neatly solving this problem.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-01-14 |title=Nearly Zero Energy Buildings Requirements for New Public Buildings |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/926574/nZEBS_circular_letter.pdf |access-date=2022-08-04 |website=Ministry of Housing, Communities, & Local Government}}</ref>

===United States===
{{update section|date=September 2019}}
[[File:Net Zero Court.jpg|thumb|right|Figure 3: Net Zero Court zero emissions office building prototype in [[St. Louis, Missouri]]]]
In the [[United States|US]], ZEB research is currently being supported by the [[US Department of Energy]] (DOE) Building America Program,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.buildingamerica.gov/|title=Building America: Bringing Building Innovations to Market – Department of Energy|website=Building America|access-date=2008-01-07|archive-date=2008-08-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080821100528/http://buildingamerica.gov/}}</ref> including industry-based consortia and researcher organizations at the [[National Renewable Energy Laboratory]] (NREL), the [[Florida Solar Energy Center]] (FSEC), [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] (LBNL), and [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] (ORNL). From [[fiscal year]] 2008 to 2012, DOE plans to award $40 million to four Building America teams, the Building Science Corporation; IBACOS; the Consortium of Advanced Residential Buildings; and the Building Industry Research Alliance, as well as a consortium of academic and building industry leaders. The funds will be used to develop net-zero-energy homes that consume 50% to 70% less energy than conventional homes.<ref name=solardec>{{cite web | title = U.S. DOE – 2007 Solar Decathlon Closing Ceremony and Awards | url = https://www.energy.gov/news/5648.htm | access-date = 2008-04-14 | date = October 2007 | archive-date = 2008-03-21 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080321061812/http://www.energy.gov/news/5648.htm }}</ref>

DOE is also awarding $4.1 million to two regional building technology application centers that will accelerate the adoption of new and developing [[Efficient energy use|energy-efficient]] technologies. The two centers, located at the [[University of Central Florida]] and [[Washington State University]], will serve 17 states, providing information and training on commercially available energy-efficient technologies.<ref name=solardec/>

The U.S. [[Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007]]<ref>{{cite web | title = U.S. Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 | url = http://www.thomas.gov/cgi-bin/query/z?c110:H.R.6.ENR: | access-date = 2007-12-23 | archive-date = 2016-01-15 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160115001453/http://www.thomas.gov/cgi-bin/query/z?c110%3AH.R.6.ENR%3A }}</ref> created 2008 through 2012 funding for a new [[solar air conditioning]] research and development program, which should soon demonstrate multiple new technology innovations and [[mass production]] [[economies of scale]].

The 2008 [[Solar America Initiative]] funded research and development into future development of cost-effective Zero Energy Homes in the amount of $148 million in 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/fy2008/energy.html|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20070820164033/http://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/fy2008/energy.html|archive-date=2007-08-20|title=Budget of the United States Government, FY 2008: Department of Energy }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2005/08/20050808-4.html|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|title=Fact Sheet: President Bush Signs Into Law a National Energy Plan|date=2005-08-08}}</ref>

The Solar Energy Tax Credits were extended until the end of 2016.{{cn|date=February 2025}}

By [[Executive Order 13514]], U.S. President Barack Obama mandated that by 2015, 15% of existing Federal buildings conform to new energy efficiency standards and 100% of all new [[Zero-Net-Energy USA Federal Buildings|Federal buildings be Zero-Net-Energy]] by 2030.

====Energy Free Home Challenge====
In 2007, the philanthropic [[Siebel Foundation]] created the Energy Free Home Foundation. The goal was to offer $20 million in global incentive prizes to design and build a 2,000 square foot (186 square meter) three-bedroom, two bathroom home with (1) net-zero annual utility bills that also has (2) high market appeal, and (3) costs no more than a conventional home to construct.<ref>Goals of the Siebel Foundation Energy Free Home Challenge</ref>

The plan included funding to build the top ten entries at $250,000 each, a $10 million first prize, and then a total of 100 such homes to be built and sold to the public.

Beginning in 2009, [[Thomas Siebel]] made many presentations about his Energy Free Home Challenge.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://video.forbes.com/fvn/tech/zero-energy-homes|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090606152224/http://video.forbes.com/fvn/tech/zero-energy-homes|archive-date=June 6, 2009|title=Forbes Video|website=Forbes}}</ref> The Siebel Foundation Report stated that the Energy Free Home Challenge was "Launching in late 2009".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.fvgroup.com/Siebel_08AR_web.pdf|title=2008 Siebel Foundation Report|access-date=2011-04-03|archive-date=2011-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007175651/http://www.fvgroup.com/Siebel_08AR_web.pdf}}</ref>

The [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] participated in writing the "Feasibility of Achieving Zero-Net-Energy, Zero-Net-Cost Homes"<ref>{{cite web|url=http://escholarship.org/uc/item/740114f0#page-4|title=Feasibility of Achieving a Zero-Net-Energy, Zero-Net-Cost Homes|first=Al-Beaini|last=S.|date=26 February 2010}}</ref> for the $20-million Energy Free Home Challenge.

If implemented, the Energy Free Home Challenge would have provided increased incentives for improved technology and consumer education about zero energy buildings coming in at the same cost as conventional housing.

====US Department of Energy Solar Decathlon====
The [[Solar Decathlon|US Department of Energy Solar Decathlon]] is an international competition that challenges collegiate teams to design, build, and operate the most attractive, effective, and energy-efficient solar-powered house. Achieving zero net energy balance is a major focus of the competition.

=====California=====
* The State of California has proposed that all new low- and mid-rise residential buildings, and all new commercial buildings, be designed and constructed to ZNE standards beginning in 2020 and 2030, respectively.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cpuc.ca.gov/uploadedFiles/CPUC_Public_Website/Content/Utilities_and_Industries/Energy/Energy_Programs/Demand_Side_Management/EE_and_Energy_Savings_Assist/ZNERESACTIONPLAN_FINAL_060815.pdf|title=New Residential Zero Net Energy Action Plan 2015-2020|publisher=California Energy Commission|access-date=March 3, 2016|archive-date=March 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304143914/http://www.cpuc.ca.gov/uploadedFiles/CPUC_Public_Website/Content/Utilities_and_Industries/Energy/Energy_Programs/Demand_Side_Management/EE_and_Energy_Savings_Assist/ZNERESACTIONPLAN_FINAL_060815.pdf|date=June 2015}}</ref> The requirements, if implemented, will be promulgated via the California Building Code, which is updated on a three-year cycle and which currently mandates some of the highest energy efficiency standards in the United States. California is anticipated to further increase efficiency requirements by 2020, thus avoiding the trends discussed above of building standard housing and achieving ZNE by adding large amounts of renewables. The California Energy Commission is required to perform a cost-benefit analysis to prove that new regulations create a net benefit for residents of the state.
* West Village, located on the [[University of California, Davis|University of California campus in Davis]], California, was the largest ZNE-planned community in North America at the time of its opening in 2014.<ref name="UC Davis West Village">{{Cite web |title=UC Davis West Village |url=http://westvillage.ucdavis.edu |access-date=2016-03-04 |website=UC Davis West Village}}</ref> The development contains student housing for approximately 1,980 UC Davis students as well as leasable office space and community amenities including a community center, pool, gym, restaurant and convenience store. Office spaces in the development are currently leased by energy and transportation-related University programs. The project was a public-private partnership between the university and West Village Community Partnership LLC, led by Carmel Partners of San Francisco, a private developer, who entered into a 60-year ground lease with the university and was responsible for the design, construction, and implementation of the $300 million project, which is intended to be market-rate housing for Davis. This is unique as the developer designed the project to achieve ZNE at no added cost to themselves or to the residents. Designed and modeled to achieve ZNE, the project uses a mixture of passive elements (roof overhangs, well-insulated walls, radiant heat barriers, ducts in insulated spaces, etc.) as well as active approaches (occupancy sensors on lights, high-efficiency appliances and lighting, etc.). Designed to out-perform California's 2008 Title 24 energy codes by 50%, the project produced 87% of the energy it consumed during its first year in operation.<ref name="UC Davis West Village" /> The shortcoming in ZNE status is attributed to several factors, including improperly functioning heat pump water heaters, which have since been fixed. Occupant behavior is significantly different from that anticipated, with the all-student population using more energy on a per-capita basis than typical inhabitants of single-family homes in the area. One of the primary factors driving increased energy use appears to be the increased miscellaneous electrical loads (MEL, or [[plug load]]s) in the form of mini-refrigerators, lights, computers, gaming consoles, televisions, and other electronic equipment. The university continues to work with the developer to identify strategies for achieving ZNE status. These approaches include incentivizing occupant behavior and increasing the site's renewable energy capacity, which is a 4 MW photovoltaic array per the original design. The West Village site is also home to the Honda Smart Home US,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hondasmarthome.com/|title=Honda Smart Home US|last=Honda|website=Honda Smart Home US|access-date=2016-03-04|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304000643/http://www.hondasmarthome.com/}}</ref> a beyond-ZNE single-family home that incorporates cutting-edge technologies in energy management, lighting, construction, and [[water efficiency]].
* The IDeAs Z2 Design Facility<ref>{{Cite magazine |last1=Kaneda |first1=David |last2=Pumsey |first2=Peter |last3=Shell |first3=Scott |date=Fall 2010 |url=http://www.hpbmagazine.org/images/stories/articles/Ideas.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101012183148/http://www.hpbmagazine.org/images/stories/articles/Ideas.pdf |archive-date=2010-10-12 |access-date=2010-10-08 |website=High Performing Buildings |title=Less Than Zero}}</ref> is a net zero energy, zero carbon retrofit project occupied since 2007. It uses less than one fourth the energy of a typical U.S. office<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eia.doe.gov/emeu/cbecs/cbecs2003/detailed_tables_2003/2003set14/2003pdf/c3a.pdf|title=Energy Information Administration (EIA) – Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey (CBECS)|website=www.eia.doe.gov}}</ref> by applying strategies such as daylighting, radiant heating/cooling with a ground-source heat pump and high energy performance lighting and computing. The remaining energy demand is met with renewable energy from its [[Building-integrated photovoltaics|building-integrated photovoltaic]] array. In 2009, building owner and occupant Integrated Design Associates (IDeAs) recorded actual measured energy use intensity of {{convert|21.17|e3Btu/sqft|kWh/m2}} per year, with {{convert|21.72|e3Btu/sqft|kWh/m2}} per year produced, for a net of {{convert|-0.55|e3Btu/sqft|kWh/m2}} per year. The building is also carbon neutral, with no gas connection, and with [[carbon offset]]s purchased to cover the embodied carbon of the building materials used in the renovation.
* The Zero Net Energy Center, scheduled to open in 2013 in [[San Leandro, California|San Leandro]], is to be a 46,000-square-foot electrician training facility created by the [[International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers]] Local 595 and the Northern California chapter of the [[National Electrical Contractors Association]]. Training will include energy-efficient construction methods.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.prweb.com/releases/2012/10/prweb10011365.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003114145/https://www.prweb.com/releases/2012/10/prweb10011365.htm |archive-date=October 3, 2020 |title=Assemblywoman Mary Hayashi to Present Resolution to Red Top Electric |date=15 October 2012 | work=[[PRWeb]] }}</ref>
* The Green Idea House is a net zero energy, zero-carbon retrofit in Hermosa Beach.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.wconline.com/articles/88184-a-good-idea |title=A Good Idea |publisher=Wall and Ceiling Magazine |first=John |last=Wyatt |work=wconline.com |date=6 November 2012 |access-date=January 21, 2013}}</ref>
* George LeyVa Middle School Administrative Offices,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vista Solar Helps Leyva Middle School Earn Net-Zero Energy Distinction |url=https://www.prweb.com/releases/Vista-Solar/Leyva/prweb9599914.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220616233720/https://www.prweb.com/releases/vista-solar/leyva/prweb9599914.htm |archive-date=June 16, 2022 |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=PRWeb}}</ref> occupied since fall 2011, is a net zero energy, net zero carbon emissions building of just over 9,000 square feet. With daylighting, variable refrigerant flow HVAC, and displacement ventilation, it is designed to use half of the energy of a conventional California school building, and, through a building-integrated solar array, provides 108% of the energy needed to offset its annual electricity use. The excess helps power the remainder of the middle school campus. It is the first publicly funded NZE K–12 building in California.
* The Stevens Library at Sacred Heart Schools in California is the first net-zero library in the United States, receiving Net Zero Energy Building status from the [[International Living Future Institute]], part of the PG&E Zero Net Energy Pilot Project.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wrnsstudio.com/stewardship/sacred-heart-stevens-net-zero-library-first-in-the-us-to-achieve-net-zero-energy-building-certification|title=Sacred Heart Stevens Net-Zero Library: First In The U.S. To Achieve Net Zero Energy Building Certification|website=WRNS Studio|language=en|access-date=2018-02-23}}</ref>
* The Santa Monica City Services Building is among the first net-zero energy, net-zero water public/municipal buildings in California. Completed in 2020, the 50,000-square-foot addition to the historic Santa Monica City Hall building was designed to provide its own energy and water, and to minimize energy use through efficient building systems.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Shapiro|first=Gideon Fink|date=2021-07-21|title=Phase-Change Architecture at the Santa Monica City Services Building|url=https://www.architectmagazine.com/technology/architectural-detail/phase-change-architecture-at-the-santa-monica-city-services-building_o|access-date=2021-08-17|website=Architect Magazine}}</ref>
* At 402,000 square-feet, the [[California Air Resources Board]] Southern California Headquarters – Mary D. Nichols Campus, is the largest net-zero energy facility in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=CARB dedicates new Southern California headquarters in Riverside {{!}} California Air Resources Board|url=https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/carb-dedicates-new-southern-california-headquarters-riverside|access-date=2021-11-19|date=2021-11-17|website=The California Air Resources Board}}</ref> A photovoltaic system covers 204,903 square-feet between the facility rooftop and parking pavilions.<ref>{{Cite web|title=California Air Resources Board Southern California Headquarters, Mary D. Nichols Campus|url=https://www.zgf.com/work/3828-california-air-resources-board-southern-california-headquarters-mary-d-nichols-campus|access-date=2021-11-19|website=ZGF}}</ref> The +3.5 megawatt system is anticipated to generate roughly 6,235,000 kWh reusable energy per year. The facility was dedicated on November 18, 2021.

=====Colorado=====
* The Moore House achieves net-zero energy usage with passive solar design, 'tuned' heat reflective windows, super-insulated and air-tight construction, natural daylighting, solar thermal panels for hot water and space heating, a photovoltaic (PV) system that generates more carbon-free electricity than the house requires, and an energy-recovery ventilator (ERV) for fresh air.<ref>{{cite book |last=Doerr |first=Thomas |author-link=Thomas Doerr |year=2012 |title=Passive Solar Simplified |url=http://alitheiapress.com/ |access-date=October 24, 2012}}</ref> The green building strategies used on the Moore House earned it a verified [[home energy rating]] system (HERS) score of −3.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.doerr.org/casestudies/net-zero-energy.html |title=Case Studies: Net-Zero Energy House in Evergreen, Colorado |publisher=Doerr.org |access-date=25 June 2014}}</ref>
* The NREL Research Support Facility in Golden is a class A office building. Its energy efficiency features include: Thermal storage concrete structure, transpired solar collectors, 70 miles of radiant piping, high-efficiency office equipment, and an energy-efficient data center that reduces the data center's energy use by 50% over traditional approaches.<ref name="Net Zero">{{cite web |title=Net Zero Examples |url=https://sftool.gov/plan/422/net-examples |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303211023/https://sftool.gov/learn/about/422/net-examples |archive-date=2016-03-03 |access-date=1 October 2015 |website=Sustainable Facilities Tool |publisher=The Office of Federal High-Performance Green Buildings}}</ref>
* Wayne Aspinall Federal Building in Grand Junction, originally constructed in 1918, became the first Net Zero Energy building listed on the National Register of Historic Places. On-site renewable energy generation is intended to produce 100% of the building's energy throughout the year using the following energy efficiency features: Variable refrigerant flow for the HVAC, a geo-exchange system, advanced metering and building controls, high-efficient lighting systems, thermally enhanced building envelope, interior window system (to maintain historic windows), and advanced power strips (APS) with individual occupancy sensors.<ref name="Net Zero"/>
* Tutt Library at Colorado College was renovated to be a net-zero library in 2017, making it the largest ZNE academic library.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.coloradocollege.edu/newsevents/newsroom/cc-s-net-zero-energy-library-opens|title=CC's Net-Zero Energy Library Opens • Colorado College|website=www.coloradocollege.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-02-23|archive-date=2018-02-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180224112859/https://www.coloradocollege.edu/newsevents/newsroom/cc-s-net-zero-energy-library-opens}}</ref> It received an Innovation Award from the National Association of college and University Business Officers.

=====Florida=====
* The 1999 side-by-side [[Florida Solar Energy Center]] Lakeland demonstration project<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fsec.ucf.edu/en/research/buildings/zero_energy/lakeland/|title=ZEH: Lakeland, FL|website=www.fsec.ucf.edu}}</ref> was called the "Zero Energy Home". It was a first-generation university effort that significantly influenced the creation of the U.S. Department of Energy, Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, Zero Energy Home program.

=====Illinois=====
* The Walgreens store located on 741 Chicago Ave, Evanston, is the first of the company's stores to be built and or converted to a net zero energy building.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 21, 2013 |title=Walgreens Debuts Nation's First Net Zero Energy Retail Store in Evanston, Ill. |url=https://news.walgreens.com/press-center/news/walgreens-debuts-nations-first-net-zero-energy-retail-store-in-evanston-ill.htm |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=news.walgreens.com |language=en}}</ref> It is the first net zero energy retail stores to be built and will pave the way to renovating and building net zero energy retail stores in the near future. The Walgreens store includes the following energy efficiency features: Geo-exchange system, energy-efficient building materials, LED lighting and daylight harvesting, and carbon dioxide refrigerant.
* The Electrical and Computer Engineering building at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, which was built in 2014, is a net zero building.<ref name="Net Zero"/>

=====Iowa=====
*  The MUM Sustainable Living Center was designed to surpass [[Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design|LEED Platinum qualification]]. The Maharishi University of Management (MUM) in Fairfield, Iowa, founded by [[Maharishi Mahesh Yogi]] (best known for having brought [[Transcendental Meditation]] to the West) incorporates principles of Bau Biology (a German system that focuses on creating a healthy indoor environment),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.baubiologie.de/site/home.php|title=Institut für Baubiologie + Nachhaltigkeit IBN|website=Institut für Baubiologie + Nachhaltigkeit IBN|access-date=2012-06-11|archive-date=2011-01-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110131132156/http://www.baubiologie.de/site/home.php}}</ref> as well as Maharishi Vedic Architecture (an Indian system of architecture focused on the precise orientation, proportions and placement of rooms).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.earthtechling.com/2012/05/net-zero-is-bliss-at-maharishi-university-in-iowa/|title=Net Zero Is Bliss At Maharishi University In Iowa |website=www.earthtechling.com|date=27 May 2012 }}</ref> The building is one of the few in the country to qualify as net zero, and one of even fewer that can claim the banner of grid positive via its solar power system. A rainwater catchment system and on-site natural waste-water treatment likewise take the building off (sewer) grid with respect to water and waste treatment. Additional green features include natural daylighting in every room, natural and breathable earth block walls (made by the program's students), purified rainwater for both potable and non-potable functions; and an on-site water purification and recycling system consisting of plants, algae, and bacteria.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ecovibz.com|title=EcoVibz|website=EcoVibz}}</ref>

=====Kentucky=====
* Richardsville Elementary School, part of the Warren County Public School District in south-central Kentucky, is the first Net Zero energy school in the United States. To reach Net Zero, innovative energy reduction strategies were used by CMTA Consulting Engineers and Sherman Carter Barnhart Architects including dedicated outdoor air systems (DOAS) with dynamic reset, new IT systems, alternative methods to prepare lunches, and the use of solar photovoltaics. The project has an efficient thermal envelope constructed with insulated concrete form (ICF) walls, geothermal water source heat pumps, low-flow fixtures, and features daylighting extensively throughout. It is also the first truly wireless school in Kentucky.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nxtbook.com/nxtbooks/ashrae/hpb_2012fall/#/36|title=High Performing Buildings – Fall 2012|website=www.nxtbook.com}}</ref>
* [[Locust Trace AgriScience Center]], an agricultural-based vocational school serving Fayette County Public Schools and surrounding districts, features a Net Zero Academic Building engineered by CMTA Consulting Engineers and designed by Tate Hill Jacobs Architects. The facility, located in Lexington, Kentucky, also has a greenhouse, riding arena with stalls, and a barn. To reach Net Zero in the Academic Building the project utilizes an air-tight envelope, expanded indoor temperature setpoints in specified areas to more closely model real-world conditions, a solar thermal system, and geothermal water source heat pumps. The school has further reduced its site impact by minimizing municipal water use through the use of a dual system consisting of a standard leach field system and a constructed wetlands system and using pervious surfaces to collect, drain, and use rainwater for crop irrigation and animal watering.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nxtbook.com/nxtbooks/ashrae/hpb_2015winter/index.php?startid=28#/32|title=High Performing Buildings – Winter 2015 – Locust Trace AgriScience Center|website=www.nxtbook.com|access-date=2015-01-21|archive-date=2015-01-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150121183347/http://www.nxtbook.com/nxtbooks/ashrae/hpb_2015winter/index.php?startid=28#/32}}</ref>

=====Massachusetts=====
* The government of [[Cambridge, Massachusetts|Cambridge]] has enacted a plan for "net zero" carbon emissions from all buildings in the city by 2040.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cambridgema.gov/CDD/Projects/Climate/NetZeroTaskForce|title=Net Zero Action Plan – CDD – City of Cambridge, Massachusetts|first=City of|last=Cambridge|website=www.cambridgema.gov}}</ref>
* [[John W. Olver Transit Center]], designed by [[Charles Rose (architect)|Charles Rose Architects Inc]], is an intermodal transit hub in [[Greenfield, Massachusetts]]. Built with [[American Recovery and Reinvestment Act]] funds, the facility was constructed with solar panels, geothermal wells, copper heat screens and other energy efficient technologies.

=====Michigan=====
* The Mission Zero House<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.MissionZeroHouse.com|title=THRIVE|website=THRIVE}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mnn.com/your-home/green-building-remodeling/blogs/mission-zero-achieved-in-ann-arbor|title='Mission Zero' achieved in Ann Arbor|website=www.mnn.com|access-date=2010-12-07|archive-date=2010-11-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101120232117/http://www.mnn.com/your-home/green-building-remodeling/blogs/mission-zero-achieved-in-ann-arbor}}</ref> is the 110-year-old Ann Arbor home of Greenovation.TV host and Environment Report contributor [[Matthew Grocoff]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.greenovation.tv/|title=THRIVE|website=THRIVE|access-date=2010-12-07|archive-date=2011-05-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501002328/http://www.greenovation.tv/}}</ref> As of 2011, the home is the oldest home in America to achieve net-zero energy.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oldhouseweb.com/blog/americas-oldest-net-zero-solar-house/|title=America's Oldest Net Zero Solar House – Old House Web Blog|website=www.oldhouseweb.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=http://content.usatoday.com/communities/greenhouse/post/2010/06/century-plus-victorian-renovated-to-power-itself/1 | work=USA Today | first=Wendy | last=Koch | title=110-Year-Old Home Gets Net Zero Energy Rehab | date=11 June 2010}}</ref> The owners are chronicling their project on Greenovation.TV and ''[[The Environment Report]]'' on public radio.
* The Vineyard Project is a Zero Energy Home (ZEH) thanks to the Passive Solar Design, 3.3 Kws of Photovoltaics, Solar Hot Water and Geothermal Heating and Cooling. The home is pre-wired for a future wind turbine and only uses 600 kWh of energy per month while a minimum of 20 kWh of electricity per day with many days net-metering backwards. The project also used ICF insulation throughout the entire house and is certified as Platinum under the LEED for Homes certification. This Project was awarded Green Builder Magazine Home of the Year 2009.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://viewer.zmags.com/publication/277aa969#/277aa969/31|title=Green Builder Magazine|date=December 2009 |pages= 31–34 }}</ref>
* The Lenawee Center for a Sustainable Future, a new campus for Lenawee Intermediate School District, serves as a living laboratory for the future of agriculture. It is the first Net Zero education building in Michigan, engineered by CMTA Consulting Engineers and designed by The Collaborative, Inc. The project includes solar arrays on the ground as well as the roof, a geothermal heating and cooling system, solar tubes, permeable pavement and sidewalks, a sedum green roof, and an overhang design to regulate building temperature.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://detroit.cbslocal.com/2013/06/10/lenawee-isd-opens-high-tech-education-showplace/|title=Lenawee ISD Opens High-Tech Education Showplace|date=10 June 2013}}</ref>

=====Missouri=====
* In 2010, architectural firm [[Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum|HOK]] worked with energy and daylighting consultant The Weidt Group to design a {{convert|170,735|sqft|m2|adj=on}} net zero carbon emissions Class A office building prototype in [[St. Louis, Missouri|St. Louis]], Missouri.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.metropolismag.com/uncategorized/a-net-zero-office-today/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205002811/http://www.metropolismag.com/pov/20101119/a-net-zero-office-today|title=A Net Zero Office Today|date=November 19, 2010|archive-date=December 5, 2010}}</ref> The team chronicled its process and results on Netzerocourt.com.

=====New Jersey=====
* The [[31 Tannery Project]], located in Branchburg, New Jersey, serves as the corporate headquarters for Ferreira Construction, the Ferreira Group, and [[Noveda Technologies]]. The 42,000-square-foot (3,900&nbsp;m<sup>2</sup>) office and shop building was constructed in 2006 and is the first building in the state of [[New Jersey]] to meet New Jersey's [[Executive order (United States)#State governors' executive orders|Executive Order]] 54. The building is also the first Net Zero Electric Commercial Building in the United States.

=====New York=====
* Green Acres, the first true zero-net energy development in America,<ref>[http://www.bolder-architecture.com/Mid-HudsonE_CWinterNewsletter.pdf "Nation's First Zero-Net Energy Home Development"], Mid-Hudson Energy $mart Communities newsletter, Winter 2011 Edition</ref> is located in New Paltz, about {{convert|80|mi|km}} north of New York City. Greenhill Contracting began construction on this development of 25 single family homes in summer 2008,<ref>[http://www.bolder-architecture.com/greenacresNPT2008-08-07.pdf "Green Acres: Developer to Build Zero Energy Homes in New Paltz"], New Paltz Times, August 7, 2008</ref> with designs by BOLDER Architecture. After a full year of occupancy, from March 2009 to March 2010, the [[solar panels]] of the first occupied home in Green Acres generated 1490 kWh more energy than the home consumed. The second occupied home has also achieved zero-net energy use. As of June 2011, five houses have been completed, purchased and occupied, two are under construction, and several more are being planned. The homes are built of [[insulated concrete forms]] with [[spray foams (insulation)|spray foam insulated]] rafters and triple pane casement windows, heated and cooled by a [[Geothermal heat pump|geothermal system]], to create extremely energy-efficient and long-lasting buildings.<ref>[http://bestplaces.nydailynews.com/stories/kid-soho-builds-countrys-first-zero-energy-development-new-york "On the House"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110410183728/http://bestplaces.nydailynews.com/stories/kid-soho-builds-countrys-first-zero-energy-development-new-york |date=2011-04-10 }}, [[Daily News (New York)|Daily News]], April 8, 2011</ref> The [[heat recovery ventilator]] provides constant fresh air and, with low or no [[volatile organic compound|VOC]] (volatile organic compound) materials, these homes are very healthy to live in. To the best of our knowledge, Green Acres is the first development of multiple buildings, residential or commercial, that achieves true zero-net energy use in the United States, and the first zero-net energy development of single family homes in the world.<ref>[http://www.solartoday-digital.org/solartoday/20100708#pg48 "Going Net-Zero in New York State"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110827120641/http://www.solartoday-digital.org/solartoday/20100708#pg48 |date=2011-08-27 }}, ''Solar Today'', July / August 2010</ref><ref>[http://www.newyorkhousemagazine.com/view/full_story/3041868/article-Off-the-Grid? "Zero-Net Energy Homes"], ''New York House'', August 2009</ref>
* Greenhill Contracting has built two luxury zero-net energy homes in Esopus, completed in 2008. One house was the first Energy Star rated zero-net energy home in the Northeast and the first registered zero-net energy home on the US Department of Energy's Builder's Challenge website.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www1.eere.energy.gov/buildings/challenge/about.html |title=Builders Challenge: About Builders Challenge |access-date=2011-06-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903011241/http://www1.eere.energy.gov/buildings/challenge/about.html |archive-date=2011-09-03 }}</ref> These homes were the template for Green Acres and the other zero-net energy homes that Greenhill Contracting has built, in terms of methods and materials.
* The headquarters of Hudson Solar, a dba of Hudson Valley Clean Energy, Inc., located in Rhinebeck and completed in 2007, was determined by NESEA (the Northeast Sustainable Energy Association) to have become the first proven zero-net energy commercial building in New York State and the ten northeast United States (October 2008). The building consumes less energy than it generates, using a solar electric system to generate power from the sun, geothermal heating and cooling, and solar thermal collectors to heat all its hot water.<ref>NESEA Letter October 2008{{full citation needed|date=August 2020}}</ref>

=====Oklahoma=====
* The first {{convert|5000|sqft|m2|adj=on}} zero-energy design<ref>{{cite web  | title = Zero Energy Design Abundant Energy In Harmony With Nature | url = http://www.zeroenergydesign.com/ | access-date = 2011-03-27 }}</ref> home was built in 1979 with support from President Carter's new [[United States Department of Energy]]. It relied heavily on [[passive solar building design]] for space heat, water heat and space cooling. It heated and cooled itself effectively in a climate where the summer peak temperature was 110 degrees Fahrenheit, and the winter low temperature was −10 F. It did not use [[active solar]] systems. It is a [[double envelope house]] that uses a gravity-fed [[natural convection]] air flow design to circulate passive solar heat from {{convert|1000|sqft|m2}} of south-facing glass on its [[greenhouse]] through a thermal buffer zone in the winter. A swimming pool in the greenhouse provided thermal mass for winter heat storage. In the summer, air from two {{convert|24|in|mm|adj=on}} {{convert|100|ft|m|adj=mid|-long}} underground [[earth tube]]s is used to cool the thermal buffer zone and exhaust heat through 7200 cfm of outer-envelope roof vents.

=====Oregon=====
* Net Zero Energy Building Certification launched in 2011, with an international following. The first project, Painters Hall,<ref>{{cite web |title=Painters Hall |url=https://ilbi.org/lbc/casestudies/paintershall/home |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150403124316/https://ilbi.org/lbc/casestudies/paintershall/home |archive-date=2015-04-03 |website=International Living Future Institute}}</ref> is Pringle Creek's Community Center, café, office, art gallery, and event venue. Originally built in the 1930s, Painters Hall was renovated to LEED Platinum Net Zero energy building standards in 2010, demonstrating the potential of converting existing building stock into high‐performance, sustainable building sites. Painters Hall features simple low-cost solutions for energy reduction, such as natural daylighting and [[passive cooling]] lighting, that save money and increase comfort. A district ground-source geothermal loop serves the building's GSHP for highly efficient heating and air conditioning. Excess generation from the 20.2&nbsp;kW rooftop solar array offsets pumping for the neighborhoods geo loop system. Open to the public, Painters Hall is a hub for gatherings of friends, neighbors, and visitors at the heart of a neighborhood designed around nature and community.

=====Pennsylvania=====
* The Phipps Center for Sustainable Landscapes in [[Pittsburgh]] was designed to be one of the greenest buildings in the world. It achieved Net Zero Energy Building Certification from the Living Building Challenge in February 2014 and is pursuing full certification.<ref>{{cite web|title=Phipps Conservatory – Center for Sustainable Landscapes|url=http://phipps.conservatory.org/project-green-heart/green-heart-at-phipps/center-for-sustainable-landscapes.aspx|website=Phipps Conservatory|access-date=1 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111111075503/http://phipps.conservatory.org/project-green-heart/green-heart-at-phipps/center-for-sustainable-landscapes.aspx|archive-date=11 November 2011}}</ref> The Phipps Center uses [[energy conservation]] technologies such as solar hot water collectors, carbon dioxide sensors, and daylighting, as well as renewable energy technologies to allow it to achieve Net Zero Energy status.<ref name="Net Zero" />
* The Lombardo Welcome Center at [[Millersville University]] became the first building in the state to become zero-energy certified. This was the largest step in [[Millersville University]]'s goal to be [[carbon neutral]] by 2040. According to the International Living Future Institute, The Lombardo Welcome Center is one of the highest-performing buildings throughout the country generating 75% more energy than currently being used.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Negley |first1=Erin |title=Here's how Pennsylvania's first zero-energy building, at Millersville, generated almost twice the energy used |url=https://lancasteronline.com/features/heres-how-pennsylvanias-first-zero-energy-building-at-millersville-generated-almost-twice-the-energy-used/article_a9a58eea-f5ce-11e9-a8be-c7cbf906f08a.html#:~:text=WhatsApp-,Here's%20how%20Pennsylvania's%20first%20zero%2Denergy%20building%2C%20at%20Millersville%2C,almost%20twice%20the%20energy%20used&text=WhatsApp-,The%20Lombardo%20Welcome%20Center%20at%20Millersville%20University%20is%20a%20net,much%20energy%20as%20it%20consumes. |website=Lancaster Online |date=24 October 2019 |publisher=LNP Media Group |access-date=October 24, 2019}}</ref>

=====Rhode Island=====
* In Newport, the Paul W. Crowley East Bay MET School is the first Net Zero project to be constructed in Rhode Island. It is a 17,000 sq ft building, housing eight large classrooms, seven bathrooms and a kitchen. It will have PV panels to supply all necessary electricity for the building and a geothermal well which will be the source of heat.

=====Tennessee=====
* civitas, designed by [[archimania]], Memphis, Tennessee.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hill |first=David |date=October 5, 2017 |title=What It Takes to Go Net-Zero |url=http://www.architectmagazine.com/practice/what-it-takes-to-go-net-zero_o |access-date=2018-06-21 |website=Architect Magazine}}</ref> civitas is a case study home on the banks of the Mississippi River, currently under construction. =====Texas=====
* The University of North Texas (UNT) constructed a Zero Energy Research Laboratory<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.unt.edu/news-releases/unt-build-zero-energy-research-laboratory |title=UNT to build Zero Energy Research Laboratory |work=University of North Texas |date=30 June 2011 |access-date=25 June 2014 |archive-date=27 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427130135/http://news.unt.edu/news-releases/unt-build-zero-energy-research-laboratory }}</ref> on its 300-acre research campus, Discovery Park, in Denton, Texas. The project was funded at over $1,150,000 and will primarily benefit students in mechanical and energy engineering (UNT became the first university to offer degrees in mechanical and energy engineering in 2006). This 1,200-square-foot structure is now competed and held ribbon-cutting ceremony for the University of North Texas' Zero Energy Laboratory on April 20, 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.unt.edu/news-releases/lab-designed-study-green-energy-technologies-completed-unt |title=Lab designed to study green energy technologies completed at UNT |work=University of North Texas |date=10 April 2012 |access-date=25 June 2014 |archive-date=27 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140427151204/http://news.unt.edu/news-releases/lab-designed-study-green-energy-technologies-completed-unt }}</ref>
* The [[West Irving Library]] in [[Irving, Texas]], became the first net zero library in Texas in 2011, running entirely off solar energy.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nbcdfw.com/news/green/Irving-Library-Goes-Green-147826445.html|title=Irving Library Operates on Solar Power|work=NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth|access-date=2018-02-23|language=en}}</ref> Since then it has produced a surplus. It has LEED gold certification.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dfwsolartour.org/locations/irvingwestlibrary/index.html|title=Irving West Library – DFW Solar Home Tour|website=dfwsolartour.org|access-date=2018-02-23|archive-date=2018-02-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180224052921/http://dfwsolartour.org/locations/irvingwestlibrary/index.html}}</ref>

=====Vermont=====
* The [[Putney School]]'s net zero Field House was opened on October 10, 2009. In use for over a year, as of December 2010, the Field House used 48,374 kWh and produced a total of 51,371 kWh during the first 12 months of operation, thus performing at slightly better than net-zero.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.putneyschool.org/putneynews/?p=1328 |work=The Putney School |title=Putney School's Net-Zero Fieldhouse Is Net-Zero |access-date=2010-12-22 |archive-date=2010-12-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101228184540/http://www.putneyschool.org/putneynews/?p=1328 }}</ref> Also in December, the building won an AIA-Vermont Honor Award.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.putneyschool.org/putneynews/?p=1296 |title=AIA-Vermont Honor Award |work=The Putney School |access-date=2010-12-22 |archive-date=2010-12-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101228191731/http://www.putneyschool.org/putneynews/?p=1296 }}</ref>
* The Charlotte Vermont House designed by Pill-Maharam Architects is a verified net zero energy house completed in 2007. The project won the Northeast Sustainable Energy Association's Net Zero Energy award in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nesea.org/inspirationawards/zeroenergy/2009winner/ |title=Zero Energy 2009 Winner |work=Northeast Sustainable Energy Association |access-date=2010-10-05 |archive-date=2010-10-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101030151303/http://www.nesea.org/inspirationawards/zeroenergy/2009winner/ }}</ref>
